05. Sequential and User-History Modeling: From GRU4Rec to Lifelong Sequences and Foundation User Models

Overview

Most modern recommender systems are, at heart, systems for turning a user's history into a prediction. A user's ordered stream of actions (clicks, views, saves, purchases, hides, searches) is the richest signal a platform owns. Over the last decade the industry has moved through four broad generations of models for that stream:

  1. Session RNNs (2015 to 2017). GRU4Rec showed that a recurrent network over a session could beat item-to-item similarity for next-click prediction [1], although later benchmarks showed tuned nearest-neighbour baselines remained strong [2].
  2. Self-attention for next-item prediction (2018 to 2023). SASRec [3] and BERT4Rec [4] brought Transformers to sequential recommendation. A long replicability debate followed [5][6].
  3. Target-attention and Transformers inside industrial CTR rankers (2018 onward). Alibaba's DIN/DIEN line [8], BST [7], and the long-sequence family MIMN [9], SIM [10], ETA [11], SDIM [13], TWIN [14] and TWIN V2 [15] put user histories of 10^2 to 10^5 behaviours into the ranking stage under tight latency budgets. Pinterest's TransAct [20] and TransAct V2 [21] do the same for real-time and lifelong action sequences.
  4. User representations and foundation user models (2020 onward). PinnerSage [18] and PinnerFormer [19] produce reusable user embeddings. PinFM [23], Meta's HSTU generative recommenders [24], Netflix's foundation model [25][26] and ByteDance's LONGER [17] pretrain large sequence models on billions of interactions and share them across many surfaces.

This chapter walks through each design: what problem it solved, how it is built, the public scale numbers, the key tricks, and what the industry learned. The last sections give a comparison table and design takeaways.

A note on sources: every number below comes from the cited paper or blog. Figures that only appear in secondary summaries are marked "reported" or "approximately".

                     The user-history design space
  +-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
  |                 short (10^1-10^2)    long (10^3-10^4)    lifelong (10^5+) |
  | retrieval       GRU4Rec, SASRec,     PinnerFormer,       PinFM, HSTU,     |
  | (user tower)    BERT4Rec, KuaiFormer Netflix FM          Netflix FM       |
  | ranking         DIN, BST, TransAct   MIMN, LONGER,       SIM, ETA, SDIM,  |
  | (target-aware)                       TransAct V2         TWIN, TWIN V2    |
  +-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
     cost grows with length x candidates x model depth -> most tricks attack this

1. Academic foundations: next-item prediction

1.1 GRU4Rec (Hidasi et al., 2015)

Problem. In e-commerce and media sites, many sessions are anonymous and short. The standard approach before 2015 was item-to-item similarity (for example "people who viewed X also viewed Y"), which uses only the last item and ignores the rest of the session [1].

Architecture. GRU4Rec feeds the session's item sequence, one item per step, into a GRU. The hidden state after each step is scored against all items to predict the next click. The paper made RNNs practical for this task with several changes [1]:

  • Session-parallel mini-batches. Sessions have very different lengths, so the batch is built from many sessions in parallel. When one session ends, the next one takes its slot and the hidden state is reset.
  • Sampled output. Scoring every item is too expensive, so the loss uses other items in the mini-batch as negatives (an early form of in-batch negatives).
  • Ranking losses. The paper introduced pairwise ranking losses (BPR and TOP1) in place of plain cross-entropy.

Lessons. Jannach and Ludewig (RecSys 2017) showed that a simple session-based nearest-neighbour method beat GRU4Rec in most of their tested configurations, and the best results often came from combining the two [2]. Hidasi and Karatzoglou later published a follow-up ("Recurrent Neural Networks with Top-k Gains", 2017) on loss functions and sampling for RNN session recommenders. The lasting lesson: sequence models need careful loss and negative-sampling choices, and strong simple baselines should always be reported.

1.2 SASRec (Kang and McAuley, 2018)

Problem. Markov-chain models use only the last few actions and work well on sparse data. RNNs can use the full history but are slow and need dense data. SASRec aimed to get both: capture long-range dependencies, but make predictions that depend mostly on a few relevant actions [3].

Architecture. A causal (left-to-right) Transformer encoder over item embeddings plus learned position embeddings. At each position the output is matched by dot product to the next item's embedding. The original training used binary cross-entropy with one sampled negative per positive.

Results. The authors report SASRec beat MC, CNN and RNN baselines on both sparse and dense datasets, and was about an order of magnitude more efficient than comparable CNN/RNN models [3]. SASRec became the default academic baseline and, later, the conceptual ancestor of most industrial "user tower" Transformers.

1.3 BERT4Rec (Sun et al., 2019)

Problem. Left-to-right models only use past context. BERT4Rec argued that this unidirectional design limits how well hidden representations capture the history [4].

Architecture. A bidirectional Transformer encoder trained with a Cloze (masked item) task: a share of items in each sequence is replaced by a [mask] token and predicted from both left and right context. At inference a [mask] token is appended to the end of the sequence and its final hidden state is used to predict the next item [4]. The paper notes that masking k items in a sequence of length n gives C(n, k) possible training samples, versus n for next-item training.

1.4 The replicability debate and gSASRec

Petrov and Macdonald (RecSys 2022) reviewed published BERT4Rec versus SASRec comparisons [5]. They found:

  • BERT4Rec was not consistently better than SASRec across the literature.
  • They could not reproduce the original BERT4Rec results with the default configuration.
  • The original results could be reproduced if training ran much longer, up to about 30x.
  • Their Hugging Face Transformers based implementation reproduced the results on 3 of 4 datasets with up to 95% less training time.

Their follow-up, gSASRec (RecSys 2023), pins down the cause [6]. Negative sampling raises the share of positives the model sees during training, so the model becomes overconfident: it overestimates the probability of positive interactions. gSASRec keeps the SASRec architecture but uses more negatives and a generalized BCE (gBCE) loss that corrects for the sampling rate. They report gSASRec can beat BERT4Rec (for example +9.47% NDCG on MovieLens-1M) while training about 73% faster, and that it scales to catalogues with over 1 million items, where BERT4Rec's full softmax does not [6].

Lesson for system designers. The training objective and negative-sampling scheme often matter more than uni- versus bidirectional attention. This is why most industrial user towers use a causal model with sampled softmax plus logQ correction (see PinnerFormer, KuaiFormer and PinFM below).

2. Target attention in industrial rankers: DIN, DIEN and BST (Alibaba)

2.1 DIN and DIEN

The Alibaba advertising team introduced target attention for CTR models. In DIN, a local activation unit weights each historical behaviour by its relevance to the candidate ad, so the user representation changes with each candidate (as summarised in the DIEN paper [8]). DIN does not model relationships between items within the sequence.

DIEN (AAAI 2019) adds two layers [8]:

  • An interest extractor GRU over the behaviour sequence, with an auxiliary loss that supervises each hidden state with the next behaviour.
  • An interest evolving layer, AUGRU, which scales the GRU update gate by the attention score against the target item, so behaviours unrelated to the target have less effect on the hidden state.

The DIEN paper reports deployment in Taobao display advertising with a 20.7% CTR improvement [8]. However, sequential GRUs are slow to serve, which limited DIEN in production to about 50 behaviours according to the MIMN paper [9].

2.2 BST: Behavior Sequence Transformer (Taobao, 2019)

Problem. Embedding-and-MLP models such as WDL and DIN mostly concatenate or pool features and ignore the order of user behaviours [7].

Architecture.

  other features (user profile, context, cross)        target item
          |                                                 |
     embeddings                     behaviour seq: item_1 .. item_n
          |                                 |  (item_id, category_id,
          |                                 |   position = t_now - t_click)
          |                         +-------v-------------------+
          |                         | Transformer layer          |
          |                         | (self-attn over seq+target)|
          |                         +-------+-------------------+
          +-------------+-------------------+
                        |  concat
                   MLP (3 layers) -> sigmoid -> pCTR

Key choices reported for BST [7]:

  • Each sequence token is built from item_id and category_id embeddings plus a position feature defined as the time gap between the recommendation time and the click time, not sinusoidal positions.
  • The target item is appended to the sequence so self-attention can mix candidate and history.
  • It runs in the ranking stage of Taobao recommendation.

Results. In the paper's table BST reached offline AUC 0.7894 versus 0.7734 for WDL and 0.7866 for DIN, and an online CTR gain of +7.57% versus +4.55% for DIN [7]. Secondary summaries report online latency rising from about 13 ms to 20 ms (approximate). The paper found that a single Transformer block worked best on its data; stacking more blocks did not help.

Lesson. BST is the template that TransAct and many later rankers follow: a short recent sequence, a light Transformer, candidate-aware fusion, and the result concatenated into a standard DNN ranker.

3. Long and lifelong sequences in ranking

The obvious next step is to use much longer histories. Lifelong histories on Taobao, Kuaishou or Pinterest contain 10^4 to 10^5 behaviours. Full target attention costs O(L x d) per candidate, and a ranker scores hundreds to thousands of candidates per request, so naive attention is not affordable. Each design below cuts this cost in a different way.

3.1 MIMN and the User Interest Center (Alibaba, KDD 2019)

Problem. Production DIEN used about 50 behaviours due to serving pressure, while longer histories clearly helped offline [9].

Design. A system and algorithm co-design:

  • UIC (User Interest Center) is a separate serving module that keeps per-user interest state and updates it incrementally whenever a behaviour event arrives, not at request time.
  • MIMN (Multi-channel user Interest Memory Network) is a memory-network model (based on Neural Turing Machine style memory with multiple channels) whose memory is exactly what UIC stores and updates.

At ranking time the model reads the precomputed memory, so latency is constant regardless of history length. The authors claim the design could in principle handle unlimited length, and it handled sequences in the thousands [9].

Results. On an Alibaba dataset MIMN improved AUC over DIEN by about 0.01. In an online A/B test from 2019-03-30 to 2019-05-10, MIMN with UIC gave +7.5% CTR and +6% RPM over DIEN [9].

Lesson. The memory is user-only (not candidate-aware), so it compresses away target-specific detail. The SIM paper later reported that MIMN accuracy drops when sequences grow 10x or more [10].

3.2 SIM: Search-based Interest Model (Alibaba, CIKM 2020)

Problem. Model lifelong histories (up to 54,000 behaviours) in CTR prediction while staying candidate-aware [10].

Architecture. Two cascaded search units:

 lifelong behaviours (10^4 - 10^5)
          |
 +--------v-------------------------------+
 | GSU: General Search Unit                |
 |  hard search: behaviours with the same  |
 |   category as the candidate             |   offline: User Behavior Tree
 |  soft search: MIPS on embeddings        |<--  key1 = user_id
 +--------+-------------------------------+     key2 = category_id
          | top-K sub-sequence (SBS)            value = behaviour items
 +--------v-------------------------------+     (distributed, ~22 TB)
 | ESU: Exact Search Unit                  |
 |  multi-head target attention on SBS     |
 |  + time-interval embeddings             |
 +--------+-------------------------------+
          v
   concat with short-term DIN features -> MLP -> pCTR
  • Soft search embeds behaviours and uses maximum inner product search to get the top-K.
  • Hard search simply keeps behaviours in the same category as the candidate.
  • The authors found top-K lists from the two methods were very similar, and hard search was much cheaper. They deployed hard search online [10].
  • The hard-search index is a two-level User Behavior Tree (UBT): first key user ID, second key category ID, value the behaviour items. It is built offline, is distributed, and reaches about 22 TB [10].

Results. Deployed in Alibaba display advertising since 2019, with +7.1% CTR and +4.4% RPM, and a maximum modelled length of 54,000, about 54x MIMN [10]. Secondary write-ups report the added serving latency as only a few milliseconds (approximate) [28].

Lesson. SIM established the two-stage GSU/ESU pattern that nearly every later lifelong-sequence model adopts. Its weakness is that the GSU relevance metric (category match or a separately trained embedding) differs from the ESU's attention metric.

3.3 ETA and SDIM: hashing the GSU

ETA (Alibaba, 2021). ETA replaces the separate GSU with locality-sensitive hashing inside the model so retrieval is end-to-end trainable [11]. Each item embedding is turned into a binary signature with SimHash (random projections, keep the sign). The top-k behaviours are chosen by Hamming distance to the candidate's signature, which needs only cheap bit operations. Multi-head target attention then runs on those k items. Because the hash uses the same embeddings the attention uses, the GSU and ESU stay roughly consistent. The paper reports a 3.1% GMV gain [11]; the extended ETA-Net version reports +1.8% CTR and +3.1% GMV on Taobao over two-stage methods [12].

SDIM (Meituan, CIKM 2022). SDIM goes further and drops the attention step [13]. It hashes the candidate and every behaviour with several hash functions, then gathers (sums) the behaviours that share the candidate's signature. The authors prove this sampling approximates target attention's pattern. Behaviour hashing is moved into a separate Behavior Sequence Encoding (BSE) service, so the CTR model only does a lookup. Meituan reports +2.98% CTR and +2.69% VBR in its search system [13].

3.4 TWIN: TWo-stage Interest Network (Kuaishou, KDD 2023)

Problem. In SIM-like systems, the GSU's relevance metric differs from the ESU's target attention. The GSU therefore misses behaviours the ESU would rate highly and keeps ones the ESU would ignore [14].

Key idea: consistency. TWIN makes the GSU and ESU "twins". The Consistency-Preserved GSU (CP-GSU) uses the same target-attention relevance as the ESU, with the same architecture and parameters [14]. CP-GSU scores all ~10^4 long-term behaviours and keeps the top 100. The ESU then does weighted pooling (multi-head target attention) over those 100 finalists [14].

Making full attention affordable. Running real target attention on 10^4 to 10^5 behaviours per candidate would be too slow. TWIN splits behaviour features:

  • Inherent item features (video ID, author, tags, duration and so on) do not depend on the user. Their linear projections (the keys) can be precomputed and cached per item, and shared across all users.
  • User-item cross features (for example when the user watched it and how long they played it) are user-specific. TWIN compresses them to a cheap scalar bias added to the attention logit, avoiding a full projection.
  per behaviour j:  K_j = W * inherent_j     (cached offline per item)
                    b_j = w . cross_j         (cheap, per user)
  per candidate c:  score_j = (Q(c) . K_j) / sqrt(d) + b_j
  CP-GSU: top-100 by score_j  ->  ESU: multi-head attention over top-100

Scale. Offline experiments use a production dataset of about 46 billion samples. With optimized online infrastructure the authors report a 99.3% reduction in the compute bottleneck, which allowed deployment on Kuaishou's main traffic [14]. Secondary summaries report watch-time gains of about 1.3% to 6.2% across the Featured-Video, Discovery and Slide tabs (approximate; check the paper's tables) [29].

3.5 TWIN V2 (Kuaishou, CIKM 2024)

Problem. Users' full life-cycle histories now exceed 10^5 to 10^6 behaviours, beyond what even TWIN can scan online [15].

Design: divide and conquer.

  1. Offline hierarchical clustering. Each user's behaviours are grouped into clusters of similar items. Secondary descriptions say this is recursive k-means that splits clusters until each leaf has at most a set number of items (gamma) [29]. Limiting cluster size compresses sequences well beyond 10^5 to a length manageable online [15].
  2. Cluster representation. Each cluster becomes one virtual behaviour (aggregated features).
  3. Cluster-aware target attention. The GSU/ESU run on clusters, and attention scores are adjusted by cluster size so large clusters (strong interests) carry their weight [15].

Results. Deployed on primary traffic serving hundreds of millions of daily active users. The paper's Table 5 lists watch-time gains of +0.672%, +0.800% and +0.728% on the Featured-Video, Discovery and Slide tabs; the authors note that a 0.1% gain is significant at Kuaishou [15].

3.6 LONGER (ByteDance, RecSys 2025)

Problem. Two-stage retrieval (SIM, TWIN) is lossy. ByteDance wanted end-to-end Transformer modelling of sequences up to 10,000 items in ranking [17].

Design [17][33]:

  • Global tokens (for example the target item and user tokens) that attend across the whole context to stabilise attention over long sequences.
  • Token merge: adjacent behaviours are merged into fewer tokens, with lightweight InnerTransformers that keep detail inside each merged group.
  • Hybrid attention: cross-attention from a small set of query tokens over the long sequence, followed by self-attention layers on the short output, to cut quadratic cost.
  • Engineering: mixed-precision training, activation recomputation, and KV-cache serving so the user-only part is computed once per request and shared across candidates.

Results. Consistent offline and online gains in advertising and e-commerce. The v2 paper says LONGER is fully deployed in dozens of ByteDance scenarios serving billions of users [17].

4. Pinterest: real-time, batch and lifelong user sequences

Pinterest has published one of the most complete public lines of user-history work, so it is worth following in order.

4.1 PinnerSage (KDD 2020): multi-embedding users

Problem. One user vector cannot represent users with many unrelated interests (for example recipes, tattoos and home decor) [18].

Design. Take the user's action pins from the last 90 days, cluster their PinSage embeddings with Ward hierarchical clustering, and represent each cluster by its medoid (a real pin from the user's history, which keeps clusters coherent and robust to outliers). Clusters get an importance score; at retrieval time the system samples a few medoids and uses each as an ANN query [18]. A/B tests showed it beat single-embedding methods.

4.2 PinnerFormer (KDD 2022): a batch user embedding trained for the long term

Problem. Pinterest wanted a single user embedding, computed in a daily batch job, that works nearly as well as a real-time embedding, and that predicts long-term engagement rather than only the next action [19].

Architecture.

 last N actions (pin, action type, surface, time features)
      |  each pin: 256-d PinSage embedding (frozen) + learned feature embeddings
 +----v------------------------------+
 | causal Transformer encoder         |
 +----+------------------------------+
      v
 user embedding (L2-normalised), computed daily for every user
      |
      v  ANN retrieval / ranking feature, matched against pin embeddings

Dense all-action loss. Instead of predicting only the next action (SASRec style), each position's embedding is trained to predict all positive engagements (repins, close-ups, clicks) in a future window of up to 28 days [19]. Training uses sampled softmax with a mix of in-batch and random negatives and logQ correction [19].

Why it matters. The objective makes the embedding robust to staleness. Moving from real-time to daily batch inference cut Recall@10 by 13.9% with the SASRec-style next-action objective, but only by 8.3% with the dense all-action objective [19]. A/B tests showed better engagement and retention than the previous user representation, and it has been in production since fall 2021 [19]. A secondary summary reports the team did not scale beyond about 256 actions (approximate).

Lesson. For an embedding that will be computed offline and reused, train it to forecast a window of future behaviour, not one next click.

4.3 TransAct (KDD 2023): real-time actions inside the ranker

Problem. PinnerFormer is updated daily, so Homefeed ranking could not react to what a user did seconds ago. A real-time sequence model is needed, but running a full user model on every action is expensive [20].

Hybrid design. TransAct is a module inside Pinterest's Homefeed ranking model (Pinnability) that encodes the most recent actions in real time, while PinnerFormer and other batch features provide long-term context [20].

   real-time action stream (Kafka-like)                  candidate pin
          |                                                    |
   latest ~100 actions: PinSage emb + action type + time       |
          |                                                    |
   early fusion: concat each action with candidate embedding <-+
          |
   Transformer encoder (small: ~2 layers, reported)
          |
   output compression: first K tokens + max pooling -> flatten
          |
   concat with PinnerFormer user emb + other features -> DCN-style ranker
          |
   multi-head outputs (repin, click, hide, ...) -> utility score

Key tricks reported in the paper [20]:

  • Early fusion of the candidate with every sequence item (concatenation), which made the Transformer candidate-aware.
  • Action type embeddings were important; positional encodings added little.
  • Random time-window masking during training: hide actions from a random recent window so the model does not over-rely on the last few actions and recommendations stay diverse.
  • Serving on GPUs, since the per-candidate Transformer is expensive.

Results and challenges. A third-party summary of the paper reports +11% Homefeed repin volume and -10% hides in online A/B tests (approximate). TransAct was deployed in Homefeed, Related Pins, Notifications and Search [20]. The paper discusses three production problems: high serving complexity, reduced diversity, and engagement decay (gains shrink if the model is not retrained often), which led to frequent retraining.

4.4 TransAct V2 (2025): lifelong sequences in ranking

Problem. TransAct used only recent actions (about 100). TransAct V2 extends Homefeed ranking to lifelong histories of about 16,000 actions, roughly 160x more [21][22][31].

Architecture.

  lifelong seq (~16k, int8 PinSage, offline store)  real-time seq   impression seq
          \                                           |             /
           +------- nearest-neighbour selection by candidate -------+
                   (dot product in PinSage space; always keep
                    the most recent real-time actions)
                              |
                      short selected sequence
                              |
                Transformer (fused single-kernel)
                              |
              features -> ranker heads  +  Next Action Loss (aux)
  • Each token holds timestamp, a multi-hot action type, surface, and a 32-dimensional PinSage embedding; lifelong actions are stored losslessly with int8 quantization [21][22].
  • Candidate-anchored nearest-neighbour (NN) selection picks a short subsequence from the lifelong, real-time and impression sequences. It is a SIM-style GSU, with the most recent actions always kept [21].
  • Next Action Loss: an auxiliary loss that asks the model to predict what the user does next, not only engagement probability [21][31].
  • Serving: a fused Triton kernel combines dequantization to float16, normalisation and NN search, cutting model latency by 20% versus native PyTorch. A single-kernel Transformer (SKUT) is reported 6.6x faster than PyTorch in the forward pass. A broadcast-free NN search reportedly cut PCIe transfers for sequences by 8x. End-to-end inference latency improved by 103x (p50), 338x (p90) and 250x (p99) versus the unoptimised baseline [21].

Results. Pinterest reports +6.35% repins, +1.41% time spent, a 12.8% drop in hides [31], and a 13.31% increase in top-3 repin hit rate [22].

4.5 PinFM (RecSys 2025): a foundation model for user activity

Problem. Many Pinterest surfaces each trained their own sequence modules. Pinterest wanted one large pretrained model of user activity to share across surfaces [23].

Design.

  • Pretraining. A Transformer with more than 20 billion parameters (most in ID embedding tables) is pretrained on about two years of user actions, with contrastive next-token, multi-token and future-token losses (in the PinnerFormer tradition) [23].
  • Fine-tuning. The pretrained Transformer and embedding tables are plugged into ranking models for each application and fine-tuned with the ranking losses; the pretraining losses can optionally be kept [23]. An ablation found that switching to bidirectional attention in fine-tuning cost 1.4% in evaluation metrics, so causal attention is kept [23].
  • DCAT (Deduplicated Cross-Attention Transformer). At serving, there are about 1,000 candidates per unique user sequence (about 10 in training). DCAT splits the model into a context part that runs the Transformer once on the user history and caches its KV, and a crossing part that scores each candidate against the cached history [23]. It raised throughput by 600% on internal data. Embeddings are int4-quantized [23].
  • Cold start. A conference talk describes ID noise, age-dependent dropout and a class token for fresh pins (secondary).

Results. +20% engagement on new items, deployed to Home Feed and Related Items for more than half a billion users at neutral cost and marginal latency increase [23].

4.6 PinRec (2025): generative retrieval from the same sequences

PinRec uses a user-sequence Transformer as a generative retriever, with outcome conditioning (for example generating for saves versus clicks) and multi-token generation [32]. It shows the same history encoder moving from ranking into retrieval.

5. Kuaishou: sequence models for retrieval

KuaiFormer (2024)

Problem. Single-vector two-tower retrieval squeezes all user interests into one vector and handles long sequences poorly [16].

Design [16]:

  • Multiple learnable query tokens (like BERT's [CLS]) appended to the sequence, each producing one interest vector for multi-interest ANN retrieval.
  • Adaptive sequence compression. Older behaviours are merged in groups of 64, middle behaviours in groups of 16, each group aggregated by a single-layer bidirectional Transformer; recent items are kept as-is. For example, 256 behaviours are fed as 55 tokens.
  • A causal Transformer over the compressed sequence, trained with a smoothed in-batch softmax with logQ correction.

Scale. In production since May 2024 in Kuaishou's short-video recommendation, serving more than 400 million daily active users [16]. Kuaishou has since published generative recommenders for long sequences, such as GEMs (2026) with a multi-stream decoder [34].

6. Generative recommenders and foundation user models

6.1 Meta HSTU and Generative Recommenders (ICML 2024)

Problem. Classic deep learning recommenders (DLRMs) did not keep improving with more compute. Meta asked whether a sequence model of user actions, scaled like an LLM, would [24].

Reformulation. Meta rewrote ranking and retrieval as sequential transduction. The user's history becomes one chronological stream mixing content and actions. Retrieval predicts the next content item; ranking predicts the action on an inserted candidate. Most hand-built features are replaced by the sequence itself [24].

HSTU (Hierarchical Sequential Transduction Unit) [24][30]:

  • Pointwise aggregated attention. Scores go through SiLU instead of row-wise softmax and are scaled by sequence length. This keeps the intensity of user preferences (how many related actions there are) and suits non-stationary, streaming vocabularies.
  • Relative attention bias from both position and time gaps.
  • A fused, simplified layer (fewer linear layers than a standard Transformer block) that uses less memory, enabling deeper stacks.
  • Efficiency: HSTU is 5.3x to 15.2x faster than FlashAttention2 Transformers at length 8,192 [24]. The paper also describes stochastic length (sampling sub-sequences of long histories) to cut cost. At inference, M-FALCON batches many candidates into one pass with attention masks so the user history cost is shared.

Results. Up to 65.8% better NDCG than baselines on public and synthetic data; a 1.5-trillion-parameter generative recommender improved online A/B metrics by 12.4% across multiple surfaces of a platform with billions of users. Model quality followed a power law of training compute across three orders of magnitude, reaching GPT-3/LLaMa-2 scale [24]. Attention dominates inference time (over 90% in one characterisation study), which drove fused kernels such as NVIDIA's cuDNN HSTU attention [30].

6.2 Netflix foundation model for personalization (2025)

Problem. Netflix ran many specialised models ("Continue Watching", "Today's Top Picks" and others), each trained separately on similar data. Maintenance was expensive and improvements did not transfer between models [25][35].

Design (from the Netflix tech blog [25] and secondary summaries [35]):

  • An LLM-style, autoregressive Transformer trained on hundreds of billions of interactions from more than 300 million users, roughly the token scale of an LLM.
  • Interaction tokenization. Raw events are merged into meaningful tokens (for example consecutive related events grouped), balancing sequence length and detail, similar to BPE for text.
  • Very long histories are handled with sparse attention and sliding-window sampling in training (Netflix published a separate sliding-window training paper [27]), plus KV caching at inference.
  • Objectives. Next-item prediction, with auxiliary targets (for example genre or original language) and multi-token prediction of several future items, which also reduces myopia.
  • Cold start. Item embeddings combine learnable ID embeddings with metadata embeddings, so new titles get useful vectors before anyone watches them. Training supports incremental updates with unseen entities.
  • Reported scaling from millions to billions of parameters, with gains following scaling laws (secondary).

Integration [26][35]. Netflix describes three ways downstream teams consume the model:

Pattern How it works Trade-off
Embeddings Precomputed user/item embeddings published to an Embedding Store Cheap and easy; can be stale
Subgraph FM layers embedded in the downstream model and trained with it Fresh, adaptable; downstream must build the FM's inputs
Fine-tuning FM fine-tuned directly for a task Best fit; most compute and ops cost

6.3 LinkedIn and others

LinkedIn has publicly described a large foundation ranking model (360Brew, reported at about 150B parameters) that reads member history as part of its input, but public details on its user-history component come mainly from secondary sources and are not covered here.

8. Recurring design patterns

8.1 Split the user part from the candidate part

The single most important serving trick is to compute the user-only part once per request and reuse it across all candidates:

  request -> [ user history encoder ]  ---- once per request (or cached / batch)
                    |   KV cache / embedding
          +---------+----------+----------+
          v         v          v          v
       cand_1    cand_2  ...  cand_1000      cheap cross-attention or dot product

Examples: MIMN/UIC (precompute memory), SDIM's BSE service, TWIN's cached item keys, LONGER's KV-cache serving, PinFM's DCAT, HSTU's M-FALCON, PinnerFormer's daily embeddings.

8.2 Retrieve, then attend

For histories past about 10^3, every production system first selects a short relevant subsequence and then runs exact attention: category search (SIM), LSH (ETA, SDIM), shared attention scores (TWIN), clustering (TWIN V2, PinnerSage), and embedding NN search (TransAct V2). TWIN's lesson is that the selection metric should match the final model's metric.

8.3 Choose the objective for how the representation is used

  • Batch embeddings: forecast a future window (PinnerFormer's dense all-action loss).
  • Real-time ranking: candidate-aware target attention with a multi-task ranking head (TransAct), plus an auxiliary next-action loss (TransAct V2).
  • Foundation models: next-token, multi-token and future-token losses (PinFM, Netflix).
  • With sampled negatives, correct for sampling (logQ, gBCE) or the model becomes overconfident [6].

8.4 Real-time versus batch

Pinterest's hybrid (daily PinnerFormer + real-time TransAct) is the clearest public example of splitting long-term and short-term interest across infrastructure tiers. Real-time models react within seconds but cost more and can reduce diversity (hence random time-window masks); batch models are cheap but stale (hence objectives robust to staleness).

8.5 Scale like an LLM

HSTU, PinFM, Netflix's model and LONGER all report that larger sequence models trained on more interactions keep improving, which DLRM-style models did not [24][25]. The cost is dominated by attention on long sequences, so these systems invest in custom kernels (Triton, cuDNN HSTU attention), quantization (int8/int4 embeddings), and KV reuse.

9. Key takeaways for system designers

  1. History is the main feature. Moving from ~50 to 10^4 or more behaviours has repeatedly given multi-percent online gains (MIMN, SIM, TWIN, TransAct V2). Plan storage and serving for lifelong histories from the start.
  2. Never pay O(L) per candidate if you can pay it once per request. Split user-only computation from candidate crossing and cache it (KV cache, precomputed keys, embeddings).
  3. Use two stages for very long sequences, and keep them consistent. A cheap GSU picks about 100 behaviours; an exact ESU attends. Share parameters or metrics between them (TWIN), or make retrieval differentiable (ETA).
  4. Compress the old, keep the recent exact. Clustering (TWIN V2), group merging (KuaiFormer, LONGER) and always-keep-recent rules (TransAct V2) are cheap and effective.
  5. Pick the training target for the consumer. Daily embeddings should forecast a window of future behaviour; rankers should be candidate-aware and multi-task.
  6. Mind negative sampling. In-batch and sampled negatives need logQ correction or a calibrated loss such as gBCE; otherwise models are overconfident and benchmarks mislead.
  7. Do not trust academic leaderboards blindly. BERT4Rec versus SASRec showed that training time and loss choices can flip conclusions; also compare against strong kNN baselines.
  8. Real-time features cause decay and diversity problems. Retrain often, use random time window masks or similar regularisation, and monitor hides and diversity, not just clicks.
  9. Positional encodings matter less than action types and timestamps. BST uses time gaps; TransAct found action-type embeddings and early fusion mattered more than position.
  10. Foundation user models are now standard at the largest platforms. Pretrain once on billions of interactions, then serve through embeddings, subgraphs or fine-tuning (Netflix) or as a module inside rankers (PinFM). Budget for custom kernels and quantization.
  11. Cold start needs explicit handling in ID-heavy sequence models. Combine ID embeddings with content/metadata embeddings (Netflix) and regularise new IDs (PinFM).

06. Generative Recommenders (2023-2026): HSTU, Semantic IDs, OneRec, MTGR and the Foundation-Model Turn

Between 2023 and 2026 the industrial recommender stack went through its largest architectural change since deep learning recommendation models (DLRMs) replaced matrix factorization. Three ideas drove it:

  1. Recommendation as sequence transduction. Meta's HSTU paper ("Actions Speak Louder than Words") recast retrieval and ranking as generative modeling over a user's chronological stream of (item, action) tokens. It reported power-law quality scaling with compute and production models of about 1.5 trillion parameters [1][2].
  2. Items as token sequences (semantic IDs). Google's TIGER replaced atomic item IDs with short tuples of discrete codes learned by residual quantization (RQ-VAE). Retrieval then becomes autoregressive decoding of the next item's code tuple [4][5].
  3. One model instead of a cascade. Kuaishou's OneRec, Meituan's MTGR and EGA, Tencent's GPR, and others replaced parts or all of the retrieve -> pre-rank -> rank -> re-rank cascade with a single generative model, often post-trained with reinforcement learning against a reward model [10][11][12][16][41].

At the same time, Netflix, LinkedIn and Pinterest published "foundation model" approaches. Each pre-trains one large user-sequence model and feeds many downstream recommenders from it [25][27][29]. X (formerly Twitter) open-sourced a For You pipeline whose main ranker, Phoenix, is a transformer over the viewer's engagement sequence with candidate-isolated attention [31].

This chapter covers each design: the problem it targets, its architecture and data flow, model and scale numbers where public, the key tricks, and the lessons learned. It ends with a comparison table and takeaways for system designers.

Source note: this chapter was compiled when only some primary hosts could be fetched directly. Facts marked "(approx.)" or "as reported" come from abstracts or secondary technical notes, not from a full read of the paper. Check them against the cited primary source before you depend on an exact figure.

1. The conceptual shift: from DLRM to generative recommenders

A classical DLRM ranker scores each (user, candidate) pair independently. It uses hundreds of hand-built features, very large sparse embedding tables, and a feature-interaction network (DCN, DeepFM, and similar). Three structural problems limited further scaling:

  • Hardware inefficiency. Embedding tables often hold more than 90% of DLRM parameters, and those parameters are sparse and memory-bound [22][21]. Secondary analyses put DLRM model FLOPs utilization (MFU) at roughly 4-5%, against 40-60% for LLM training [23].
  • Cascade information loss. Items dropped by an early stage are never seen by later, stronger models. Each stage also optimizes a different objective [22].
  • Per-impression training cost. Each impression is a separate training example, so a user with 500 interactions gets 500 separate forward passes over almost the same history [18].

Generative recommenders (GRs) address all three. They model the user as a single token sequence, run one causal forward pass that produces supervision at every position, and use dense, GEMM-heavy transformer compute that scales the way LLMs do.

 Classical cascade (DLRM era)            Generative recommender (GR era)
 ----------------------------            --------------------------------
 user feats ─┐                           [item0, act0, item1, act1, ... , itemN]
 item feats ─┼─> Retrieval (two-tower)              │ causal transformer (HSTU,
 cross feats ┘      │ ~10^3-10^4                     │  decoder-only, enc-dec)
                    v                                v
             Pre-rank (light DNN)        retrieval head: p(next item | history)
                    │ ~10^2-10^3         ranking head:  p(action | history, item)
                    v                    or: decode semantic-ID tokens directly
             Rank (DLRM, MTL)                        │
                    │ ~10^1-10^2                     v
                    v                    (optional) RL post-training vs reward model
             Re-rank / blend

2. Meta HSTU: "Actions Speak Louder than Words"

2.1 Problem

Meta wanted to know whether recommendation quality scales with compute the way language modeling does, and what architecture would allow it on high-cardinality, non-stationary streaming data with billions of users [1]. Standard transformers did not fit well. Softmax attention normalizes away the intensity of user interest, and the FFN-heavy blocks used too much activation memory for the very large batches that industrial training needs [18].

2.2 Problem formulation

HSTU interleaves content tokens (Φ) and action tokens (a) into one chronological sequence [Φ0, a0, Φ1, a1, ..., Φn-1, an-1] of length 2n_c. Other categorical features are merged onto this timeline by timestamp, and runs of identical values are compressed [18]. Both main tasks then become sequence transduction:

  • Ranking: p(a_i | Φ0, a0, ..., Φi). This is target-aware, because the candidate item is in the context when the action is predicted.
  • Retrieval: p(Φ_i | Φ0, a0, ..., a_{i-1}). This predicts the next item.

Under a causal mask, one forward pass yields n_c supervision signals. For a user with about 500 interactions, the secondary analysis estimates roughly a 500x reduction in training forward passes compared with impression-level DLRM training [18].

2.3 The HSTU block

Each layer has three parts [1][18]:

  1. Pointwise projection: U, V, Q, K = Split(SiLU(f1(X))).
  2. Pointwise aggregated attention: A(X)V(X) = SiLU(Q K^T + rab_{p,t}) ⊙ V. There is no softmax, so the weights do not sum to 1 and the absolute strength of interest is preserved. rab_{p,t} is a relative attention bias over both position and time differences.
  3. Pointwise transformation: Y = f2(Norm(A(X)V(X)) ⊙ U(X)). The gate U replaces the usual 4x-wide FFN.
   X ──> Linear ──> SiLU ──> split ──> U, V, Q, K
                                      │
            SiLU(Q·K^T + rab(pos,time)) ⊙ V      <- no softmax; rel. pos+time bias
                                      │
                       LayerNorm(·) ⊙ U          <- gating replaces the FFN
                                      │
                            Linear ──> + X (residual)

The secondary analysis reports per-layer activation memory falling from about 33x hidden dimension (standard transformer) to about 14x [18]. This matters because industrial batch sizes run from tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands, and activation memory is usually the limit [18].

2.4 Efficiency tricks

  • Stochastic Length (SL). Long user histories are sparsely subsampled during training, so attention cost grows sub-quadratically. The secondary notes report 80%+ sparsity with almost no loss in quality [18].
  • Efficient attention kernels. The paper reports HSTU running 5.3x to 15.2x faster than FlashAttention2-based transformers on 8192-length sequences [1]. The open-source repo now includes Triton kernels, an HSTU attention kernel based on FlashAttention-3 for H100 GPUs, and row-wise FP8 GEMMs [2].
  • M-FALCON (inference). To score m candidates against one history, the candidates are appended to the sequence with an attention mask so that candidates see only the history and not each other. They are processed in micro-batches, and the history's K/V cache is shared across micro-batches. The secondary analysis attributes speedups of tens to hundreds of times to the combination [18].

2.5 Scale and results

  • Up to 65.8% NDCG improvement over baselines on public and synthetic datasets [1].
  • 1.5-trillion-parameter models deployed on multiple surfaces of a billion-user platform, with a reported +12.4% on online A/B metrics [1].
  • Quality scales as a power law of training compute across three orders of magnitude, up to roughly GPT-3/LLaMa-2 training compute [1]. Secondary notes give the fitted laws as HR@100 = 0.15 + 0.0195 ln C for retrieval and NE = 0.549 - 0.0053 ln C for ranking. The sweep covered sequence lengths 512-8192, hidden dimensions 256-1024, and up to 24 layers [18].
  • Public benchmark reproduction from the repo: on ML-20M, HSTU-large reaches HR@10 0.3556 against 0.2889 for SASRec (+23.1%). On Amazon Books it reaches NDCG@10 0.0262 against 0.0164 (+60.7%) [2].

2.6 Follow-ups

The repo also contains a "DLRM-v3" ranker built on HSTU with an MLCommons LoadGen inference harness, and "HSTU Ultra", which adds semi-local and target-aware attention and FP8 projections [2]. In 2026 Meta published "Bending the Scaling Law Curve in Large-Scale Recommendation Systems" (listed under the ULTRA-HSTU name), and an analysis of how well generative recommenders generalize [35][45].

Lessons. (1) Softmax is not sacred: for recommendation, unnormalized SiLU attention plus a relative time bias works better. (2) Most of the value comes from restructuring training (one sequence per user, causal supervision), not only from model size. (3) Inference needs its own algorithm (M-FALCON) to make target-aware ranking over many candidates affordable.

3. Semantic IDs and TIGER (Google)

3.1 Problem

Atomic item IDs carry no meaning: item 81723 and item 81724 are unrelated unless behavior links them. Very large ID vocabularies also make softmax retrieval expensive, and brand-new items have no trained embedding at all. TIGER ("Recommender Systems with Generative Retrieval", NeurIPS 2023) proposed describing every item with a short tuple of discrete semantic codes and training a sequence model to generate the next item's code tuple [4][5].

3.2 Pipeline

 item text/metadata ──> frozen text encoder (e.g., Sentence-T5) ──> dense emb e
                                                                    │
                       RQ-VAE: encoder -> z
                       level 1: c1 = argmin ||z - C1[k]||, r1 = z - C1[c1]
                       level 2: c2 = argmin ||r1 - C2[k]||, r2 = r1 - C2[c2]
                       level 3: c3 = ...
                                                                    │
                    Semantic ID = (c1, c2, c3 [, dedup token])  e.g. (10, 5, 42)
                                                                    │
 user history = [SID(item1), SID(item2), ...] ──> Transformer seq2seq (T5-style)
                                                ──> beam-decode SID of next item
                                                ──> map SID -> item (lookup)
  • RQ-VAE loss. Reconstruction error, plus a codebook term and a commitment term (weight β) at each level. Gradients pass through the quantizer with the straight-through estimator [21].
  • Hierarchy. On the Beauty dataset, the first codeword tracks broad categories and later codewords refine them. Items that share a prefix are semantically similar, so knowledge transfers between related items [4].
  • Cold start. A new item gets its semantic ID from its content embedding with no interaction history. The authors report better behavior on cold items [4].
  • Collisions. When two items get the same code tuple, an extra disambiguation token is appended. Decoding can also be restricted to valid prefixes so that every output maps to a real item [6].
  • Commonly reported TIGER configuration (approx.): a 768-d Sentence-T5 embedding, 3 RQ levels with 256 codes each, plus the collision token. The open-source reproduction uses smaller toy settings in its quick-start (codebook 16, 3 levels) [6].

3.3 Variations on semantic IDs

Variant Idea Where used
RQ-VAE Learned encoder + residual codebooks, end to end TIGER [4]; EGA (3 levels x 1024) [24]
RQ-KMeans Residual k-means on frozen embeddings; decoupled from representation learning; new items assigned by nearest-centroid search OneRec (3 levels, about 8K codes per level) [20][21]
RQ-KMeans+ Improved init/utilization; codebook utilization reported 65% -> 92%, reconstruction error -15% Tencent GPR [24]
RQ + OPQ suffix 3 RQ layers (4096/1024/512) plus 2 OPQ codes (2 x 256) to separate near-duplicates Kuaishou OneSearch [21][43]
Constrained RQ-KMeans Balancing and dedup layer for conflicting items MiniOneRec [15]
Hybrid sparse + dense Generate SID, then refine with a dense vector Baidu COBRA [40], Meta LIGER [39]

Known pathologies and practical guidance:

  • The "hourglass" effect. Intermediate RQ levels can collapse onto a few codes, which limits the ceiling of generative retrieval. A 2024 analysis proposes fixes [9].
  • Codebook collapse and imbalance cause collisions. Uniform allocation, capacity limits, and k-means-based assignment all reduce it [21].
  • Snap's GRID framework and its "Practitioner's Handbook" (CIKM 2025) benchmark RQ-VAE, RVQ and RQ-KMeans tokenizers inside a TIGER-style model on a common pipeline [8]. A companion study looks at how semantic-ID generative recommenders scale with model size [36].
  • Google's PLUM (2025) adapts pre-trained LLMs to industrial generative recommendation with semantic IDs [38].

Lessons. The semantic-ID tokenizer is the "vocabulary design" of a generative recommender, and it is a first-class system component. Its collision rate, codebook utilization, refresh cadence, and how well it reflects collaborative signal, not only content, matter as much as the sequence model.

4. Kuaishou OneRec family

OneRec is the most complete public example of replacing an entire recommendation cascade with a single generative model in a short-video app serving hundreds of millions of users.

4.1 OneRec (V1) - February 2025 paper and June 2025 technical report

Problem. Remove the retrieve/pre-rank/rank cascade. Generate a session of recommended videos end to end, and align the generator with user preference through RL [10][11].

Tokenizer.

  • Inputs (title, tags, ASR, OCR, cover, sampled frames) are compressed by a multimodal LLM (miniCPM-V-8B) to 1280 tokens, then by a QFormer to 4 query vectors.
  • An item-pair contrastive loss injects collaborative signal, and title generation is used as an auxiliary task.
  • RQ-KMeans then produces 3 code levels [20].

Encoder. Four pathways [20]:

  • Static user features, through two dense layers.
  • Short-term behavior: the last 20 interactions.
  • Positive-feedback behavior: the last 256 high-engagement interactions.
  • Lifelong history: up to 100,000 records. These are compressed by hierarchical k-means to 2,000 items, then by a QFormer to 128 tokens.

The encoder context is 1 + 20 + 256 + 128 = 405 tokens.

Decoder. A [BOS] token plus semantic-ID tokens, with causal self-attention, cross-attention to the encoder, and MoE feed-forward layers with top-k routing [20].

 user static ─┐
 short seq 20 ├─> Encoder (Transformer, RMSNorm) ──> 405 ctx tokens
 pos-fb 256  ─┤                                          │ cross-attn
 lifelong 1e5 ─> hier-kmeans 2000 ─> QFormer 128 ─┘      v
                         [BOS] s1 s2 s3 ──> Decoder (causal + MoE FFN)
                                                         │ beam search over SIDs
                                                         v
                       candidate sessions ──> Reward model (P-Score: CTR/LTR/VTR..)
                                                         │
                         preference alignment (DPO-style IPA in V1 paper;
                         ECPO = early-clipped GRPO in technical report)

Alignment and RL.

  • The original paper used Iterative Preference Alignment (IPA). A reward model scores sampled sessions, and chosen/rejected pairs drive DPO-style updates [10].
  • The technical report moved to ECPO, an early-clipped variant of GRPO that prevents exploding gradients on negative-advantage samples [20].
  • It also added format rewards so the model generates only legal semantic IDs.
  • "SIR" industrial alignment down-weights viral content. It is reported to cut viral-content exposure by 9.59% while keeping core metrics stable [20].

Scale (as reported, approx.). The technical report claims:

  • Training MFU of about 24% and inference MFU of about 29%.
  • Operating cost of about 10% of the previous cascade.
  • Deployment on the main Kuaishou and Kuaishou Lite feeds, handling about a quarter of their traffic.
  • App stay-time gains of about 0.5-1.2%.

These figures come from the report's abstract and should be verified there [11].

4.2 OneRec-V2 (August 2025)

Problem. In V1 most compute went into the encoder. Only a small fraction trained the generator, and RL from a learned reward model risked reward hacking [20].

Lazy decoder-only architecture.

  • A context processor computes key/value pairs once and shares them across decoder layers. There is no per-layer KV projection, and the shared KV uses GQA.
  • The decoder input is only [BOS] plus the first two semantic-ID tokens.
  • Each layer has lazy cross-attention, causal self-attention, and an FFN, with MoE in the deeper layers [20].

At 1B parameters, the encoder-decoder used 296.36 GFLOPs and reached a converged loss of 3.28. The lazy decoder-only model used 18.89 GFLOPs and reached 3.27. That is about 94% less compute and about 90% less training resource for the same quality [20]. Secondary notes put OneRec-V2 MFU at 20%+, against roughly 5-10% for encoder-decoder setups [22].

Scaling law.

  • Dense models from 0.1B to 8B parameters fit L(N) = E + A / N^α, with E = 3.13, A = 3660, α = 0.489.
  • Converged loss falls from 3.57 (0.1B) to 3.19 (8B).
  • A 4B-total / 0.5B-active MoE reaches 3.22, better than a 2B dense model [20].

RL from real user feedback.

  • Rewards come directly from logged watch time, which is log-bucketed. The top 25% within a bucket get advantage +1, explicit negative feedback gets -1, and the rest get 0.
  • GBPO (Gradient-Bounded Policy Optimization) keeps gradients for all samples but bounds the RL gradient by the BCE gradient [20].

Reported online stay-time gains are again in the sub-1% range (approx.) [12].

4.3 OneRec-Think, OpenOneRec, MiniOneRec

  • OneRec-Think (Oct 2025). Built on Qwen3 with a vocabulary extended by semantic-ID tokens. Training runs in three stages: itemic alignment (mapping item tokens into text space), reasoning activation (chain-of-thought SFT), and reasoning enhancement with a reward that allows multiple valid answers. It reports a further +0.159% app stay time online [13].
  • OpenOneRec (Dec 2025). Kuaishou's open release.
    • Model checkpoints: OneRec-1.7B and 8B, trained on about 33B tokens, and "-Pro" variants trained on about 130B tokens, including industrial data. All use Qwen3 backbones.
    • Items are represented as three-level "itemic tokens".
    • Post-training pipeline: multi-task SFT, then on-policy distillation to restore general reasoning, then RL.
    • RecIF-Bench: 8 tasks over 100M interactions from 200K users in short video, ads, and products [14].
  • MiniOneRec (Oct 2025). A community open-source reproduction. It builds text-embedding semantic IDs (RQ-VAE / RQ-KMeans / constrained RQ-KMeans) and SFT co-trained with language alignment. It then applies GRPO with a rank-aware reward and a KL penalty, and decodes with constrained beam search through a logits processor [15].

Kuaishou extended the same recipe to e-commerce search (OneSearch), query suggestion (OneSug), live streaming (OneLive), and local services (OneLoc) [43][44].

Lessons.

  • (1) In a generative recommender the encoder is mostly a context compressor, and compute belongs in the generating decoder. This is V2's main lesson.
  • (2) RL post-training needs guardrails: format rewards, clipping and bounding of policy gradients, and anti-virality shaping.
  • (3) Lifelong histories of about 10^5 events are compressed (clustering, then QFormer) instead of being attended to directly.

5. Meituan MTGR (and MTGRBoost, DFGR, EGA)

5.1 Problem

Meituan's food-delivery ranking depends heavily on cross features: user x item statistics such as the user's historical CTR on a category, or their preference by hour of day. Pure HSTU-style generative ranking drops these features. Meituan found that this hurt so much that even the largest generative model without cross features performed worse than a mid-sized DLRM [19].

5.2 Architecture

MTGR is a hybrid: a transformer encoder with HSTU-style user-level sequence compression, trained with a discriminative (CTR/CTCVR) objective [16][19].

  • Token groups:
    • User tokens: static attributes, one token per attribute.
    • Sequence tokens: long-term history, one per item.
    • Real-time tokens: recent events.
    • Candidate tokens: MLP(concat(item embedding, cross-feature embedding)), plus position and exposure time.
  • Cross features stay on candidate tokens and never enter the history, which avoids causal leakage.
  • Group LayerNorm (GLN): separate normalization statistics and affine parameters per token group.
  • Dynamic masking: static tokens are visible to all. Real-time tokens are causal, and a candidate can see them only if their timestamp is before that candidate's exposure time. Candidates cannot see each other (a diagonal block), so all candidates for a user are scored in one pass.
  • Loss is computed only at candidate positions. Encoding the history once and scoring m candidates in parallel costs O((n+m)^2), against O(m·n^2) when candidates are scored separately [19].
 [U1..Uk | S1 ... Sn | R1 ... Rr | C1  C2  ...  Cm]
   static   long seq   real-time   candidates (item ⊕ cross feats)
 mask: U,S -> visible to all; R causal & time-gated per candidate; Ci ⟂ Cj
 heads: CTR / CTCVR on C positions only

Scale (as reported, approx.). The paper reports per-sample inference compute about 65x that of the DLRM baseline. It describes this as the largest offline and online gain in about two years, deployed on Meituan's delivery recommendation [16]. Training was supported by MTGRBoost, a companion system paper on large-scale generative-model training infrastructure [17].

Related Meituan work:

  • DFGR ("Action is All You Need: Dual-Flow Generative Ranking Network") restructures action and item flows.
  • EGA-V1/V2 build fully generative advertising. EGA uses RQ-VAE semantic IDs (3 levels x 1024 codes) and decomposes generation into P(POI) x P(creative | POI). It puts auction mechanics into the model with token-level bids and a payment network that guarantees individual rationality (payment never exceeds bid). Incentive compatibility is enforced approximately through a Lagrangian on ex-post regret [24][42].

Lessons. Generative architecture and discriminative objectives can coexist. Keep the scaling benefits of user-level sequence encoding and parallel candidate scoring, and keep the cross features that a pure next-token model throws away.

6. Other generative ranking systems worth knowing

  • Xiaohongshu GenRank ("Towards Large-scale Generative Ranking", 2025).
    • Trained on hundreds of billions of exposure logs.
    • An action-oriented sequence makes actions the main tokens and folds items in as attributes. This halves the sequence (2n_c -> n_c), cuts attention compute by 75%, and speeds up training by 78.7%.
    • ALiBi-style parameter-free position and time biases raise the total speedup to 94.8%.
    • Loss at history positions hurt AUC, and so did removing the causal mask. Real-time features stayed important while most historical aggregate features lost value [22][32].
  • ByteDance RankMixer (2025).
    • Not a generative model, but part of the same scaling trend.
    • Self-attention is replaced by parameter-free token mixing, plus per-token FFNs and a dense-train / sparse-infer MoE.
    • Raises ranking MFU from about 4-5% to about 45% [23][33].
    • Successors: OneTrans and TokenMixer-Large [44].
  • Tencent GPR (2025, WeChat Channels ads).
    • Four token types (user, organic, environment, ad), RQ-KMeans+ semantic IDs, and a heterogeneous hierarchical decoder with "thinking tokens".
    • Value-guided trie beam search.
    • Reported results: latency from 200ms+ to about 80ms, and 5 models collapsed into 1 [24][41].
  • Alibaba LUM (2025). A three-step paradigm: pre-train a large user model generatively, query it, then use its outputs in discriminative models. It aims to unlock scaling laws in industrial recommendation [37].

7. Netflix: Foundation Model for Personalized Recommendation

7.1 Problem

Netflix ran many specialized models (rows, ranking, search, notifications). Each was trained on overlapping data with its own feature engineering, which made improvements hard to share. In a March 2025 tech-blog post, Netflix described consolidating user-preference learning into one large, centrally trained foundation model in the spirit of LLMs. Downstream systems consume it [25].

7.2 Design elements (as described in the blog; summarized via a public reimplementation's mapping)

  • Interaction tokenization. User interaction events are tokenized, and adjacent related actions are merged, much like BPE in language models. Sequences stay informative but shorter [25][26].
  • Long-context handling. Sparse or local attention, plus sliding-window sampling over long histories during training [25][26].
  • Multi-token / multi-attribute prediction. Heads predict several future items and attributes such as genre, not only the next item ID. This reduces myopia [25][26].
  • Cold start. Metadata-based embeddings are mixed with learned ID embeddings, with a gate weighted by item "age". New titles lean on metadata, and the model is incrementally retrained to add new IDs [25][26].
  • Embedding stability. A projection, described as an orthogonal transformation, keeps embedding spaces comparable across retrains, so downstream consumers do not break [25][26].
  • Downstream use. Three modes: (a) the model directly as a predictive model, (b) exported user and item embeddings, and (c) fine-tuning for specific surfaces [25].
 member events ──> tokenizer (merge adjacent actions) ──> FM transformer
                                                         │   (sparse attn,
                                                         │    multi-token heads)
                    ┌────────────────────┬───────────────┴──────────┐
                    v                    v                          v
          direct prediction      user/item embeddings        fine-tuned task models
          (next-title scores)    (stable via projection)     (rows, search, notifs)

Netflix reported that performance kept improving as it scaled the model and data, consistent with scaling-law behavior (approx.; see [25]).

Lessons. For companies with many surfaces, the main gain is organizational: one representation learner, with stable embedding contracts, feeding many consumers. The engineering work is concentrated in tokenization, cold-start mixing, and keeping embeddings stable across retrains.

8. LinkedIn 360Brew

360Brew ("A Decoder-only Foundation Model for Personalized Ranking and Recommendation", 2025) takes the most radical "LLM-as-recommender" route of the systems here [27][28].

  • Problem. Replace many task-specific ranking models and their hand-engineered features with one model that reasons over textual member profiles and histories.
  • Interface. Each task is written as a natural-language prompt. For example: given the member's profile and past job interactions (applied, viewed, dismissed), predict whether they will apply to, view, or dismiss a given job. No manual feature engineering is needed [28].
  • Scaling observations. Performance improved with (a) more training tokens across five releases over nine months, (b) longer context, meaning more interaction history, and (c) larger model size [28].
  • Scale (approx.). The paper abstract describes a decoder-only model of about 150B parameters covering 30+ ranking tasks across LinkedIn surfaces, matching or beating production models without task-specific fine-tuning. Verify the figures in [27].

Lessons. Text-native foundation rankers trade very high serving cost for much less feature and model sprawl, plus zero-shot transfer to new surfaces. In practice they are often distilled or used for some surfaces rather than as the single high-QPS scorer.

9. Pinterest PinFM (and PinRec, UniPinRec)

PinFM ("Foundation Model for User Activity Sequences at a Billion-scale Visual Discovery Platform", 2025) pre-trains a large transformer on user activity sequences and then fine-tunes it inside multiple downstream ranking models [29].

  • Pre-train / fine-tune split. Large-scale pre-training on lifelong activity sequences. The module is then fine-tuned inside each downstream ranker, for example home-feed or related-pins ranking, and not served as a separate system [29].
  • Serving efficiency (approx.). The abstract describes a deduplicated cross-attention design (DCAT). It computes the user-sequence part once per request and shares it across all candidates, and is reported to improve throughput substantially (approx. 600%). It also reports gains in engagement with new items. Verify the figures in [29].
  • Model size (approx.). The parameter count is reported in the tens of billions (approx. 20B+) [29].
  • Related work. PinRec (2025) is an outcome-conditioned, multi-token generative retrieval model [30]. UniPinRec (2026) unifies generative retrieval and ranking at Pinterest scale [46].

Lessons. The "user-sequence foundation model plus downstream fine-tune" pattern deploys incrementally. It slots into an existing ranker as a learned feature extractor. Dedup and KV-sharing tricks like DCAT (similar to M-FALCON and MTGR's masking) are what make it affordable.

10. X (Twitter) For You: Phoenix transformer ranker

X's open-sourced x-algorithm repository describes the 2025-2026 For You pipeline [31]. (Public commentary often calls Phoenix "Grok-based". The repository itself says only that it is a transformer. "Grox" is a separate set of LLM content classifiers [31].)

  • Home-mixer pipeline: query hydration, then candidate sources, then hydration, then filters, then scoring, then selection, then post-selection visibility filtering, then blending.
  • Candidate sources:
    • Thunder: an in-memory store of recent posts from followed accounts.
    • Phoenix retrieval: embedding nearest-neighbor search for out-of-network posts.
    • SimClusters.
    • Popular posts.
  • Phoenix ranker. Its main input is the viewer's recent engagement sequence. It predicts per-action probabilities for engagement (favorite, reply, repost, quote, share), clicks, attention (dwell, video view), follow, and negative actions (not interested, mute, block, report). Training and serving are written in JAX with a Rust serving layer [31].
  • Candidate isolation. "During transformer inference, candidates cannot attend to each other - only to the viewer context." Each post's score is therefore independent of how candidates are batched. This is the same masking idea as M-FALCON and MTGR [31].
  • Hash embeddings. Retrieval and ranking both use multiple hash functions for embedding lookup, so there is no ID vocabulary to maintain [31].
  • Value model. Final score = Σ w_i · P(action_i). It is followed by an author-diversity decay, an out-of-network discount, a new-author boost, and a DPP-based re-ranker (VMRanker) that trades score for diversity [31].
 viewer engagement seq ─┐
 Thunder (in-network)  ─┼─> candidates ─> filters ─> Phoenix transformer
 Phoenix ANN (OON)     ─┤                         (cands attend only to viewer ctx)
 SimClusters / popular ─┘                                 │ P(fav), P(reply), ...
                                                          v
                      Σ w_i P(a_i) ─> diversity/OON adj ─> DPP rerank ─> VF ─> blend

Lessons. A transformer over the engagement sequence can replace a hand-built feature ranker without becoming end-to-end generative. Multi-action prediction combined with an explicit, tunable value model keeps product control (weights, negative signals) outside the network.

11. Scaling laws for recommendation

Work Model family Scaling claim (as reported)
HSTU (Meta, 2024) [1][18] Sequential transducer Power law in compute over 3 orders of magnitude; HR@100 and NE linear in ln(compute)
Wukong (Meta, 2024) [34] Stacked factorization machines (DLRM-style) Scaling law for dense interaction stacks across two orders of magnitude in complexity (approx.)
OneRec-V2 (Kuaishou, 2025) [20] Lazy decoder-only + MoE L(N) = 3.13 + 3660 / N^0.489, 0.1B-8B
360Brew (LinkedIn, 2025) [28] Text decoder LLM Gains with tokens, context length, model size
LUM (Alibaba, 2025) [37] Generative pre-trained user model Scaling unlocked by three-step generative -> discriminative paradigm
SID scaling study (Snap, 2025) [36] Semantic-ID GR Studies model-size scaling limits of SID-based GR
ULTRA-HSTU (Meta, 2026) [35] HSTU successor "Bending" the scaling curve via architecture/efficiency

Common findings:

  • (a) Gains are roughly logarithmic in compute, so each 10x buys a fixed increment. For HSTU this is about 4.5 points of HR@100 and about 1.2 points of NE per 10x, per secondary analysis [18].
  • (b) Sequence length is a scaling axis on equal footing with depth and width.
  • (c) MoE gives better loss per active FLOP [20].
  • (d) Embedding-table size alone does not scale. Dense compute does.

12. Comparison table

System Org / year Paradigm Item representation Stage replaced Notable scale / result (as reported)
HSTU / GR Meta 2024 Causal sequential transducer Atomic IDs + actions interleaved Retrieval & ranking models 1.5T params; +12.4% online; 5.3-15.2x faster attention [1]
TIGER Google 2023 Seq2seq generative retrieval Semantic IDs (RQ-VAE) Retrieval SOTA on Amazon datasets; cold-start gains [4]
OneRec V1 Kuaishou 2025 Enc-dec + MoE + RL (IPA/ECPO) 3-level RQ-KMeans SIDs Whole cascade MFU about 24%/29%; OPEX about 10% (approx.) [11]
OneRec-V2 Kuaishou 2025 Lazy decoder-only + RL from real feedback SIDs Whole cascade 94% less compute at equal loss; 8B scaling [20]
MTGR Meituan 2025 Hybrid generative-encoder, discriminative loss Atomic IDs + cross features Ranking about 65x FLOPs/sample vs DLRM (approx.) [16]
GenRank Xiaohongshu 2025 Action-oriented generative ranking Actions as tokens Ranking 94.8% training speedup [22]
GPR Tencent 2025 Decoder + value-guided trie search RQ-KMeans+ SIDs Ads cascade 5 models -> 1; latency to about 80ms [24]
Netflix FM Netflix 2025 Central foundation model Merged interaction tokens + metadata Feeds many models Scaling with data/params (approx.) [25]
360Brew LinkedIn 2025 Text decoder LLM ranker Natural-language prompts Many task rankers about 150B params, 30+ tasks (approx.) [27]
PinFM Pinterest 2025 Pre-trained user-seq FM, fine-tuned downstream IDs + content Feature extractor in rankers about 20B+ params; DCAT about 600% throughput (approx.) [29]
Phoenix X 2025-26 Transformer ranker + ANN retrieval Hash embeddings Main ranker Candidate-isolated attention; multi-action heads [31]

Key takeaways for system designers

  1. Restructure training before you scale. Moving from impression-level samples to one causal sequence per user (HSTU, GenRank, MTGR) gives order-of-magnitude efficiency gains before any parameters are added.
  2. Candidate-isolated attention is the universal serving trick. M-FALCON (Meta), dynamic masking (Meituan), DCAT (Pinterest) and Phoenix (X) all encode the user context once, share its KV, and let candidates attend only to the context. This makes target-aware transformer ranking linear in the number of candidates.
  3. Treat the tokenizer as infrastructure. Semantic IDs need a pipeline: embedding model, RQ-VAE or RQ-KMeans, collision handling, valid-prefix tries for constrained decoding, and a refresh policy. Monitor codebook utilization, collision rate, and the "hourglass" effect [9][21].
  4. Keep the features that carry signal. MTGR shows that dropping cross features to be "purely generative" can lose more than scaling gains back. Hybrid designs are legitimate.
  5. Put compute in the generator. OneRec-V2's lazy decoder-only design matched encoder-decoder quality with about 94% less compute. Compress long context (clustering, QFormer) instead of attending over 10^5 raw events.
  6. RL post-training needs stabilization. Use format rewards, clipped or bounded policy gradients (ECPO, GBPO), rewards grounded in real user feedback, and anti-virality or diversity shaping. Learned reward models alone invite reward hacking.
  7. MFU is the new north-star infrastructure metric. Going from about 5% (DLRM) to 20-45% (OneRec, RankMixer) changes what model sizes are affordable.
  8. Foundation models win organizationally. Netflix, PinFM and 360Brew show that one user-sequence model feeding many consumers, with stable embeddings, reduces duplicated feature work. Plan for embedding-versioning contracts.
  9. Keep business control explicit. Even end-to-end systems keep value models, auction or payment modules, diversity re-rankers and visibility filters outside or on top of the generator (X value model, EGA payment network).
  10. Expect logarithmic returns. Budget for about 10x compute per fixed metric increment, and use MoE and sequence-length scaling to stretch the curve.
