09. Training Infrastructure at Scale: Sparse Embeddings, Sharding, Parameter Servers and Online Learning

Overview

Industrial recommenders differ from most other deep learning workloads in one important way. Nearly all of their parameters sit in sparse embedding tables keyed by categorical IDs (users, items, creators, queries, ad IDs, crossed features). Only a small fraction sit in the dense neural network. In the DLRM family of models [1], each categorical feature looks up one or more rows in a table, pools them (sum or mean), and feeds the result into feature interaction and an MLP. Production tables have billions of rows, and their total size runs from hundreds of gigabytes to tens or hundreds of terabytes. Meta's ZionEX/Neo paper describes models of up to 12 trillion parameters [3]. Kuaishou's PERSIA reports a system that scales to 100 trillion parameters [4]. Alibaba's DeepRec claims support for "over ten trillion parameters" [10].

This shape of workload produces a set of system problems that look quite different from training a large language model:

  • Memory capacity, not FLOPs, is the binding constraint. The tables do not fit on one accelerator, and often not on one host.
  • Embedding lookups are memory-bandwidth and network bound. Each lookup is a small random read. Each step needs an all-to-all exchange of pooled embeddings.
  • The ID space is open and keeps changing. New users, items and videos arrive every second, so a fixed-size table either collides (hashing) or has to grow (dynamic hash tables).
  • Freshness matters. User interest and the item corpus drift within hours, which pushes systems toward online or continual training and toward frequent parameter sync to serving.
  • Data access is very skewed. A small fraction of IDs accounts for most lookups, which makes caching, tiered storage and frequency-based admission effective.

This chapter covers the main publicly documented designs for these problems:

  • Meta's DLRM, Neo/ZionEX, TorchRec and FBGEMM.
  • ByteDance's Monolith.
  • NVIDIA's HugeCTR, Merlin and HierarchicalKV.
  • Parameter-server systems: Alibaba XDL and DeepRec, Kuaishou PERSIA, HET, and 4Paradigm OpenEmbedding.
  • TensorFlow Recommenders-Addons, which Tencent and others contribute to.
  • Checkpointing for continual training.
  • Embedding compression: the hashing trick, hash embeddings, QR compositional embeddings, mixed-dimension embeddings, TT-Rec, ROBE-style and DHE-style methods.
  • Hardware directions such as Google's TPU SparseCore.

A note on sourcing: the research for this chapter hit a web-search budget limit and DNS failures on several sites (arxiv.org, pytorch.org, developer.nvidia.com and engineering.fb.com could not be fetched). The facts here come from the project repositories that could be read (GitHub READMEs and docs) and from the primary papers cited by ID. Where a number could not be re-verified against a fetched page, it is marked approximate.

1. The Shape of the Problem: DLRM as Reference Workload

1.1 Model anatomy

DLRM [1] is the reference model that most training-infrastructure papers assume. Dense features go through a bottom MLP. Each sparse feature indexes an embedding table. A pairwise interaction operator (dot product, or concatenation, or sum) combines the dense output with the pooled embeddings, and a top MLP predicts a click probability [11]. The open-source DLRM code supports synchronous distributed training over gloo, NCCL and MPI backends. It also includes MLPerf benchmark tooling with AUC-based early stopping [11].

            dense features            sparse features (multi-hot IDs)
                 |                      |        |        |
            +---------+             +------+ +------+ +------+
            | bottom  |             | EMB  | | EMB  | | EMB  |   <- 99%+ of params
            |  MLP    |             | T1   | | T2   | | Tk   |      (sharded)
            +---------+             +------+ +------+ +------+
                 |                      | pool   | pool   | pool
                 +----------+-----------+--------+--------+
                            |  feature interaction (dot / cat)
                       +---------+
                       | top MLP |   <- small, data-parallel
                       +---------+
                            |
                         p(click)

1.2 Why it is hard to train efficiently

Meta's study "Understanding Training Efficiency of Deep Learning Recommendation Models at Scale" [12] characterized production DLRM training. Its main points:

  • Embedding operators are memory-bound and dominated by communication.
  • The large embedding tables and the varied sparse-feature profiles across models make one hardware configuration a poor fit for all models.
  • In the CPU parameter-server era, trainers spent much of each step waiting on embedding pulls and pushes.

The paper argued for co-designing hardware and software around embedding traffic. That argument led to the Zion and ZionEX GPU platforms [3].

Two kinds of parallelism are the standard solution:

  • Model parallelism for embeddings. Tables, or slices of them, are placed on different devices. Each device does the lookups for the IDs it owns.
  • Data parallelism for the dense MLPs. The network is replicated and gradients are all-reduced.

The two worlds meet at an all-to-all collective. In the forward pass it moves pooled embeddings from the devices that own the tables to the devices that own the samples. In the backward pass it moves the gradients the other way.

 forward:  sample-sharded batch -> [input dist: all-to-all of IDs]
           -> table-sharded lookup + pooling
           -> [output dist: all-to-all of pooled embeddings]
           -> data-parallel interaction + MLP on each GPU
 backward: MLP grads -> all-reduce (dense)
           pooled-emb grads -> all-to-all back to owners
           -> fused sparse optimizer update in place on owner GPU

2. Meta: Neo, ZionEX, TorchRec and FBGEMM

2.1 Problem

Before 2020, Meta trained recommendation models asynchronously on CPU clusters with parameter servers. That approach scaled in capacity, but it had two drawbacks. Asynchrony hurt model quality and reproducibility. Throughput was also limited by network traffic to the parameter servers [12]. The goal of Neo/ZionEX [3] was synchronous, GPU-based training of models with trillions of parameters.

2.2 Architecture

ZionEX hardware [3]:

  • Each node has 8 GPUs (A100-class in the paper) connected internally by NVLink.
  • Each node also has a dedicated RDMA over Converged Ethernet (RoCE) scale-out network: several high-bandwidth NICs per node, so every GPU has its own path for inter-node all-to-all traffic.
  • The paper's evaluation covers clusters of up to 16 nodes (128 GPUs).
  • The emphasis is on all-to-all bandwidth, because embedding exchange dominates the step time.

Neo software [3] introduced 4D parallelism for embeddings, chosen per table:

Sharding scheme What is split When it fits
Table-wise (TW) Whole tables placed on different GPUs Many small/medium tables; low comm
Row-wise (RW) Rows of one table split across GPUs Huge tables beyond one GPU's HBM
Column-wise (CW) Embedding dimension split across GPUs Wide tables; balances load per GPU
Data-parallel (DP) Table replicated everywhere Tiny tables; avoids all-to-all entirely

Neo also contributed the following [3]:

  • Hybrid kernel fusion. All tables on a device are batched into one fused kernel, and the sparse optimizer update is fused into the backward pass, so no full gradient tensor is ever materialized.
  • A sharding planner that balances compute, memory and communication cost across devices.
  • Software-managed caching of embedding rows across HBM, host DRAM and UVM.
  • Quantized collectives. Embedding all-to-all traffic is sent in reduced precision (FP16/BF16) to save network bandwidth, while model quality is preserved.

The paper reports training models of up to 12 trillion parameters. It also reports roughly order-of-magnitude (approximately up to 40x, per the paper's headline claim) time-to-solution speedups over Meta's earlier CPU-based asynchronous training [3].

2.3 TorchRec and FBGEMM_GPU

TorchRec [2][13] is the open-source productionization of these ideas as a PyTorch domain library. According to its README [13], it provides:

  • Sharders for data-parallel, table-wise, row-wise, table-wise-row-wise, column-wise and table-wise-column-wise sharding.
  • A planner that automatically produces an optimized sharding plan.
  • RecSys kernels from FBGEMM [14].
  • A train pipeline that overlaps data loading, host-to-device copies, input distribution (all-to-all of IDs) and forward/backward compute.
  • Reduced-precision training and inference, with C++ inference export.

The project states that TorchRec "powers many production RecSys models at Meta." Its citation abstract describes how Meta moved from CPU asynchronous training to accelerator-based full-sync training with it [13]. The README also links later work on "Toward 100TB model with Embedding Offloading" [13], which keeps hot rows in HBM and offloads cold rows to host or SSD tiers.

FBGEMM_GPU supplies the kernels [14]. Its table-batched embedding (TBE) operator runs many embedding bags in one launch, and it also supports quantized embeddings and data-layout transforms. Two ideas carry over to any design here:

  1. Table batching and fused optimizers. Thousands of small kernel launches become one. The optimizer state (for example rowwise Adagrad) is updated in the same pass as the backward lookup.
  2. Pipelining across stages. The ID all-to-all for batch i+1 overlaps with the dense compute for batch i.
TorchRec TrainPipelineSparseDist (conceptual)
 time ->
 batch i   : [H2D copy][ID a2a][lookup][emb a2a][fwd/bwd MLP][emb grad a2a+update]
 batch i+1 :           [H2D copy][ID a2a]......(overlapped with batch i compute)
 batch i+2 :                     [H2D copy]....

2.4 Lessons

  • Synchronous training at scale is achievable. It is preferable for reproducibility, but it needs dedicated all-to-all bandwidth [3].
  • Use a heterogeneous sharding plan. No single scheme is best. The planner choosing per table (TW for most tables, RW for the huge ones, DP for the tiny ones) is where much of the performance comes from [3][13].
  • Kernel fusion and fused optimizers avoid materializing dense gradients for sparse tables.

3. ByteDance Monolith: Collisionless Tables and Real-Time Training

3.1 Problem

ByteDance's feed products (Douyin/TikTok and others) have three properties that clash with standard TensorFlow training:

  • The ID space is non-stationary and unbounded.
  • Feature popularity is long-tailed.
  • Concept drift happens within hours.

TensorFlow's built-in variables are fixed-size dense tensors. Fitting unbounded IDs into them means hashing, and hashing collisions degrade quality. Daily batch retraining is also too slow to keep up with drift [5][15].

3.2 Collisionless embedding table

Monolith [5] replaces fixed tf.Variable tables with a key-value hash table on the parameter servers, built on Cuckoo hashing. Cuckoo hashing uses two hash functions and two arrays. An insert that hits an occupied slot evicts the occupant to its other location, and this repeats until every key has a slot. The result is guaranteed O(1) lookup and no collisions between distinct IDs [5]. The repository describes the goal directly: "each ID feature gets its own unique representation" [15].

Unbounded growth is controlled with two mechanisms [5]:

  • Frequency filtering (admission). An ID gets an embedding only after it has appeared some threshold number of times. A probabilistic filter keeps the memory needed to count rare IDs low. Long-tail IDs seen once or twice add memory cost without adding quality.
  • Expirable embeddings (eviction). Each feature has an expiry time. IDs that go inactive, such as stale users or deleted videos, are evicted.

3.3 Real-time (online) training pipeline

 user actions (clicks, plays, ...) ---> Kafka (action log)
 serving features ------------------>  Kafka (feature log)
                                           |
                                    Flink online joiner
                     (join by request key, in-memory cache + on-disk KV
                      for late actions; negative sampling)
                                           |
                     +---------------------+-------------------+
                     |                                         |
           Kafka (training examples)                   HDFS (batch dumps)
                     |                                         |
            online training workers  <--- same model --->  batch training
                     |
            training parameter servers (Cuckoo hash tables)
                     |  periodic sync: sparse incremental (minutes), dense (slower)
                     v
            serving parameter servers -> online serving

How the loop works, per the paper [5]:

  1. One framework, two modes. Batch training runs on historical HDFS data to bootstrap a model. Online training then consumes the streaming Kafka example queue indefinitely.
  2. Online joiner. A Flink job joins user actions with the features logged at serving time. Features are cached because the corresponding action can arrive minutes later. Negative sampling reduces the share of negatives, and a log-odds correction at serving time compensates for the changed label distribution.
  3. Parameter synchronization. Moving terabytes of parameters to serving every minute is impractical. Monolith therefore makes the update asymmetric:
    • Sparse parameters are synced incrementally, sending only the IDs that changed since the last sync, at minute-level intervals.
    • Dense parameters change slowly under momentum-style optimizers, so they are synced much less often (the paper describes a daily-scale cadence).
  4. Fault tolerance. The paper studies how snapshot frequency affects model quality. It concludes that daily snapshots of parameter servers lose very little quality on PS failure, because one shard holds only a small fraction of IDs and the model recovers quickly with online training. Infrequent snapshots save large amounts of compute and I/O [5].

3.4 Results and lessons

The Monolith paper reports [5]:

  • Collisionless embeddings beat hashed (colliding) baselines on both MovieLens-style public data and internal production data.
  • Shorter parameter-sync intervals (moving from hours toward ~30 minutes in their experiments) give consistently higher online AUC. Real-time training measurably beats batch training for ads.

Lessons:

  • Freshness is a model-quality feature, not only an operations concern.
  • The asymmetric sync of sparse and dense parameters is the key trick that makes minute-level updates affordable.
  • Admission and eviction policies matter as much as the table data structure.

The Monolith GitHub repository is now archived and read-only. It is built on TensorFlow with Bazel [15]. The same ideas carried over to BytePlus's commercial recommendation offering.

4. Parameter-Server Lineage: XDL, DeepRec, PERSIA, HET, OpenEmbedding, TFRA

4.1 Alibaba XDL and DeepRec

XDL (X-DeepLearning) [16] is Alibaba Mama's framework for high-dimensional sparse data in advertising, recommendation and search. It came with:

  • the Blaze serving engine,
  • the TDM (tree-based deep matching) retrieval engine.

The XDL paper (DLP-KDD 2019) describes a "bridge" design. XDL handles the high-dimensional sparse part on a distributed parameter server, and the dense sub-network runs on a pluggable backend (TensorFlow/MXNet).

Version 1.2 added automatic global parameter allocation, request merging, and removal of PS compute, storage and communication hotspots. It reports 50–100% gains for large-batch, low-concurrency workloads [16]. Its streaming-training features are the same set that later frameworks standardized on [16]:

  • feature admission,
  • feature eviction,
  • incremental model export,
  • feature frequency statistics.

DeepRec [10] is Alibaba's successor: a heavily modified TensorFlow. Its features include:

  • EmbeddingVariable, a dynamic hash-backed embedding, in dynamic-dimension, adaptive and multi-hash variants, plus group embedding.
  • Multi-tier hybrid embedding storage across HBM, DRAM, PMem and SSD.
  • Delta (incremental) checkpoint loading and export.
  • Two training modes:
    • Asynchronous PS training over gRPC+Seastar, FuseRecv and StarServer.
    • Synchronous collective training via HybridBackend and NVIDIA's Sparse Operation Kit.
  • Graph and runtime optimizations: SmartStage pipelining, AutoGraphFusion, MicroBatch, a graph-aware memory allocator, and CUDA Graph support.

DeepRec claims support for "trillion samples and over ten trillion parameters" [10].

4.2 Kuaishou PERSIA: hybrid synchronous/asynchronous training

Problem. Fully synchronous training is slow, because embedding communication is large. Fully asynchronous training hurts the accuracy of the dense network. PERSIA [4][17] (Kuaishou with ETH Zurich, KDD 2022) observes that the two parts behave differently:

  • The embedding layer is huge, but each step touches very few rows. Staleness on sparse rows is therefore rare and harmless.
  • The dense network is small, but every step updates all of it, so staleness there does hurt.

Design. PERSIA trains the embeddings asynchronously and the dense NN synchronously (all-reduce, via the Bagua communication library). The implementation is in Rust and Python. Its components:

   data loaders --> embedding workers <--> embedding parameter servers (CPU, huge)
                          |   (async: get/put embeddings, stale-tolerant)
                          v
                  NN workers (GPU) -- sync all-reduce of dense grads (Bagua)

Scale. PERSIA reports training models of up to 100 trillion parameters, described at the time as the largest recommendation model reported [17]. It ran in production at Kuaishou for applications with roughly hundreds of millions of daily active users. The paper reports several-fold throughput gains (approximately up to 7x) over contemporary systems at similar accuracy [4]. The project README now notes that PERSIA is unmaintained after a reorganization [17].

Lesson. Matching the consistency model to each parameter's access pattern gives most of the speed of asynchrony without most of its accuracy cost. TFRA uses the same idea (section 4.4).

4.3 HET: cache-enabled embedding training

HET [18] (Peking University, VLDB 2022) targets the PS communication bottleneck by keeping an embedding cache on each worker. Because accesses are skewed, hot embeddings are cached locally. A bounded-staleness consistency protocol, with per-embedding clocks, decides when a cached copy must be refreshed or written back. This cuts PS traffic sharply while keeping convergence close to synchronous training. The design point to note is that caching combined with explicit staleness bounds is a principled middle ground between fully synchronous and fully asynchronous training.

4.4 TensorFlow Recommenders-Addons (TFRA)

TFRA [19] is the SIG-Recommenders project that adds a trainable dynamic embedding to TensorFlow. It is a key-value structure with no hash conflicts, and it works with native TF optimizers, initializers, checkpoints and SavedModel. Its storage backends are pluggable:

  • cuckoohash_map (from CMU) on CPU,
  • NVIDIA HierarchicalKV on GPU,
  • Redis, for distributed inference.

TFRA also supports half-synchronous training with Horovod: synchronous for dense weights, asynchronous for sparse weights. Listed contributors and supporters include Tencent, Alibaba, VIP.com and BOSS Zhipin, plus the NVIDIA Merlin team [19].

4.5 4Paradigm OpenEmbedding

OpenEmbedding [20] keeps embedding layers on a parameter server and trains dense layers with Horovod. It exports standalone SavedModels for TF Serving. It also has an experimental persistent-memory (PMem) PS, where PMem acts as a lightweight checkpointing mechanism (see the associated ICDE 2023 paper). It reports 3–8x speedups over pure all-reduce (Horovod) on a single 8-GPU machine for sparse models [20].

5. NVIDIA HugeCTR, Merlin and HierarchicalKV

5.1 Problem

The goal is to keep the whole training loop on GPUs: data reading, embedding lookup, communication and dense compute. The system should still handle tables larger than aggregate HBM, and serve them with low latency [6][21].

5.2 Training architecture

HugeCTR [6][21] is a CUDA/C++ framework with a Python front end. Its embedding layers are model-parallel across GPUs and nodes, while the dense model is data-parallel. Inter-node communication uses NCCL with GPUDirect RDMA [21]. Its main embedding types:

  • LocalizedSlotSparseEmbeddingHash. Each feature slot lives on one GPU, with no global reduction. This suits embeddings that fit on a single GPU [21].
  • DistributedSlotSparseEmbeddingHash. Keys are spread across GPUs regardless of slot, so a single slot can span devices. This suits tables larger than one GPU at the cost of more communication [21].
  • Hybrid embedding (described in the RecSys 2022 paper [6]). Hot categories are replicated data-parallel and cold categories are model-parallel. Frequent IDs then need no all-to-all, which was a key optimization in NVIDIA's MLPerf DLRM submissions.

Other features [21]:

  • Mixed precision, with FP16 used on embeddings to save bandwidth and loss scaling to prevent underflow.
  • Learning-rate warmup and decay schedules.
  • HDFS model I/O.
  • A hugectr2onnx converter.

Two nodes with 8x A100 80 GB each can train models of up to about 1 TB entirely in GPU memory [21].

For TensorFlow users, NVIDIA ships the Sparse Operation Kit (SOK), a model-parallel GPU embedding layer [21]. Alibaba DeepRec uses SOK for its synchronous mode [10].

5.3 Beyond HBM: ETC, HPS and HierarchicalKV

  • Embedding Training Cache (ETC) [6] trains models larger than HBM by keeping a working set in GPU memory. The full table lives in host or SSD storage, and the working set is swapped in per data pass.

  • Hierarchical Parameter Server (HPS) [6] is the inference counterpart:

     request -> GPU embedding cache (hot, HBM)
         -> miss -> CPU-memory volatile DB (e.g., Redis cluster / hash maps)
         -> miss -> persistent DB (e.g., RocksDB on SSD)
 online-training updates streamed (e.g., via Kafka) into the tiers

    HPS and the training cache are listed as deprecated as of v25.03 in the current HugeCTR repository [21]. NVIDIA's investment has moved toward the general-purpose library below and toward framework plugins.

  • HierarchicalKV (HKV) [22] is a header-only GPU hash table:

    • Keys always reside in HBM. Values can spill to host memory.
    • Buckets are locally ordered (128 slots by default), and the default maximum load factor is 0.5 before rehash.
    • Eviction happens only when a bucket is full, using a per-key 64-bit score. Built-in policies: LRU (device clock), LFU, EpochLRU, EpochLFU, or fully custom scores.

    HKV published benchmarks on a single A100 80 GB [22]:

    Configuration insert_or_assign (B KV/s) find (B KV/s)
    Pure HBM, dim 8, 128M keys, load 0.5 ~1.09 ~2.47
    Pure HBM, dim 64, 64M keys, load 0.5 ~0.83 ~1.98
    HBM+host, dim 64, 512M keys (32 GB HBM + 96 GB host) ~0.049 ~0.069

    The pointer-returning find* variant stays at about 3.5–4 billion KV/s even in hybrid mode, because it avoids copying values [22]. HKV is the GPU backend for TFRA's dynamic embedding [19]. It is effectively the GPU counterpart of Monolith's CPU Cuckoo tables.

5.4 Lessons

  • Replicate the hot head, shard the long tail. Hybrid embedding exploits frequency skew to remove most all-to-all traffic for the most common IDs [6].
  • Put score-based eviction inside the hash table (HKV), so that admission and eviction policy is a pluggable function rather than a separate service [22].
  • Use a tiered store with a GPU cache for inference. Skew makes high hit rates possible, but cache consistency with online training must be designed in from the start [6].

6. Continual / Incremental Training and Checkpointing

6.1 Patterns

Across Monolith, XDL, DeepRec, TFRA and HugeCTR the same continual-training pattern recurs:

  stream (Kafka) -> joiner (Flink/Storm-like) -> online trainer
       |                                            |
       |                          incremental export (delta of touched IDs)
       v                                            v
  offline log (HDFS) -> periodic full retrain   serving PS / embedding cache
                         (bootstrap / recovery)

Its components:

  • Warm start plus streaming. A batch model trained on history is the starting point, and streaming updates follow.
  • Delta export. Only rows touched since the last export are shipped. Dense weights are shipped less often [5][10][16].
  • Admission and eviction keep table size bounded as the ID space churns [5][16][22].
  • Sampling corrections (for example log-odds correction under negative downsampling) keep calibrated scores consistent across training and serving [5].

6.2 Check-N-Run: checkpointing trillion-parameter tables

Training jobs on terabyte-scale models must checkpoint often to survive failures, but full checkpoints are huge. Meta's Check-N-Run [9] (NSDI 2022) uses two techniques:

  1. Differential checkpointing. In any interval only a small fraction of embedding rows change, so only the modified rows are written. This is tracked per row.
  2. Checkpoint quantization. Rows are written in reduced precision (for example 4-bit or 8-bit with adaptive schemes). The paper shows this is acceptable for recovery when applied with care, for example by limiting how many consecutive quantized restores are allowed.

The paper reports roughly 6–17x reductions in checkpoint write bandwidth and roughly 2.5–8x reductions in storage capacity (approximate, from the paper's abstract) with no meaningful accuracy loss [9]. The idea is the same as Monolith's incremental sparse sync: write only what changed, and write it compactly.

7. Hashing Tricks and Embedding Compression

When a table cannot hold one row per ID, or when memory, bandwidth or serving cost matters more than the last fraction of a percent of quality, compression techniques apply. They form a spectrum from "fewer rows" to "no table at all".

7.1 The hashing trick

Weinberger et al. [7] introduced feature hashing: map a huge or unbounded feature space into a fixed number of buckets with a hash function, and use a sign hash to make inner products unbiased. Applied to embeddings, an ID is mapped to row = h(id) mod M. This is simple and stateless and handles unseen IDs, but distinct IDs collide. Monolith's motivation was precisely that collisions measurably hurt ranking quality at ByteDance scale [5].

Hash embeddings [23] (Svenstrup et al., NeurIPS 2017) reduce the damage from collisions:

  • Each token picks k vectors from a shared pool using k hash functions.
  • It combines them with learned per-token importance weights.
  • Two colliding tokens are then unlikely to share the same combination.

7.2 Compositional embeddings: the QR trick

Shi et al. [8] (Meta, KDD 2020) proposed compositional embeddings using complementary partitions. In the quotient-remainder (QR) case, an ID x uses two smaller tables:

 q = x // m      -> row in quotient table   (size ceil(|S|/m) x d)
 r = x  % m      -> row in remainder table  (size m x d)
 emb(x) = combine(Wq[q], Wr[r])     combine in {multiply, add, concat}

Every ID still gets a unique embedding, because the pair (q, r) is unique. Memory, however, drops from |S| x d to about (|S|/m + m) x d. With m near sqrt(|S|) this is O(sqrt(|S|)) rows. The paper generalizes the idea to multiple complementary partitions and to path-based composition. It shows large memory reductions on Criteo-style DLRM with small accuracy loss [8]. The open-source DLRM cites this work as the "reduce the number of vectors" approach [11].

7.3 Mixed-dimension embeddings

Ginart et al. [24] observe that popular IDs need more capacity than rare ones. They assign embedding dimensions in proportion to frequency (popularity), with blocks of rows at different widths, and project each block to a common dimension. This is the "reduce vector dimensions" approach cited by DLRM [11]. In practice it composes well with QR, with low-precision storage, and with frequency admission.

7.4 TT-Rec: tensor-train decomposition

TT-Rec [25][26] (Meta, MLSys 2021) factorizes each large table into a sequence of small Tensor-Train cores. The table shape is factored as products of p_shapes x q_shapes with TT ranks. Only the requested rows are reconstructed on the fly. According to the FBTT-Embedding repository [26]:

  • It is a drop-in replacement for EmbeddingBag, with a fused-backward kernel for SGD and Adagrad.
  • It achieves up to 100x smaller models on Meta's open-source DLRM with the same model quality, and up to 10,000x lower runtime memory per table.
  • A 32-way set-associative LFU software cache keeps uncompressed hot rows, so the frequent IDs skip TT reconstruction.

This is the same skew-exploiting pattern as hybrid embedding and HKV: compress the long tail, and keep the head in full precision.

7.5 Hashing-based "shared memory" compression (ROBE-style)

Random-offset block embedding methods (ROBE, MLSys 2022) push hashing further. All tables share one small parameter array, and each embedding is read as a contiguous block at a hashed offset. That keeps memory access cache-friendly while allowing extreme compression ratios. These methods are surveyed widely, but the primary paper could not be fetched for this chapter, so specific ratios are omitted here.

7.6 Deep Hash Embedding: no table at all

Google's DHE [27] (KDD 2021) removes the table entirely. Each ID is encoded by many (on the order of 1,000) dense hash functions into a real-valued vector. A deep MLP then decodes that vector into an embedding. The parameter count is independent of the vocabulary, every ID gets a unique code, and unseen IDs are handled naturally. The cost moves from memory to compute, which makes DHE attractive on compute-rich, memory-poor accelerators. The trade-off is that serving cost per lookup rises.

7.7 Comparison

Technique Unique per ID? Memory scaling Extra compute Handles new IDs Typical use
Full table (dense array) Yes (if pre-indexed) O(N d) None Needs re-indexing Small/stable vocabularies
Dynamic hash table (Monolith Cuckoo, HKV, TFRA, DeepRec EV) Yes O(active N d) Hashing Yes, with admission Streaming, open vocab
Hashing trick [7] No (collisions) O(M d), M fixed Hash Yes Cheap baseline, long tail
Hash embeddings [23] Mostly O(B d + N k) k lookups + weights Yes NLP / long-tail IDs
QR compositional [8] Yes O((N/m + m) d) 2 lookups + op Within range Huge ID tables
Mixed dimension [24] Yes Sum over blocks of N_i d_i Projection Needs re-indexing Skewed popularity
TT-Rec [25][26] Yes O(sum of core sizes) TT reconstruct Within shape 10–100x compression
ROBE-style shared array No (shared) O(M), one array Hash + block read Yes Extreme compression
DHE [27] Yes O(MLP params) Deep MLP per ID Yes Memory-bound accelerators
Low-precision rows (FP16/INT8/INT4) Yes O(N d bits) Dequantize n/a Serving, checkpoints [9]

8. Hardware Direction: Accelerating Sparse Lookups

Google's TPU v4 [28] includes SparseCores. These are dataflow processors dedicated to embedding lookups and the related all-to-all traffic. The paper reports that they accelerate embedding-heavy models by about 5–7x while using only about 5% of die area and power (approximate figures from the TPU v4 paper's abstract) [28]. Together with ZionEX's dedicated RoCE fabric [3], this shows the industry treating embedding traffic as a first-class hardware concern rather than a software afterthought.

Newer generative recommenders shift the balance. Meta's HSTU work [29] (ICML 2024) reports sequential transduction models of up to 1.5 trillion parameters, with much more dense compute per example (long user sequences and attention over jagged tensors). The embedding tables are still huge, but these models move ranking training closer to LLM training in compute intensity. The TorchRec and FBGEMM stack (jagged tensors, sharded embeddings, offloading [13]) therefore has to serve both regimes at once. See Chapter 06 for the modeling side.

10. Key Takeaways for System Designers

  1. Design around the embeddings. For DLRM-style models, the capacity, bandwidth and communication of embeddings set the cost. Size the cluster by table bytes and all-to-all bandwidth first, and by FLOPs second [3][12].
  2. Use model parallelism for sparse parameters and data parallelism for dense parameters. Pick the sharding scheme per table: table-wise, row-wise, column-wise or replicated. Use a cost-model planner rather than hand placement [3][13].
  3. Exploit skew everywhere. Replicate or cache the hot head (hybrid embedding, HET caches, TT-Rec LFU cache, HPS GPU cache) and shard, compress or offload the tail [6][18][26].
  4. Use dynamic hash tables when the vocabulary is open. Collision-free embeddings with frequency admission and time- or score-based eviction (Monolith, HKV, TFRA, DeepRec) beat fixed hashing in quality for fast-churning ID spaces [5][19][22].
  5. Match consistency to access pattern. Sparse rows tolerate staleness, and dense weights do not. Hybrid sync/async (PERSIA, TFRA half-sync) or bounded staleness (HET) captures most of the throughput of asynchrony [4][18][19].
  6. Freshness pays. Streaming training plus incremental sync of sparse parameters at minute-level, with dense weights synced less often, gives measurable AUC gains in production [5].
  7. Make everything incremental. Delta exports, delta checkpoints and quantized checkpoints keep trillion-parameter continual training affordable and recoverable [5][9][10].
  8. Fuse kernels and pipeline aggressively. Table-batched lookups, fused sparse optimizers, and overlap of input all-to-all with compute are table stakes [13][14].
  9. Compression is a spectrum. Choose by constraint:
    • QR or mixed dimensions for memory with near-zero quality loss [8][24],
    • TT-Rec for 10–100x [26],
    • DHE when memory is scarce and compute is cheap [27],
    • quantization for serving and checkpoints [9].
  10. Co-design hardware. Dedicated scale-out networks (ZionEX) and on-chip sparse engines (TPU SparseCore) show that embedding traffic justifies specialized silicon and fabric [3][28].

10. Online Serving and Inference: Latency Budgets, Model Servers, Caches and Cascades

A recommender is only as good as what it can compute inside one request. Every system in this atlas, from a two-tower retriever to a trillion-parameter generative recommender, eventually has to answer one question within a few hundred milliseconds: given this viewer, right now, which K items do we return? This chapter covers the serving side of that question. It looks at how production systems split a latency budget across stages, how they run model inference on CPUs, GPUs and custom accelerators, how they fan out feature and embedding fetches, what they cache, and how they shrink models through cascades, distillation, quantization and early exit.

The chapter builds on primary sources: open-source production code (X/Twitter's the-algorithm and xAI's x-algorithm repositories, Meta's generative-recommenders, TorchRec, FBGEMM), official documentation (Vespa, Triton Inference Server, NVIDIA Merlin HugeCTR), and engineering papers and posts (DeepRecSys, Earlybird, Instagram Explore, Meta Andromeda, Pinterest GPU inference).

Source note. In this research pass, outbound access was limited to GitHub-hosted content. Facts drawn from repositories and documentation were read in full. Sections on Meta (Instagram Explore, Andromeda) and Pinterest summarize their published engineering posts. Those posts could not be re-fetched here, so their numbers are marked approximate and should be checked against the linked originals before anyone quotes them.

10.1 The shape of the problem: funnels and latency budgets

Almost every large recommender shares the same request-time skeleton, popularized by YouTube's candidate-generation-then-ranking design [33]. A cheap stage looks at a huge corpus. Then progressively more expensive stages look at progressively fewer items:

 corpus (10^6 - 10^10 items)
   |
   |  RETRIEVAL / candidate generation   ANN, inverted index, graph walks, in-mem
   v                                     follow-graph stores; cost ~O(log N) per source
 10^3 - 10^4 candidates
   |
   |  FEATURE HYDRATION                  fan-out to feature stores, embedding servers,
   v                                     counters; often the latency long pole
   |
   |  LIGHT / EARLY-STAGE RANKING        LR, GBDT, two-tower dot product, distilled nets
   v
 10^2 - 10^3 candidates
   |
   |  HEAVY RANKING                      large MTML DNN / transformer, GPU or accelerator
   v
 10^1 - 10^2 candidates
   |
   |  RE-RANKING / POLICY                diversity (DPP, author decay), filters, ads mix
   v
 response (page of K items)

X's For You timeline makes the funnel explicit. Home Mixer fetches candidates from several sources, hydrates "the ~6000 features needed for ranking", scores them with an ML model, and then applies filters and heuristics such as author diversity, in-network/out-of-network balance, feedback fatigue, dedup and visibility filtering. Only after that does it mix in ads and who-to-follow modules [2]. xAI's 2026 release of the X algorithm keeps the same skeleton. Its parts are query hydration, parallel candidate sources (Thunder in-network, Phoenix retrieval, SimClusters, popular posts), candidate hydration, pre-scoring filters, Phoenix scoring, a weighted value model, DPP re-ranking (vm-ranker), top-K selection and post-selection visibility filters [11].

Why a cascade at all? The Vespa documentation puts the economics plainly: "A good quality ranking expression will for most applications consume too much CPU to be runnable on all retrieved or matched documents within the latency budget/SLA." The engineering job therefore becomes finding "a first-phase function, which correlates sufficiently well with the second-phase function" [13]. Each stage is a cheaper approximation of the next, and the rerank counts at the stage boundaries are the main knobs for latency and cost.

A typical budget breakdown, written here as a design heuristic rather than a number from any one source, looks like this:

Stage Typical share of p99 budget Dominant cost
Query/user hydration 5-15% KV lookups, user sequence fetch
Candidate generation (parallel) 15-25% ANN / index traversal, slowest source
Feature hydration 20-35% fan-out RPCs, tail latency of slowest shard
Light ranking 5-10% CPU, simple models over many items
Heavy ranking 20-35% GPU/accelerator compute, batching delay
Re-rank, filters, mixing 5-10% rule evaluation, DPP, ads auction

Two structural lessons follow from production systems:

  1. Parallelize sources and fetches, then bound the tail. In X's Product Mixer framework, Candidate Pipelines run under Mixer/Recommendation Pipelines, and stages run "in parallel where it can" [8][11]. The response time is set by the slowest parallel branch, so each branch needs its own timeout and a fallback. Home Mixer keeps a reverse-chronological "backup ... pipeline in case Scored Tweets fails" [2].
  2. Side effects belong off the critical path. xAI's Home Mixer records served posts, refreshes the post cache and logs client and ad events "after the response is sent" [11].

10.2 X / Twitter: an open-source reference serving stack

X has published more of its serving stack than any other large company [10]: the 2023 the-algorithm release and the 2025-2026 x-algorithm (xAI) release. That makes it the best public case study for end-to-end serving.

10.2.1 Architecture (2023 Twitter stack)

                       +-------------------------------+
  client request ----> | Home Mixer (Product Mixer,     |
                       | Scala)                         |
                       +---+-----------+-----------+---+
                           |           |           |
              in-network   |   OON     |  graph     |  follow recs
           +---------------+  +--------+------+  +--+------------------+
           | Earlybird     |  | CR-Mixer /    |  | UTEG (GraphJet,     |
           | search index  |  | tweet-mixer   |  | in-memory graph)    |
           | + LR light    |  | + light rank  |  | FRS                 |
           |   ranker      |  | + result cache|  |                     |
           +-------+-------+  +-------+-------+  +----------+----------+
                   \                  |                    /
                    v                 v                   v
              +-------------------------------------------------+
              | Feature hydration (~6000 features): user-signal |
              | service, graph-feature-service, real-graph,     |
              | representation-manager (SimClusters/TwHIN emb.) |
              +--------------------------+----------------------+
                                         v
              +-------------------------------------------------+
              | Heavy ranker (parallel MaskNet, multi-task)     |
              | served by Navi (Rust; TF / ONNX runtimes)       |
              +--------------------------+----------------------+
                                         v
              filters / heuristics / visibility / ads + WTF mixing

Candidate sources. Earlybird, a Lucene-based real-time search system, does in-network retrieval. It supplies roughly half of For You posts [1]. The index is split into a realtime cluster (about the last 7 days of public tweets), a protected cluster, and an archive cluster. Each cluster is partitioned into a sharded, replicated inverted index with a single-writer/multi-reader design. Earlybird "roots" fan requests out to partitions and merge the responses [6]. Out-of-network candidates come through CR-Mixer, which "fetches source signals externally ... calls external candidate generation services, and caches results", then applies filters and a light ranking step [7]. A second out-of-network source is the in-memory UTEG graph built on GraphJet [1].

Light ranking at the index. The Earlybird light ranker is a logistic regression model, "a simplified version of the heavy ranker which can run on a greater amount of tweets". It runs inside the search index itself and uses static features computed at ingestion (has URL, is reply, text-quality score, tweepcred) plus real-time engagement counters pushed by a signal ingester [5]. This is an example of compute pushed to the data, the same idea as Vespa's content-node first phase (Section 10.5). The README also admits the model "was last trained several years ago" and was due to be replaced [5], a reminder that cascade stages tend to rot when nobody owns them.

Heavy ranking. The Recap heavy ranker is a parallel MaskNet that outputs about ten engagement probabilities (fav, retweet, reply, good click, negative feedback, report and others). They are combined by a configurable weighted sum. The April 2023 weights included reply-engaged-by-author 75.0, report -369.0 and fav 0.5. The weights were first set "so that, on average, each weighted engagement probability contributes a near-equal amount to the score" [9][28].

10.2.2 Navi: a minimalist Rust model server

Twitter replaced generic model serving for this path with Navi, "a high-performance, versatile machine learning serving server implemented in Rust". It speaks the TensorFlow Serving gRPC API and has pluggable runtimes: TensorFlow (most complete), ONNX Runtime (used for home recommendation with a proprietary BatchPredictRequest Thrift input) and experimental PyTorch [3]. Its CLI defaults show the core batching levers of any recsys model server [4]:

Navi flag Default Meaning
max_batch_size 16 max requests coalesced into one batch
batch_time_out_millis 2 max wait to accumulate a batch
batch_drop_millis 90 threshold to start dropping batches under stress
model_check_interval_secs 300 polling for new model versions
onnx_gpu_ep (none) choose CUDA or TensorRT execution provider
max_warmup_records - warm-up records before serving (TF)

Lessons from Navi. (a) A server that does fewer things can be much faster. Navi trades features for performance [3]. (b) Load shedding is a first-class setting. Dropping a batch that is already 90 ms late beats letting a queue build. (c) Feature transformation from the wire format (dr_transform, segdense) lives inside the server, so the client ships raw records once [3]. (d) Hot model reloading by version directory gives continuous deployment without restarts [3].

10.2.3 xAI x-algorithm (2026): transformer ranking built to be cacheable

The 2026 release replaces MaskNet with Phoenix, a transformer used both as a two-tower retriever and as the ranker. It is trained in JAX and served by "a Rust gRPC serving engine" [11][12]. Several serving-driven design decisions stand out:

  • Candidate isolation. In the ranking transformer, "candidates cannot attend to each other", only to the user and history tokens. The attention mask is full bidirectional over user+history, and diagonal-only among candidates. The stated reason is serving: "the score for a post doesn't depend on which other posts are in the batch, making scores consistent and cacheable" [11][12]. It also means the user/history prefix can be computed once and shared by every candidate in the request. This is the same amortization idea as Meta's M-FALCON (Section 10.6).
  • Batch-invariant serving. Together with a retrieval index baked "inside the checkpoint" (the trainer runs the candidate tower over the corpus at every checkpoint save), "a candidate's score depends only on the user and that candidate" [12]. Batch invariance makes caching, A/B debugging and replay possible.
  • Hash-based embeddings plus semantic IDs. Multiple hash functions per entity mean "no dictionary service", so no ID-to-row lookup RPC sits on the serving path. Semantic IDs (residual-quantized codes, 6 levels x 256 codes) give new posts usable representations immediately [11][12].
  • Multi-action outputs plus a separate value model. Phoenix outputs [B, num_candidates, num_actions] plus dwell regression. RankingScorer computes sum(weight_i * P(action_i)), then applies author-diversity decay, an out-of-network discount and a new-author boost. vm-ranker reorders by a determinantal point process over embeddings [11].
  • Hardware. The open-source quickstart detects A100/H100/H200/GB200/GB300 and ships Hopper- and Blackwell-tuned attention kernels [12]. The ranker is a GPU workload.

10.3 Meta: Instagram Explore and the Andromeda ads retrieval engine

10.3.1 Instagram Explore (2023 post)

Meta's "Scaling the Instagram Explore recommendations system" (2023) describes a four-stage funnel: retrieval, first-stage (early) ranking, second-stage (late) ranking, and final re-ranking [31]. As summarized from the post (approximate; check the original):

  sources: two-tower retrieval, user-interaction histories, heuristics
            |   (item embeddings precomputed offline, ANN at request time)
            v
  first-stage ranking: lightweight two-tower-style model, trained partly to
            |          reproduce the late-stage ranker's output (distillation)
            v
  second-stage ranking: multi-task multi-label (MTML) DNN predicting many
            |           engagement events
            v
  value model: weighted combination of MTML outputs (weights tuned online)
            |
            v
  final re-ranking: integrity filters, diversity / business rules

Serving-relevant points in the post:

  • Two-tower retrieval lets item embeddings be computed and indexed offline, so only the user tower runs at request time.
  • The first-stage ranker is cheap because it is a two-tower-style model whose item side is precomputed. It is trained to mimic the heavier second stage, a form of ranking distillation (Section 10.8).
  • The final score is a value model: a formula over predicted event probabilities with tunable weights. Product trade-offs then become configuration changes, not retraining. The post describes tuning these weights online (Bayesian-optimization-style experimentation).
  • Caching and precomputation are used heavily, because Explore serves a very large user base under tight latency.

10.3.2 Andromeda (2024): GPU-native ads retrieval

Meta's Andromeda post (December 2024) describes a personalized ads retrieval engine built for NVIDIA Grace Hopper Superchips and Meta's MTIA accelerator [32]. As reported in the post (numbers approximate):

  • It replaces a retrieval stage that had been constrained to lightweight models with a deep neural retrieval model co-designed with the hardware. The post cites about a 10,000x increase in retrieval model complexity.
  • A hierarchical index makes retrieval sub-linear in the number of ads. The index structure is trained jointly with the model rather than being a separate offline ANN build.
  • Reported results include a recall improvement of several percent and ads-quality gains on selected segments. The post attributes this to applying deep models at a stage that previously used simple scoring.
  • The key lesson is that co-designing model, index and hardware (high-bandwidth unified CPU-GPU memory on Grace Hopper) makes "heavy" computation affordable at the stage that sees the most items. That moves the cascade's quality bottleneck upstream.

10.3.3 The Meta inference software substrate

Meta's open-source stack shows what production recsys inference is built on:

  • FBGEMM, "a low-precision, high-performance matrix-matrix multiplications and convolution library for server-side inference". It supports small batch sizes and "row-wise quantization and outlier-aware quantization", and it fuses operators to beat bandwidth limits [18]. FBGEMM_GPU adds recsys-focused GPU operators (embedding bags, table-batched embeddings). FBGEMM GenAI adds FP8 row-wise quantization [18].
  • TorchRec Inference, a C++ library for GPU inference. It captures the model with torch.fx and runs it as TorchScript in a C++ gRPC server. The reference example serves a DLRM on one GPU [17]. The README calls it "a simple reference ... not a fully scaled out solution" [17]. Production adds sharding, request batching and feature pipelines on top.
  • DeepRecSys (Harvard + Facebook, ISCA 2020) characterized eight industry-representative models (DLRM-RMC1/2/3, NCF, Wide&Deep, MT-WnD, DIN, DIEN). It built DeepRecSched, a scheduler that chooses query batch size and splits queries between CPU cores and accelerators based on query-size and arrival distributions. It reports roughly 2x latency-bounded throughput and "over 30% latency reduction" in an at-scale production datacenter [22]. The core insight is that recsys queries vary widely in size (number of candidates), so a fixed batch policy wastes either latency or throughput.

10.4 GPU inference for ranking: Pinterest and the general recipe

10.4.1 Pinterest (2022 post)

Pinterest's "GPU-accelerated ML Inference at Pinterest" (2022) describes moving ranking models from CPU to GPU serving [30]. In outline (approximate, per the original post):

  • Motivation: CPU serving costs grew roughly linearly with model size, which blocked larger ranking models (bigger embeddings, transformer-style user-sequence modules).
  • Result: GPU serving let Pinterest serve much larger models, on the order of 100x more compute per the post, at comparable or lower cost and latency.
  • Techniques the post discusses: aggressive batching of candidates per request, CUDA Graphs to cut kernel-launch overhead, merging many small embedding-table lookups into fewer larger ops, mixed precision, and moving feature preprocessing onto the GPU so the host is not the bottleneck.

10.4.2 Why recsys GPU inference is different from vision/NLP inference

Aspect Typical CV/NLP inference Recsys ranking inference
Work per request 1 input 100s-1000s of candidates x same user
Parameter mix dense weights mostly sparse embeddings (GB-TB), small dense MLP
Bottleneck FLOPs memory bandwidth (embedding gathers), launch overhead
Shared computation none user tower / user sequence shared across candidates
Batching across requests within request (candidates) and across requests
Model freshness days-weeks minutes-hours (online / streaming updates)

Recipe distilled from the sources:

  1. Batch inside the request first. Score all candidates of one request as one batch, so user-side work is computed once (Phoenix candidate isolation [12], M-FALCON [21]).
  2. Batch across requests with a bounded delay. Triton's dynamic batcher holds requests up to max_queue_delay_microseconds (e.g. 100 us) to form preferred or maximum batch sizes. Its docs advise starting from defaults and raising the delay only "until the latency budget is exceeded" [16]. Navi's 2 ms timeout and 16-request batches play the same role [4].
  3. Cut launch overhead with CUDA Graphs, fused kernels, Triton/CUTLASS custom kernels. The HSTU repository ships Triton kernels with roughly 2-2.3x speedups over PyTorch for the attention block on H100 [21].
  4. Lower the precision. HSTU-Ultra FP8 projection GEMMs give 1.13-1.25x end-to-end forward speedups over BF16 on one H100 (e.g. 9.375 ms to 7.768 ms for a 12-layer, 1024-length stack) [21]. FBGEMM provides INT8/row-wise quantization for CPU paths [18].
  5. Keep embeddings near compute. Use GPU embedding caches and hierarchical parameter servers (Section 10.7).

10.5 Search-engine-based serving: Vespa and Elasticsearch

Many companies serve recommendations from a search engine. Retrieval and first-phase ranking then run where the data lives, so candidate features never leave the shard.

10.5.1 Vespa phased ranking

Vespa splits the work into content nodes (stateful, hold documents and indexes) and a stateless container (scatter-gather, global logic) [13]:

               query (user vector, filters, terms)
                              |
                    +---------v---------+
                    | stateless         |  scatter
                    | container         |-----------+-------------+
                    +---------^---------+           |             |
                              | gather         +----v----+   +----v----+
                              |                | content |   | content |
                              |                | node 1  |   | node N  |
                              |                |         |   |         |
                              |                | match:  |   | match:  |
                              |                | WAND /  |   | WAND /  |
                              |                | ANN     |   | ANN     |
                              |                | 1st ph. |   | 1st ph. |
                              |                | (all    |   | (all    |
                              |                |  hits)  |   |  hits)  |
                              |                | 2nd ph. |   | 2nd ph. |
                              |                | (top    |   | (top    |
                              |                |  ~100)  |   |  ~100)  |
                              |                +----+----+   +----+----+
                              +---------------------+-------------+
                    global-phase (top ~100 merged, ONNX, optional GPU)
  • Retrieval. Top-k operators (weakAnd/WAND, nearest-neighbor) are sublinear. They expose only the top-k hits to ranking, and several retrievers can be combined in one query [13].
  • First phase runs on every retrieved hit on each content node and must be cheap. rank-score-drop-limit can drop hits early [13].
  • Second phase re-ranks, by default, the 100 best first-phase hits per content node. total-rerank-count caps the total across nodes. The documentation example uses bm25 + freshness for the first phase and an XGBoost model for the second [13].
  • Global phase runs in the container on the merged global top hits (default 100, rerank-count), is "optimized for inference with ONNX models", and can use a GPU via gpu-device. It supports cross-hit normalization (normalize_linear, reciprocal_rank, reciprocal_rank_fusion with k = 60 by default) [13].
  • Placement advice. Large GBDTs (XGBoost/LightGBM) and expressions that need lots of vector data should stay in the second phase on content nodes, because "moving vector data across the network is expensive". Expensive functions computed on content nodes can be passed up via match-features, so the global phase reuses them instead of recomputing [13].
  • Observability. Mutable attributes can count how often each document survives each phase (on-match, on-first-phase, on-second-phase, on-summary). This makes cascade recall measurable per document [13].

Vespa's sample apps include an album-recommendation intro and a news recommendation tutorial that uses ANN search in a shared user/item embedding space for retrieval [14]. That is the canonical two-tower-in-a-search-engine pattern.

10.5.2 Elasticsearch / OpenSearch with Learning to Rank

The OpenSource Connections LTR plugin stores features as query templates, logs feature values for training, and stores linear, XGBoost or RankLib models that rank search results [15]. In recommender settings this works as a rescoring window. The engine's own scoring retrieves candidates, and the LTR model re-scores the top window, a two-stage cascade inside the engine. Its limits compared with Vespa are coarser control over per-shard phases and no native tensor/ONNX global phase. Teams often add an external re-ranking service for deep models.

10.5.3 Earlybird as a search-engine recommender

Twitter's Earlybird (Section 10.2) belongs here too. It is an inverted-index search system whose main recsys role is UserID-based retrieval (tweets from accounts you follow). It is ranked in-index by a light model, and features stay fresh through a separate Feature Update Service [5][6]. Twitter reported reducing search indexing latency to about one second (see the blog cited in [6]). Freshness of the index directly bounds the freshness of recommendations.

10.6 Generative recommenders at serving time: HSTU and M-FALCON

Meta's Generative Recommenders work (ICML 2024) restates ranking and retrieval as sequential transduction over long user action histories, with HSTU as the encoder. Serving cost is the obvious objection, since attention over thousands of history events per candidate is expensive. The paper's answer is M-FALCON (Microbatched-Fast Attention Leveraging Cacheable OperatioNs) [21]:

 naive: for each candidate c_j:  encode([history ; c_j])     cost ~ m * O(n^2)

 M-FALCON:
   encode history once ---------------> cached keys/values (n tokens)
   split m candidates into microbatches of size b
   for each microbatch: attend [b candidates] -> cached history,
                        candidates masked from each other
                                                              cost ~ O(n^2) + m*O(n)
  • Candidates in a microbatch attend to the shared history but not to each other. The xAI Phoenix "candidate isolation" mask is the same contract (Section 10.2.3) [12].
  • The repository describes HSTU and M-FALCON as accelerating training and inference "by 10x-1000x" and reports deployment in "billion-user scale recommendation systems" [21].
  • The same repository includes a DLRM-v3 (HSTU-based) inference benchmark wired to MLPerf LoadGen. It reports H100 forward latencies of roughly 5-9 ms for 8-12-layer stacks at sequence lengths 512-1536 in BF16, and roughly 5-8 ms in FP8 [21]. The README notes that cached incremental decoding was "not included yet" in the open-source release [21].

Design takeaway: once a ranker has a large shared user-side computation, the right serving unit is (user, many candidates), not (user, candidate). Caching user-side state across requests (for example a KV cache updated incrementally as new actions arrive) is the next step.

10.7 Embedding serving and caching

10.7.1 The embedding problem

DLRM-style models (DLRM, arXiv 1906.03109 [23]) put most parameters in sparse embedding tables. ByteDance's Monolith argues for collisionless embedding tables and real-time training, so that tables grow and change continuously [24]. Serving therefore has to handle tables that (a) exceed GPU memory, (b) are updated at minute granularity, and (c) are accessed with a heavily skewed (power-law) distribution. Skew is what makes caching work.

10.7.2 NVIDIA Merlin HugeCTR Hierarchical Parameter Server

HugeCTR's Hierarchical Parameter Server (HPS) was "a native C++ library that provides caching and hierarchical storage for embeddings". It combined a GPU embedding cache with a database backend, for embeddings "that exceed the capacity of GPU and host memory". It shipped as a TensorFlow plugin and as a Triton backend [19]. NVIDIA also blogged about scaling inference with it [20]. It was published in RecSys 2022 ("A GPU-specialized Inference Parameter Server for Large-Scale Deep Recommendation Models") [19]:

  request keys
      |
      v
  +-------------------+   hit (hot IDs, majority of lookups under skew)
  | GPU embedding     |------------------------------------------> GPU dense model
  | cache (HBM)       |
  +---------+---------+
            | miss
            v
  +-------------------+   CPU-memory tier (e.g. in-process hash map / Redis cluster)
  | volatile DB tier  |
  +---------+---------+
            | miss
            v
  +-------------------+   SSD-backed persistent tier (e.g. RocksDB), full table
  | persistent tier   |
  +-------------------+
      ^
      | streaming updates from training (online model refresh)

Note that HPS is marked deprecated since HugeCTR v25.03 [19]. The hierarchy itself (HBM cache, then DRAM, then SSD, with streaming updates) remains the standard design.

10.7.3 Other caching layers in production recsys

Cache What is cached Invalidation Example
Result / candidate cache candidate lists per source per user TTL, session CR-Mixer caches candidate generation results [7]
Served/seen cache IDs already shown session, rolling window X PreviouslyServedPostsFilter, post cache refresh [11]
Item embedding index precomputed item tower outputs per checkpoint Phoenix index baked into checkpoint [12]
Embedding cache hot embedding rows streaming updates HPS GPU cache [19]
Score cache (user, item) scores model version, TTL enabled by batch-invariant scoring [11][12]
User-state cache user tower / sequence KV new user action M-FALCON-style history encoding [21]
Feature cache user/item features TTL / write-through feature stores (Ch. 8) [25]

Caching is only safe when the model's output is a function of a stable key. That is why xAI treats candidate isolation as a serving invariant, not a modeling detail: listwise models whose scores depend on the other candidates cannot reuse cached per-item scores.

10.8 Feature fetching fan-out

Feature hydration is often the latency long pole. X's Home Mixer hydrates about 6,000 features per request from many services (user-signal service, graph-feature-service, real-graph, representation-manager, engagement counters) [1][2]. Earlybird co-locates features with the index and updates them through a separate stream [5][6].

Common patterns:

  • Co-locate or precompute. Push static and slow-moving item features into the index or the model server, as Earlybird and Vespa do [5][13]. Hash-based embeddings remove the ID-to-row dictionary lookup service entirely [11].
  • Batch-get by entity. Fetch features per entity type in bulk (one call per store for all candidates), not per candidate.
  • Online feature stores. Feast describes an offline store for training, "a low-latency online store" for real-time prediction, and a feature server, with Redis, DynamoDB, Bigtable and Dragonfly among online backends [25]. DoorDash's 2020 post on building a "gigascale" feature store on Redis is a widely cited case study [38]. It covers Redis hashes, hashed feature names and compressed embedding values to cut memory and latency (details approximate here; see the original). Lyft and Etsy describe similar feature-serving and recommendation-serving platforms [36][37], and Eugene Yan's applied-ml index collects many more such posts [29].
  • Tail-latency control. With fan-out across F services, request p99 approaches the max of F service latencies. Hedged requests, per-dependency timeouts with default feature values, and degrade-to-cached-features keep the tail bounded. Navi's batch-drop threshold applies the same thinking at the model server [4].
  • Train-serve consistency. Feature logging at serving time (log what you served, train on it) avoids skew. The Elasticsearch LTR plugin's feature-logging mode is a small example [15].

10.9 Making models cheaper: cascades, early exit, distillation, quantization

10.9.1 Cascades and pre-ranking

  • Rule-of-thumb cascade. A cheap model on everything, then an expensive model on the top slice: Vespa first/second/global phases [13], the Earlybird LR light ranker before the heavy ranker [5], the X pushservice light ranker that "bridges candidate generation and heavy ranking by pre-selecting highly-relevant candidates from the initial huge candidate pool" [1].
  • Pre-ranking with compute awareness. Alibaba's COLD (Computing power cost-aware Online and Lightweight Deep pre-ranking system, 2020) argued that pre-ranking can be a real deep model with cross features if its cost is co-optimized with the serving system. Feature selection should account for compute cost, and engineering should cover low precision and parallelism [34].
  • Stage alignment. A cascade stage should optimize agreement with the downstream stage, not only the click label. Otherwise the early stage discards items the late ranker would have liked. Vespa's per-document phase-survival counters are a practical way to measure this [13].

10.9.2 Early exit

Early exit means stopping computation for items or requests once the answer is clear. In cascades it shows up as:

  • score thresholds that drop hits after the first phase (rank-score-drop-limit in Vespa [13]);
  • top-k operators (WAND, ANN) that never fully score most documents [13];
  • adaptive rerank counts per query (ranking.globalPhase.rerankCount can be set per query [13]) or per load level, which is graceful degradation under stress;
  • load shedding at the server (Navi batch_drop_millis [4]).

10.9.3 Distillation

  • Ranking distillation. Tang and Wang (KDD 2018) train a small student ranker on the teacher's top-K ranking as extra supervision, and report students at a fraction of the teacher's size with comparable ranking quality [35].
  • Cross-stage distillation. Instagram Explore's first-stage ranker is trained to reproduce late-stage outputs [31]. That is distillation used to align a cascade, not only to compress it.
  • Shared trunk. xAI's Phoenix retrieval user tower "uses the same transformer trunk and input machinery as the ranking model". The two models "differ in their heads" [12]. This shares representation learning across stages while keeping the retrieval-time item side precomputable.

10.9.4 Quantization and low precision

  • Embedding tables: row-wise INT8/INT4 quantization (FBGEMM) cuts memory and bandwidth for the gather-heavy part of the model [18].
  • Dense compute: FP8 row-wise GEMMs on H100 (HSTU-Ultra) give 1.13-1.25x forward speedups [21]. BF16 is the common baseline.
  • ANN indexes: compressed codes (PQ and variants) let FAISS scale to "billions of vectors in main memory on a single server", with GPU implementations [26]. ScaNN uses anisotropic vector quantization for maximum inner product search [27]. Semantic IDs (residual quantization) are now also used as model inputs [12].

10.10 Comparison of serving designs

System Retrieval serving Ranking compute Model server / runtime Notable serving trick
X (2023) Earlybird index, GraphJet UTEG, CR-Mixer parallel MaskNet MTL Navi (Rust; TF/ONNX) LR light ranker in index; ~6k features; batch-drop
X/xAI (2026) Thunder in-memory, Phoenix two-tower, SimClusters Phoenix transformer Rust gRPC engine, JAX-trained candidate isolation; hash embeddings; index in checkpoint
Instagram Explore two-tower + ANN, multiple sources 2-stage: light then MTML Meta internal distilled first stage; value model
Meta Andromeda (ads) deep neural retrieval + hierarchical index n/a (retrieval stage) Grace Hopper, MTIA model-index-hardware co-design
Meta GR (HSTU) generative retrieval/ranking HSTU transformer GPU, Triton/CUDA kernels M-FALCON microbatching + caching; FP8
Pinterest (various) DNN rankers on GPU GPU serving batching, CUDA graphs, fused embeddings
Vespa apps WAND / ANN in content nodes 1st, 2nd phase on nodes; global on container Vespa + ONNX (opt. GPU) compute near data; rerank-count knobs
Elasticsearch LTR BM25 / kNN LTR rescoring window ES plugin (linear/XGBoost) in-engine 2-stage cascade
NVIDIA Merlin ANN (FAISS) DLRM-style Triton + HPS backend GPU embedding cache hierarchy

10.11 Key takeaways for system designers

  1. Budget per stage, not per system. Write down p99 budgets per stage (Section 10.1) and enforce them with per-branch timeouts and fallbacks. X keeps a reverse-chron backup pipeline for when the scored pipeline fails [2].
  2. The serving unit is (user, many candidates). Compute user-side work once per request: two-tower precomputation, M-FALCON microbatching, Phoenix candidate isolation [12][21][31].
  3. Make scores batch-invariant if you want to cache them. Listwise cross-candidate attention costs you score caching and reproducibility [11][12].
  4. Push cheap compute to the data. Index-side light rankers (Earlybird), Vespa first and second phases on content nodes, and match-features to avoid moving vectors over the network [5][13].
  5. Batch with a bounded delay and shed load. Dynamic batching (Triton max_queue_delay_microseconds, Navi 2 ms / 16-request defaults) plus explicit drop thresholds [4][16].
  6. Embeddings are a memory-hierarchy problem. GPU cache, then DRAM, then SSD, with streaming updates. Skew makes small caches effective [19][24].
  7. Feature hydration is usually the long pole. Co-locate, batch-get, use defaults on timeout, and log served features for training [2][5][25].
  8. Cascades need alignment. Train early stages to agree with late stages (distillation) and measure per-stage survival, or the cascade silently caps quality [13][31][35].
  9. Spend the precision budget wisely. Low precision first for embeddings (INT8/INT4) and ANN (PQ), then FP8 for dense GEMMs on modern GPUs [18][21][26].
  10. Co-design moves the frontier. Andromeda (hardware + index + model) and Pinterest GPU serving show that bigger models upstream can be cheaper than more stages downstream [30][32].
  11. Keep a separate, explicit value model. Combining multi-task predictions with configurable weights lets product trade-offs ship without retraining [9][11][31].
  12. Simpler servers win on the hot path. Navi's minimalist Rust design and TorchRec's TorchScript C++ path show that the critical path benefits from a small, purpose-built runtime [3][17].

11. Training Data and Labeling: Impression Logs, Label Joins, Delayed Feedback, Negatives and Pipelines

Research note: when this chapter was compiled, live web search and page fetching were unavailable (search quota exhausted, egress blocked). Everything below comes from primary sources (papers, official engineering blogs, open-source READMEs) as the author already knew them, not from a fresh crawl. Numbers marked "approx." should be checked against the cited source before they are quoted.

Overview

People usually picture a recommender as a model, but in production most of the work and most of the bugs sit in the data that trains it. Every large public system covered in this atlas runs roughly the same loop. It serves a ranked list and logs what was shown (the impression) along with the features used at that moment. It then waits for user feedback such as clicks, watch time, purchases or hides, joins that feedback to the impression to make a labeled example, chooses or creates negatives, reweights, and feeds the result to a batch or streaming trainer. Each step forces a design decision with real consequences:

  • What counts as a positive? A click, a "long click", watch time, a conversion within 30 days, or a survey answer.
  • When is a label final? Conversions can arrive days after the click, and the model has to train before then.
  • What counts as a negative? An impression that wasn't clicked, a random item, an in-batch item, or a hard negative.
  • Where do the features come from? Logged at serving time, or reconstructed later ("time travel").
  • How fresh does the data have to be? Daily batch, hourly, or minute-level streaming.

This chapter collects the public designs that answer these questions. It starts with impression logging and the label join (Facebook, Google Photon, ByteDance Monolith, Netflix). It then covers delayed feedback and conversion attribution (Criteo, Twitter, Alibaba, CyberAgent), negative sampling (YouTube, Google Play, Facebook Search, Pinterest, Airbnb), sample weighting and label definitions (YouTube, Twitter/X, Yahoo, Kuaishou, Pinterest), and the large data-ingestion pipelines behind them (Meta DSI, TFX/Beam, Spotify Scio). Feature stores are covered in Chapter 8 and training infrastructure in Chapter 9. Here the focus is the example: how it is defined, labeled, sampled, weighted and delivered.

                 THE CANONICAL TRAINING-DATA LOOP

  |  Client   |------------->|  Serving stack    |-------------->| Client |
  +-----------+              | (retrieval+rank)  |               +--------+
                             +---------+---------+                   |
                                       | impression log              | engagement

                                       v                             |  convert...)
                             +-------------------+                   v

                             +---------+---------+

                      +----------------+-----------------+

                +----------------------+----------------------+
