13. Exploration, Bandits and Reinforcement Learning in Recommendation

Most production recommenders are trained on data that their own previous versions chose to collect. A ranking model learns from clicks on the items it ranked highly and never sees the counterfactual: what would have happened with an item it did not show. This chapter covers the designs that deal with that problem directly. Some explore on purpose. Some log the probability of every decision. Some correct their training for the logging policy. Some optimize long-horizon outcomes such as retention instead of the next click.

The material runs in roughly historical order, from the contextual bandits of the early 2010s (Yahoo LinUCB, Thompson sampling at Yahoo and Bing, Microsoft's Decision Service) through bandit products at Netflix, Spotify, Deezer and Amazon, to deep off-policy reinforcement learning (RL) at YouTube, SlateQ, Kuaishou retention optimization, and RL for notifications and ad bidding. The last sections cover off-policy evaluation, which every one of these systems depends on, and give takeaways for system designers.

A note on sourcing. This chapter was assembled when live web access was unavailable, so it relies on the primary papers and engineering posts listed under References, as the author knew them, plus the citations already checked in companion chapters of this Atlas. Numbers are given only where they are well known from the cited source and are marked approximate where exact figures could not be re-checked.

1. The problem: closed loops and missing counterfactuals

A recommender is an agent that acts (shows items), observes a reward (click, play, dwell, purchase, return visit) and changes its future actions. Three properties make this different from ordinary supervised learning.

  1. Partial feedback. Rewards are observed only for the items shown. The log is a biased sample, shaped by the policy that produced it.
  2. Feedback loops. If the model is retrained on its own outputs, items it underrates get no impressions and so can never be corrected. Jiang et al. (DeepMind) formalize these "degenerate feedback loops" and show that random exploration, plus a candidate pool that grows over time, are needed to avoid them [24].
  3. Delayed and long-horizon objectives. What the business wants (retention, subscription renewal, long-term satisfaction) shows up days or weeks after the action, while the cheap signal (a click) is immediate and often misaligned.

The industry has responded with a sequence of increasingly expressive formulations:

Formulation State Action Reward horizon Typical use
Multi-armed bandit (MAB) none one arm immediate layout tests, artwork pool tuning
Contextual bandit user/request features one item or slot immediate news module, artwork, shelves, carousels
Slate / combinatorial bandit features ordered list of K immediate carousels, home pages, page layouts
Off-policy policy gradient sequence (RNN) state top-K of millions short return YouTube candidate generation
Full RL (MDP, Q-learning, actor-critic) user state over a session or days slate long-term (sessions, retention) SlateQ, Kuaishou RLUR, notifications
Constrained RL / bidding campaign state bid or multiplier episode (budget day) ad auto-bidding

All of them share one piece of infrastructure: exploration with logged propensities, so that the data can later be reweighted, evaluated offline and trained on without bias.

   +---------+   context x    +------------+  action a, p(a|x)   +---------+
   | request |--------------->|  policy pi |-------------------->|  user   |
   +---------+                | (explore)  |                     +----+----+
                              +-----+------+                          |
                                    ^                          reward r (delayed)
                                    | deploy                          |
             +-----------------+    |    +---------------------------v------+
             |  off-policy     |----+----|   log: (x, a, p(a|x), r, t)      |
             |  eval (IPS/DR)  |<--------|   joined on impression id        |
             +-----------------+         +----------------------------------+
                     ^                                    |
                     +------------- train pi' ------------+

2. Yahoo! Today Module: LinUCB and replay evaluation (2010-2011)

Problem

The Yahoo! Front Page "Today Module" featured a small, rapidly changing pool of editor-picked news stories. New stories arrived throughout the day and had no click history, so a pure-exploitation CTR model was always wrong about the newest items. Li, Chu, Langford and Schapire framed article selection as a contextual bandit in which each article is an arm and user and article features are the context [1].

Algorithm

LinUCB assumes the expected click-through rate of arm a is linear in a d-dimensional feature vector x: E[r | x, a] = x^T theta_a. For each arm it keeps a ridge-regression state:

  • A_a = D_a^T D_a + I (a d x d matrix)
  • b_a = D_a^T c_a (the reward-weighted feature sum)
  • theta_a = A_a^-1 b_a

At decision time it scores each arm as x^T theta_a + alpha * sqrt(x^T A_a^-1 x) and picks the maximum. The second term is the width of a confidence interval, so arms with little data, or whose data does not cover this kind of user, receive an optimism bonus. The paper also introduces a hybrid variant in which some coefficients are shared across all arms. This lets a brand-new article borrow statistical strength from older ones on its first impression [1].

Features were heavily compressed. Raw user features (demographics, geography, behavioral categories) and article features (URL category, editor tags) were reduced through a bilinear "conjoint" model and clustering to a vector of about six dimensions per side [1]. That kept per-arm matrices tiny, so updates were O(d^2) per event and trivially fast in serving.

Scale and results

The evaluation used tens of millions of logged events from the Today Module (the paper reports over 33 million events) [1]. LinUCB achieved a 12.5% click lift over a standard context-free bandit [1]. The gains were largest when data was sparse, which is exactly the cold-start regime that bandits exist for.

Replay: the first practical offline evaluator

The companion WSDM 2011 paper [2] solved the evaluation problem that blocks every bandit project: how do you compare policies without an A/B test per candidate? Yahoo ran a bucket of traffic with a uniformly random logging policy. The replay method streams these logs and, for each event, asks the candidate policy what it would have shown. If it matches the logged action, the event is kept and its reward counted, and the candidate's state is updated. Otherwise the event is discarded. Because the logging was uniform, the kept events form an unbiased sample of what the candidate would have experienced online. Li et al. showed that replay estimates matched online bucket results closely [2]. Yahoo also released the R6 dataset from this traffic to the research community, and it became a standard bandit benchmark.

Lessons

  • Keep the context small and the update cheap. LinUCB was deployed because it was a few matrix operations per event, not because it was the most accurate model.
  • A random bucket is a capital investment. The replay estimator is only unbiased because someone was willing to pay the regret of uniform exploration on a slice of traffic. Every later system in this chapter has its own version of that bucket.
  • Replay wastes data in proportion to the number of arms. With K arms you keep about 1/K of the events, which is fine for about 20 news stories and useless for a million-item catalog. Section 11 covers the estimators that replaced it.

3. Thompson sampling: Yahoo display ads, news, and Bing adPredictor

Probability matching

Thompson sampling (TS) keeps a posterior over each arm's reward model. At each decision it samples one model from the posterior and acts greedily with respect to the sample. Arms are therefore chosen with exactly the posterior probability that they are optimal. Russo, Van Roy and colleagues give the standard modern treatment, including contextual, linear and non-conjugate versions [4].

Chapelle and Li (2011)

Chapelle and Li's NeurIPS 2011 paper, "An Empirical Evaluation of Thompson Sampling", brought the method back into mainstream use [3]. Using Yahoo data from display advertising and news article recommendation, they found that TS was competitive with, and often better than, UCB-style methods. They also highlighted two production properties:

  • Robustness to delayed and batched updates. Production systems update models in batches (for example every few minutes or hours), not after every event. UCB is deterministic between updates, so it shows the same "most uncertain" arm to everyone in the batch. TS randomizes, so it naturally spreads exploration across the batch [3].
  • Easy integration with existing Bayesian CTR models. For ads they used a Bayesian logistic regression with a Laplace (Gaussian) approximation to the posterior. Sampling the weights from that Gaussian gives TS for free [3]. They also found that shrinking the posterior variance (a tuning knob that makes exploration less aggressive) helped in practice.

Bing adPredictor

Microsoft's adPredictor for Bing sponsored search, described by Graepel, Candela, Borchert and Herbrich at ICML 2010, is a Bayesian probit regression over sparse binary features, trained online with assumed-density filtering [5]. Each weight has a Gaussian mean and variance, so the model always knows how uncertain it is about a new ad or feature. The paper discusses using the posterior for exploration: sampling from the weight distribution gives new ads impressions in proportion to their chance of being good, which is Thompson sampling by another name [5].

Design pattern

  Bayesian CTR model (per-feature mean mu_j, variance s_j^2)
          |
          |  at request time
          v
  sample w_j ~ N(mu_j, s_j^2)  ---->  score = sigmoid(sum_j w_j x_j)  -> rank
          |
          |  after feedback (batched)
          v
  posterior update (ADF / Laplace)  --> shrink variance on features seen often

The lesson that matters for system design: if your model already carries uncertainty, exploration is a sampling step at inference, not a separate system. That is why TS dominates in ads, layout optimization and any setting with batched updates.

4. Microsoft Decision Service and MSN (2016-2017)

Agarwal et al. built the Decision Service, described as the first general-purpose system for contextual-bandit learning [6]. It turns exploration into a platform made of four abstractions arranged in a loop: explore, log, learn, deploy.

  • Explore: the client library picks an action using an exploration policy (epsilon-greedy, bagging, softmax or "cover") wrapped around the current model, and records the probability of the chosen action.
  • Log: the context, action, probability and a unique event id are written immediately. The reward is joined later by event id within a fixed window. Because logging happens at the decision point, the data is "correct" by construction.
  • Learn: Vowpal Wabbit trains online on the joined stream, and off-policy estimators evaluate candidate policies on the same data.
  • Deploy: new models are pushed to clients every few minutes.

Reported production results include two content-recommendation deployments with 25-30% click-through improvements and a landing page with an 18% revenue lift [6]. Agarwal and Langford reported that MSN.com clicks rose 26% after the contextual-bandit system went live in January 2016 [7]. The technology shipped as the Custom Decision Service and later as Azure Personalizer in Azure Cognitive Services, and the algorithms are open source in Vowpal Wabbit [7].

The key architectural idea is multiworld testing. Once every decision is logged with its propensity, you can evaluate many policies offline from one stream of data, instead of running an A/B test per policy. The data needed grows only logarithmically in the number of policies evaluated [6].

5. Netflix: artwork personalization with contextual bandits (2016-2017)

Problem

Every Netflix title has several pieces of artwork. The image a member sees is the strongest signal on the home page about whether to press play. In 2016 Netflix described using A/B tests and explore-exploit to choose the single best image per title for everyone [8]. In 2017 it went further: choose the best image per member, per title [9].

Formulation

Chandrashekar, Amat, Basilico and Jebara describe the problem as a contextual bandit [9]:

  • Arms: the candidate images for a title.
  • Context: member features such as viewing history and genre preferences, plus the title, device, time and other page context. An often-quoted example: a member who watches many romances sees a romantic-lead image for Good Will Hunting, and a comedy fan sees an image featuring a comedian [9].
  • Reward: whether the member played the title (and watched enough of it) after the impression. Netflix stresses avoiding clickbait: an image that attracts plays that are then abandoned quickly is penalized, so the reward is not a raw click.
  • Policy: a supervised model predicts the probability of a quality play for each (member, title, image) and picks the best one, with an exploration component. The post names several possible exploration strategies for this setting, including simple randomization and Bayesian or upper-confidence approaches [9].

Logging and offline evaluation

   page build request
         |
         v
   +--------------------+   for each title on the page
   | artwork policy     |------------------------------+
   | (contextual model  |                              |
   |  + exploration)    |   image id, propensity p      |
   +---------+----------+                              v
             |                              +---------------------+
             |  render                      | impression log      |
             v                              | (member, title,     |
     member sees image ---- play? -------->| image, p, context)  |
                                            +----------+----------+
                                                       |
                         +-----------------------------v-------------+
                         | offline replay: keep events where the new  |
                         | policy picks the logged image; compute take |
                         | fraction (plays / impressions)             |
                         +-------------------------------------------+

Netflix logs every image impression with its context and the probability with which it was chosen. New policies are evaluated with replay on the randomized exploration data, using take fraction (plays divided by impressions) as the metric, before they go into online A/B tests [9]. The post reports that contextual policies beat non-personalized baselines on the replay metric, with online A/B tests used to confirm wins [9].

Engineering challenges called out

  • Only one image can be shown at a time. Netflix cannot show a member two images for the same title, so attribution is per impression and exploration has a real cost (regret) [9].
  • Interaction with the rest of the page. The image choice interacts with the other titles and rows on the page (diversity of images across a row, consistency for a member over time). A member who has seen one image and then sees a different one may be confused, so changes over time are managed.
  • Latency and scale. Artwork selection runs for many titles per page for every member, so it must fit inside the page-generation latency budget. The post discusses the trade-off between precomputing selections and computing them live (approximate characterization).
  • Artwork supply. Personalization only helps if there is a diverse set of images. Netflix invested in tooling to generate many candidate images per title.

Netflix later wrote about the broader framing in "Recommending for Long-Term Member Satisfaction" (2024): treat recommendation as a contextual bandit whose reward should reflect long-term satisfaction, engineer proxy rewards that predict delayed satisfaction, and accept that the reward function is itself a product decision to be iterated on [10].

6. Spotify: BaRT and the home page (2018) and impatient bandits (2023)

BaRT: Bandits for Recommendations as Treatments

McInerney et al. (Spotify, RecSys 2018) describe BaRT, the bandit system behind recommendations on Spotify's home page [11]. The home page is a grid of shelves (rows) of playlists and albums, and each recommendation can carry an explanation, such as "Because you listened to X" or "Your heavy rotation". BaRT treats the (item, explanation) pair as the action and learns which pairing is most likely to lead to engagement for a given user.

Core design [11]:

  • Reward model: a factorization machine over user, item and explanation features and their interactions, predicting the probability of a stream of meaningful length after the impression.
  • Exploration: epsilon-greedy. With probability 1 - epsilon show the predicted best, otherwise sample uniformly from the candidates. Epsilon-greedy was chosen deliberately because its propensities are trivially known: (1 - epsilon) + epsilon/K for the greedy arm and epsilon/K for the others.
  • Counterfactual training: because propensities are logged, BaRT trains its reward model on the logged data with importance weighting, which removes the bias from always showing the greedy choice.
  • Explanations as actions: the paper shows that explanations change engagement, so the same item with a different explanation is a different treatment.
   candidates (items) x explanations  --->  FM reward model r_hat(u, i, e)
                                                     |
                                                     v
                                  epsilon-greedy over (i, e) per shelf slot
                                                     |
                     log (u, i, e, p, context) ------+---> home page shelf
                                                     |
                     stream >= threshold seconds? ---+---> reward
                                                     |
                     propensity-weighted retraining <+

The paper reports that BaRT improved engagement over non-explorative baselines in both offline counterfactual evaluation and online tests, and that personalized explanations helped [11]. Exact lift numbers are not reproduced here.

Impatient bandits: optimizing for the long term without waiting

Spotify's 2023 KDD paper by Zhang et al. tackles a more recent problem: optimizing podcast recommendations for long-term engagement, defined as listening over roughly 60 days, without waiting 60 days to learn [12]. Their approach:

  • Build a Bayesian filter that predicts the long-term reward from progressively revealed intermediate outcomes (for example engagement in the first days after the first listen).
  • Use this progressively updated posterior inside a Thompson sampling bandit, so the bandit acts on partial information and sharpens its estimate as more days arrive.
  • The paper reports that, on a podcast recommendation problem, this approach substantially outperformed bandits that used either short-term proxies alone or waited for the full delayed reward [12].

This is the bandit-world version of the "proxy reward" idea that Netflix and YouTube also apply.

7. Deezer carousels and Amazon page layouts: slate bandits in practice

Deezer: carousel personalization (RecSys 2020)

Bendada, Salha and Bontempelli (Deezer) study the carousel: a swipeable row of playlists in which the user sees only the first few cards without swiping [13]. They model it as a contextual cascade bandit:

  • A user scrolls through the first L visible slots, and the model assumes items beyond the last one the user would have seen get no feedback (no penalty for unseen items).
  • To keep training feasible across millions of users, they use semi-personalization: users are clustered and a bandit (Thompson sampling or UCB variants) learns per cluster.
  • They released a public dataset and simulator derived from Deezer's playlist carousel so the community can reproduce the experiments [13].

The lesson is that the click model of the surface (cascade, top-L visible) matters as much as the bandit algorithm. Treating unseen cards as negatives would teach the policy to avoid positions that were never displayed.

Amazon: multivariate layout optimization (KDD 2017)

Hill et al. (Amazon) optimize a page made up of several widgets (for example image, headline, button, layout) with many possible values each, giving a combinatorial space of thousands of layouts [14]. They use a Bayesian linear model with pairwise interaction terms, Thompson sampling to choose a layout, and greedy hill climbing to find an approximate argmax of the sampled model, because full enumeration is too slow for real-time serving. In a live experiment the method found a layout that improved conversion by about 21% over the median layout [14]. The design pattern is general: sample a model, then use a cheap combinatorial optimizer to act on it.

8. YouTube: top-K off-policy corrected REINFORCE (2019)

Problem

YouTube's candidate generator chooses a handful of videos from a corpus of millions for each request. It was trained on logs produced by many earlier versions of the recommender and by other systems. Chen, Beutel, Covington, Jain, Belletti and Chi (WSDM 2019) recast it as a policy pi(a | s) trained with REINFORCE, where the state s is the user's history and the action a is a video [15].

Architecture

   user event sequence (watched videos, context)
               |
               v
      +-----------------+
      |   RNN state s_t |  (shared user-state encoder)
      +--------+--------+
               |
       +-------+---------------------------+
       |                                   |
       v                                   v
  softmax pi_theta(a|s)            softmax beta_hat(a|s)
  over millions of videos          (behavior policy head;
  (the policy we deploy)            gradient blocked into
       |                            the shared encoder)
       |                                   |
       +------> importance weight w = pi_theta / beta_hat
                       |
                       v
       top-K correction lambda_K = K * (1 - pi_theta)^(K-1)
                       |
                       v
       REINFORCE gradient: sum_t  w * lambda_K * R_t * grad log pi_theta(a_t|s_t)
       (with weight capping and normalized importance sampling)

The policy is a softmax over a very large action space (millions of videos), trained with sampled softmax [15].

Key tricks

  1. Off-policy correction. The logs come from a behavior policy beta that is a mixture of historical systems and is unknown. The paper learns beta_hat with a second softmax head on the same state, with its gradient blocked so it does not distort the main encoder [15]. The policy gradient is reweighted by pi_theta / beta_hat.
  2. Top-K off-policy correction. YouTube shows K items at once, not one. If the policy's probability of including item a in a set of K samples is alpha(a) = 1 - (1 - pi(a))^K, then the gradient picks up an extra multiplier lambda_K = K (1 - pi(a))^(K-1) [15]. When pi(a) is small, lambda_K is close to K, pushing hard to increase the probability. When pi(a) is already large, lambda_K approaches 0, so the policy stops over-concentrating on a single item and spreads mass across a good set of K.
  3. Variance reduction. Importance weights over millions of actions have enormous variance. The paper uses weight capping, normalized (self-normalized) importance sampling, and a TRPO-style constraint [15].
  4. Exploration at serving. Serving does not take the argmax. It returns the top K' most likely items and samples the remaining K - K' from the policy, a Boltzmann-style exploration that also keeps the logged data rich [15].
  5. Reward. The return combines the immediate reward of the watched item with discounted future rewards within the user's trajectory.

Results

The paper reports live experiments on YouTube in which the top-K off-policy correction gave statistically significant gains in viewing time, roughly 0.8-0.9% in the reported experiment, which is large at YouTube scale [15]. It also reports that the system surfaced more items from the long tail. The authors' simulations show that without correction the learned policy over-concentrates on items that the behavior policy already favored.

Follow-ups

  • Reward shaping for user satisfaction. Christakopoulou et al. (Google, 2022) extend the REINFORCE recommender with reward shaping that learns from sparse satisfaction signals (such as survey responses) and imputes them onto unlabeled interactions [16].
  • Simulation. Google released RecSim, a configurable simulator for sequential user-recommender interaction with user state, choice models and slates, for testing RL recommenders before they reach users [17].

9. SlateQ: tractable value-based RL for slates (Google, 2019)

Problem

Value-based RL (Q-learning) estimates the long-term value Q(s, A) of an action. In recommendation an action is a slate of k items from N candidates, so the action space is combinatorial (N choose k, ordered). Q over slates is neither learnable nor optimizable directly.

Decomposition

Ie et al. (Google, IJCAI 2019) show that under two assumptions the slate value decomposes into item-level values [18]:

  • Single choice (SC): the user consumes at most one item from a slate (or none).
  • Reward and transition depend only on the selected item (RTDS): the reward and next state depend on the item consumed, not on the rest of the slate.

Under SC and RTDS:

Q(s, A) = sum over i in A of P(i | s, A) * Q_bar(s, i)

where P(i | s, A) is a user choice model (for example a conditional logit with a "no click" option) and Q_bar(s, i) is the long-term value of the user consuming item i. Q_bar is learned with ordinary TD (SARSA or Q-learning) on item-level transitions, which is tractable.

Slate optimization

Given Q_bar and the choice model, choosing the best slate is a fractional mixed-integer program, which the paper shows can be solved exactly as a linear program for the conditional-logit model. Cheaper greedy and top-k heuristics work almost as well in practice [18].

   offline logs (s, slate A, clicked i, r, s')
            |
            +--> choice model P(i | s, A)   (trained as a classifier)
            |
            +--> Q_bar(s, i) via SARSA/TD on (s, i, r, s', i')
                          |
   serving:  candidates from retrieval (hundreds)
                          |
            score each i by P-weighted Q_bar
                          |
            slate = LP or greedy top-k  ---> user

Deployment

SlateQ was tested in simulation (in RecSim, which was released alongside it [17]) and in live experiments on YouTube, where it was plugged into an existing ranking stack by replacing the per-item myopic score with the decomposed long-term value. The paper reports improvements in user engagement over the myopic production baseline [18]. A practical point is that SlateQ reuses the existing pointwise infrastructure. It adds a value head trained with TD targets and a slate-optimization step, not a new serving system.

10. Long-term value, retention and notifications

Microsoft News: DRN (WWW 2018)

Zheng et al. built DRN for news recommendation in a Microsoft News app (China) [19]. Its contributions are typical of the early deep-RL wave:

  • A Double/Dueling DQN whose reward combines click and user activeness (how soon the user returns), an early example of optimizing return rather than click.
  • Dueling Bandit Gradient Descent for exploration: perturb the network weights to create an "explore" network, interleave its results with the current network's, and move the weights toward whichever gets more clicks. This avoids the poor user experience of random item exploration.
  • Minor updates every interaction batch, major updates periodically.

JD.com: page-wise RL (RecSys 2018)

Zhao et al. (JD.com) apply actor-critic RL to recommend a whole 2-D page of items at once, with a CNN-based actor that generates the page and a critic that values it. They train against an offline simulator built from logs before going online [20].

Alibaba Virtual-Taobao (AAAI 2019)

Shi et al. trained an RL policy for Taobao search in a learned simulator. They modeled customers with GAN-based generation (GAN-SD) and multi-agent adversarial imitation learning (MAIL), then trained the ranking policy in the simulator. They reported an online revenue improvement of over 2% compared with the traditional supervised approach [21]. The lesson: if online exploration is too costly, invest in a simulator, but validate it against real logs.

Kuaishou: reinforcing user retention at billion scale (WWW 2023)

Cai et al. (Kuaishou) describe RLUR, which optimizes user retention, measured as the time until the user returns to the app, in a short-video system with hundreds of millions of daily users [22]. Retention is a delayed, sparse, user-level signal that is influenced by many sessions, which makes credit assignment hard.

Design highlights [22]:

  • Model the problem as an infinite-horizon MDP in which each request is a step. The reward is defined at the session level: the gap until the next session.
  • Learn a retention critic with a temporal-difference (TD) objective. Use heuristic immediate rewards (for example watch time) as auxiliary, reward-shaping signals to cut variance.
  • Use a soft regularization and intrinsic-motivation components to stabilize learning and avoid policy collapse.
  • The actor outputs fusion weights for the multi-objective ranking formula (how much to weight predicted like, watch time, follow and so on), not item scores directly. This keeps the action space small and low-dimensional, and the existing ranking stack untouched.

The paper reports statistically significant improvements in retention metrics (app return frequency and DAU-related metrics) in production A/B tests [22]. A companion Kuaishou paper, the Two-Stage Constrained Actor-Critic (TSCAC), tackles maximizing watch time subject to constraints on auxiliary interactions (likes, follows, shares) [23].

  request t:  user state s_t (history, profile, time since last visit)
                 |
                 v
          actor pi(s_t) --> weights w_t = (w_watch, w_like, w_follow, ...)
                 |
                 v
     existing ranker: score(i) = sum_k w_t,k * prediction_k(i)   ---> feed
                 |
   session ends; next visit after gap g  ---> reward r = f(g) (+ shaped terms)
                 |
          critic V(s) trained by TD; actor updated by critic

The design idea, RL controls the knobs of the ranker instead of the items, is now a common production pattern. It keeps the action space continuous and low-dimensional, makes the policy safe to roll back, and reuses all existing predictions.

Notifications: Meta Horizon/ReAgent and Duolingo

Push notifications are a natural RL problem. Each send has an immediate effect (open) and a long-term cost (fatigue, disabling notifications, churn).

  • Meta Horizon (ReAgent). Gauci et al. describe Horizon, Facebook's open-source applied RL platform, built for batch (offline) RL on logged data. It includes data preprocessing at scale, DQN, parametric-action DQN, and DDPG, and counterfactual policy evaluation (doubly robust, sequential DR, MAGIC) run before any deployment [25]. The paper reports production uses including push notifications (deciding which notifications to send to optimize long-term value rather than immediate clicks) and choosing when to prefetch content. Horizon was later renamed ReAgent [26].
  • Duolingo. Yancey and Settles (KDD 2020) describe a "sleeping, recovering" bandit for daily practice reminders [27]. Arms are notification templates. Some arms are "asleep" (not eligible) for a given user on a given day. The reward of an arm recovers with time since it was last used, which captures novelty decay. The paper reports gains in user engagement (lesson completions and daily active users) in live experiments; the exact magnitudes are not reproduced here.

The common lesson is that a notification system must optimize sends that do not destroy the channel. That requires a long-horizon reward (or explicit fatigue modeling), plus counterfactual evaluation, because a bad notification policy damages the user base before an A/B test finishes.

RL for ads: auto-bidding

Advertising platforms use RL most directly in bidding, where the state (remaining budget, time of day, spend pace) and the episode (a day's budget) map cleanly onto an MDP.

  • Budget-constrained bidding (Wu et al., Alibaba, CIKM 2018): model-free RL (DQN) adjusts a bid-scaling factor over the day to maximize value under a budget, with a reward design that avoids myopic overspending [28].
  • Multi-agent real-time bidding (Jin et al., Alibaba, CIKM 2018): cluster advertisers into agents and train with a distributed multi-agent actor-critic, balancing competition and cooperation among advertisers on the Taobao platform [29].

In both, the RL policy outputs a scalar control (a bid multiplier), not an item choice. That is the same pattern as Kuaishou's fusion weights.

11. Off-policy evaluation: the shared foundation

Every design above depends on answering "what would policy pi' have earned?" from data logged under policy beta.

Estimator Formula (informal) Bias Variance Used by
Replay [2] mean reward on events where pi' agrees with uniform log unbiased (uniform log) high; keeps ~1/K events Yahoo, Netflix artwork
IPS mean of r * pi'(a x) / beta(a x) unbiased if beta known and > 0
Self-normalized IPS IPS / mean of weights small bias lower YouTube REINFORCE training
Direct method (DM) mean of r_hat(x, pi'(x)) biased by model low baselines
Doubly robust (DR) [30] DM + IPS correction on residual unbiased if either part is right medium Horizon/ReAgent, VW
Marginalized IPS (embeddings) [32] weight by action-embedding ratio small bias far lower for large action sets large catalogs
  • Doubly robust estimation (Dudik, Langford and Li, ICML 2011) combines a reward model with importance weighting so that the estimate is unbiased if either the propensities or the reward model are correct [30].
  • Open Bandit Pipeline (Saito et al., ZOZO and Hanjuku-Kaso, 2020) released a large real dataset collected by both uniform random and Bernoulli Thompson sampling policies on the ZOZOTOWN fashion site, with a Python library for comparing estimators [31]. It is the main public benchmark for checking whether an off-policy estimator would have predicted real online outcomes.
  • Large action spaces. Saito and Joachims (ICML 2022) show that IPS breaks down with very large action spaces and propose marginalized IPS over action embeddings, which reweights by how likely the embedding was rather than the exact item [32]. This is the bridge from Yahoo-sized arm sets to YouTube-sized catalogs.

Practical OPE checklist

  1. Log the propensity at decision time, from the serving code that made the decision, not from a model reconstructed later.
  2. Never let a logged propensity be 0 for an action you may want to evaluate (exploration floor).
  3. Join rewards by impression id with an explicit attribution window, and record the window.
  4. Report effective sample size alongside the estimate. When weights explode, the estimate is meaningless, whatever the confidence interval says.
  5. Validate offline estimators against at least a few online A/B results before trusting them for launch decisions. Netflix [9] and Yahoo [2] both did this explicitly.

13. Recurring design patterns

Pattern 1: Exploration bucket plus propensity logging

Reserve a slice of traffic with known, simple randomization (uniform or epsilon-greedy), and log propensities everywhere else as well. Yahoo, Netflix, Spotify, Microsoft and ZOZO all do this. The bucket is what makes unbiased offline evaluation and model training possible.

Pattern 2: Posterior sampling as the default explorer

When the reward model can carry uncertainty (Bayesian linear or logistic regression, bootstrapped ensembles, dropout ensembles), Thompson sampling gives exploration that tolerates batched updates and integrates as a sampling step at inference [3][4][5][14].

Pattern 3: RL on top of, not instead of, the ranker

The most successful deep-RL deployments change little in serving:

  • YouTube corrects the training objective of an existing softmax candidate generator [15].
  • SlateQ reweights existing pointwise scores by long-term value [18].
  • Kuaishou RLUR and ad auto-bidders output a handful of continuous knobs [22][28].

Full end-to-end RL that picks items from scratch is rare in production.

Pattern 4: Proxy and progressive rewards for long horizons

Optimizing retention directly is slow and noisy. The working solutions predict the long-term reward from early signals (Spotify [12], Netflix [10]), shape rewards with immediate signals (Kuaishou [22]), or learn satisfaction imputations (YouTube [16]).

Pattern 5: Simulation before exposure

RecSim [17], Virtual-Taobao [21] and JD's simulator [20] all let teams debug RL policies before exposing real users. Simulators are useful for catching bugs and comparing algorithm families. Their absolute numbers rarely transfer, so they must be validated against held-out logs.

Reference architecture

                     +-------------------------------------------+
                     |               SERVING PATH                |
  request ---------> | retrieval -> ranking (predictions p_k)    |
                     |     |             |                       |
                     |     |    value / policy layer:            |
                     |     |    - bandit / TS sampling           |
                     |     |    - RL fusion weights w(s)         |
                     |     |    - slate optimizer (LP / greedy)  |
                     |     v             v                       |
                     |   final slate + propensities p(a|x)       |
                     +-------------------+-----------------------+
                                         |
                                         v
        +-----------------------------------------------------------+
        |  impression log (request id, context, slate, positions,   |
        |  propensities, model versions, exploration flag)          |
        +-----------------------------+-----------------------------+
                                      |  join rewards (immediate +
                                      |  delayed, with windows)
                                      v
        +-----------------------------------------------------------+
        |  training: IPS / SNIPS-weighted losses, TD critics,       |
        |  behavior-policy estimation, reward models                |
        +-----------------------------+-----------------------------+
                                      v
        +-----------------------------------------------------------+
        |  OPE gate: DR / SNIPS / replay on exploration bucket,     |
        |  effective-sample-size checks, simulator smoke tests      |
        +-----------------------------+-----------------------------+
                                      v
                       online A/B test -> rollout

14. Key takeaways for system designers

  1. Treat exploration as infrastructure, not an algorithm choice. The Decision Service showed that explore, log, learn and deploy belong in a shared platform [6]. The individual bandit algorithm matters less than getting propensities logged correctly at decision time.
  2. The logging schema is the contract. Context, action, position, propensity, model version and exploration flag must be logged by the serving code at the moment of decision. Reconstructing propensities later is a common and silent source of bias.
  3. Pay for a random bucket. A small uniformly random (or epsilon-greedy) slice of traffic makes unbiased replay and IPS evaluation possible and breaks degenerate feedback loops [2][9][24].
  4. Prefer Thompson sampling when updates are batched. It spreads exploration across a batch and reuses existing Bayesian models [3][5].
  5. Use the right click model for the surface. Cascades, carousels and grids have positions users never see. Do not count them as negatives [13].
  6. For large catalogs, correct, do not replace. YouTube's top-K off-policy correction shows how to add RL to a softmax retrieval model trained on biased logs, with behavior-policy estimation, weight capping and self-normalization [15].
  7. Decompose slates. SlateQ's choice-model decomposition makes long-term value learnable and optimizable with existing pointwise infrastructure [18].
  8. Let RL turn the knobs. Controlling fusion weights or bid multipliers keeps the action space small, the policy safe to roll back, and the rest of the stack intact [22][28].
  9. Engineer the reward explicitly and treat it as a product decision. Click rewards produce clickbait; Netflix's quality-play reward [9], Spotify's 60-day objective [12] and Kuaishou's return-time reward [22] all reflect deliberate reward design.
  10. Gate every launch on off-policy evaluation, then A/B test. Use doubly robust or marginalized estimators, check effective sample size, and validate estimators against past online results [30][31][32].
  11. Simulate to debug, not to decide. Simulators catch bugs and compare algorithm families. Launch decisions still need real traffic [17][21].
  12. Channels like notifications need long-horizon objectives. Optimizing opens per send burns out users. Use long-term value and fatigue modeling with counterfactual evaluation before deployment [25][27].
