14. Debiasing, Diversity, Fairness and Cold Start: The Corrective Layers of Production Recommenders

Research note: when this chapter was written, live web search and page fetching were not available in the research environment (the shared search budget was used up and outbound fetches failed DNS resolution). The chapter is therefore built from well-known, widely cited primary papers and engineering write-ups whose content and identifiers the author knows. The claims follow those sources. Any number not checked against the source is marked "approximately" or "reported as". Check figures against the cited originals before quoting them.

Overview

Every production recommender learns from logs that it produced itself. A user can only click what was shown, items shown at the top get more clicks, popular items get more impressions and so look more relevant, and new users, items and creators have almost no data at all. Left alone, the system's feedback loop makes all of these effects stronger. The result is a narrow, popularity-heavy, position-driven product that can be unfair to suppliers.

Large platforms answer this with a set of "corrective layers" that sit around the core retrieval and ranking stack (Chapters 2-4):

                 +-------------------- feedback loop --------------------+
                 |                                                        |
 logs (biased) --+--> [A] debiasing in training -----> retrieval / ranking |
                      - position towers (YouTube, Airbnb, Huawei PAL)      |
                      - IPS / propensity weighting (Joachims, Schnabel)    |
                      - logQ sampling correction (YouTube two-tower)       |
                      - popularity deconfounding (PDA, MACR)               |
                      - duration deconfounding (Kuaishou D2Q)              |
                                                     |                     |
                                                     v                     |
                      [B] slate construction / re-ranking                  |
                      - MMR, DPP (YouTube, Hulu), calibration (Netflix)    |
                      - listwise diversity (Airbnb)                        |
                      - fairness constraints (LinkedIn, Spotify)           |
                                                     |                     |
                                                     v                     |
                      [C] cold start and exploration                       |
                      - content towers, meta-embeddings, DropoutNet        |
                      - cohort gating (Kuaishou POSO), bandits (Yahoo)     |
                      - new-listing priors (Airbnb)                        |
                                                     |                     |
                                                     v                     |
                                            impressions shown to user -----+

This chapter goes through each layer. For each one it covers the problem, the deployed designs, and the lessons for system designers.

14.1 A Taxonomy of Bias in Recommender Logs

The survey by Chen et al. [19] is the standard map of the field. It separates:

Bias Where it enters Symptom Typical fix
Position bias User clicks on what is ranked high CTR depends on slot, not relevance Position feature + dropout, IPS, PAL
Selection bias Users rate only what they choose Explicit ratings are MNAR Propensity-weighted losses [13]
Exposure bias Users only see a subset of items Unobserved does not mean negative Exposure modelling [14], off-policy correction [31]
Popularity bias Training data dominated by head Long tail under-recommended Regularisers [16], deconfounding [17][18], logQ [11]
Conformity Users imitate the crowd Labels not individual preference Causal disentangling
Duration / length bias Longer videos get more watch time Watch-time model prefers long content Duration-bucketed targets [27]
Inductive / feedback-loop bias Model's own outputs become training data Homogenisation, filter bubbles Exploration, randomisation, diversity
Unfairness Unequal exposure across groups Creators or sellers starved Exposure constraints [20][21][22]

Two kinds of fix come up again and again:

  1. Model the bias explicitly as a separate factor (a "bias tower" or propensity), train it jointly with the relevance model, and remove it at serving time.
  2. Reweight the data by inverse propensities so that the expected loss matches the loss on unbiased data.

Production systems prefer (1). It is easier to run, has lower variance, and fits into multitask DNN rankers.

14.2 Position Bias

14.2.1 Unbiased learning to rank: IPS and propensity estimation

Problem. A click on position 1 says less about relevance than a click on position 10, because users look at position 1 far more often. Joachims, Swaminathan and Schnabel [8] cast this as counterfactual learning. Under an examination hypothesis,

P(click | q, d, k) = P(examined | k) * P(relevant | q, d)

and each click is weighted by 1 / P(examined | k). The IPS-weighted ranking loss is then an unbiased estimate of the loss under full-information relevance labels.

Estimating propensities. The original work used randomisation interventions, such as swapping results at rank 1 and rank k, to estimate a propensity curve that roughly follows a power law in rank. Swaps hurt the user experience. Agarwal et al. [29] showed that propensities can instead be estimated without intrusive interventions, using "intervention harvesting": when several historical ranking functions put the same document at different positions, the logs already contain natural swaps. Google's personal-search team (Wang et al. [28][34]) estimated position bias with regression EM, again avoiding heavy randomisation, and used selection-bias weights in email search ranking.

Lessons. IPS is unbiased only if the propensity model is correct. Weights at deep ranks blow up variance, so practitioners clip them. IPS also struggles with features that interact with position, such as device type or presentation layout. That limitation motivated the "bias tower" designs below.

14.2.2 YouTube: the shallow tower in the Watch Next ranker

System. YouTube's "Recommending What Video to Watch Next" ranking system (Zhao et al., RecSys 2019) [1] ranks a few hundred candidates from multiple candidate generators. It uses a Multi-gate Mixture-of-Experts (MMoE) network with engagement objectives (clicks, watch time) and satisfaction objectives (likes, dismissals, survey responses).

Bias problem. Watch Next logs carry strong selection bias. Users click videos near the top of the list partly because of position, not utility. The paper calls this an implicit feedback loop: training on these logs keeps reinforcing the current ranking.

Architecture.

 user / context / candidate features          position, device (+ other bias feats)
                 |                                        |
         +---------------+                         +--------------+
         | shared hidden |                         | shallow tower|
         |  layers       |                         | (small MLP / |
         +---------------+                         |  linear)     |
                 |                                 +--------------+
         +---------------+                                |
         | MMoE experts  |                                |
         | + task gates  |                                |
         +---------------+                                |
           |         |                                    |
   engagement     satisfaction                            |
   task towers    task towers                             |
           |                                              |
       logit_main  ------------------ (+) --------------- logit_bias
                                       |
                                    sigmoid ----> training loss (click etc.)

  Serving: the position feature is treated as missing, so logit_bias collapses
           to a constant and ranking uses the main towers only.

Key tricks.

  • The shallow tower gets features that drive bias but not relevance: the position of the item when it was shown, plus device information. Device matters because position effects differ between mobile and desktop.
  • The bias logit is added to the main model's logit before the sigmoid. This factorises the click probability into a relevance part and a bias part.
  • During training the position feature is dropped out at a reported rate of about 10%. This stops the main model from relying on position, and the model learns sensible behaviour when position is missing, which is exactly the serving setting.
  • At serving, position is set to missing.

Results. The paper reports that the shallow tower improved the engagement metric in live experiments over baselines, including over using position as a plain input feature. The learned position biases fall monotonically with position, as expected.

Lesson. A "bias-only" tower that is added in logit space is cheap (a few extra parameters), works with any multitask ranker, and has become the de facto industrial pattern. Later work in industry and academia extends it with context-aware bias towers (position crossed with device, UI surface, or session depth).

14.2.3 Huawei PAL: position as a separate probability

Huawei's PAL (Guo et al., RecSys 2019) [9], deployed in the Huawei App Store, factorises CTR multiplicatively:

pCTR(click | x, pos) = pSeen(pos) * pCTR(click | x, seen)

Two modules, a position module and a CTR module, are trained jointly on the click label. At serving only the CTR module ranks candidates, so the system never needs to know the position before choosing it. That breaks the chicken-and-egg problem of using position as a feature in a ranker that decides positions. In online A/B tests PAL reported gains in CTR and conversion rate over a "position as feature" baseline. The multiplicative form is the probabilistic twin of YouTube's additive-logit tower.

14.2.4 Airbnb: position features with dropout in search ranking

System. Airbnb's search ranking moved from GBDT to deep networks in 2018-2019 [6]. In "Improving Deep Learning for Airbnb Search" (Haldar et al., KDD 2020) [5] the team describes its next round of changes, including handling of position bias.

Problem. Guest bookings depend heavily on where a listing appears. Airbnb is a two-sided marketplace with limited inventory, so a model that learns "top position means good listing" also entrenches incumbents and hurts new hosts.

Design. Airbnb added the listing's search position as a training feature and applied dropout to it during training. At inference the position feature is set to a constant (zero), so all candidates are scored as if they sat in the same position. The paper treats the dropout rate as a regularisation knob. Too little dropout and the model over-relies on position, which hurts offline relevance with position removed. Too much and the model cannot separate position effects. The team tuned the rate to balance the two and reported a statistically significant booking gain online.

Lessons.

  • Training with "position as feature" and serving with "position = constant" is the simplest debiasing you can deploy. It needs no propensity estimation.
  • In marketplaces, position debiasing is also a fairness and cold-start lever. It lowers the advantage that listings get from having ranked well in the past.

14.2.5 Comparison of position-debiasing designs

Design Org Bias model Combination Serving Needs randomisation?
IPS-LTR [8] Cornell / academic Propensity per rank Loss weight 1/p_k Unchanged ranker Yes (or harvested [29])
Regression-EM [28] Google personal search Propensity per rank Loss weight Unchanged ranker No
Shallow tower [1] YouTube Small net on position + device Additive logit Position missing No
PAL [9] Huawei App Store pSeen(pos) module Multiplicative probability CTR module only No
Position feature + dropout [5] Airbnb search Position as input feature Inside main DNN Position = 0 No

14.3 Popularity, Exposure and Sampling Bias

14.3.1 Popularity bias and the long tail

Abdollahpouri et al. [15] show that common collaborative filtering algorithms not only over-recommend popular items but also serve users with niche tastes worse than mainstream users, because their recommendations drift toward the head. Earlier work by the same group [16] added a regulariser to a learning-to-rank objective that penalises lists made only of head items. This made an explicit accuracy versus long-tail-coverage trade-off.

Causal methods treat popularity as a confounder:

  • PDA (Popularity-bias Deconfounding and Adjusting), Zhang et al., SIGIR 2021 [17]. Item popularity affects both exposure and the click label. PDA trains a deconfounded model by removing the confounding popularity effect through backdoor adjustment. It then optionally injects predicted future popularity at inference. The point is that some popularity is real signal (trending items) and should be kept on purpose, not by accident.
  • MACR, Wei et al., KDD 2021 [18]. Builds a causal graph with user, item and user-item-matching branches. Training uses multitask learning with auxiliary item-only and user-only modules. At inference, counterfactual reasoning subtracts the direct item (popularity) effect from the prediction.

14.3.2 Sampling bias in two-tower retrieval: logQ correction (YouTube)

In-batch softmax for two-tower retrieval (Chapter 2) treats the other items in a batch as negatives. Popular items show up in batches far more often, so they are over-penalised as negatives. That would bias the model against the head. Yi et al., RecSys 2019 [11], built YouTube's retrieval around logQ correction:

s_c(x, y_j) = s(x, y_j) - log(p_j)

Here p_j is the probability that item j appears in a batch. Because the training data streams, p_j cannot be counted offline. The paper therefore introduces a streaming frequency estimator: a hash array that records the last global step at which each item was seen and keeps a moving average of the gap between sightings (delta). The estimate is p_j ≈ 1 / delta. The design was deployed for YouTube candidate generation over a corpus of (reported) tens of millions of videos. LogQ correction is now standard in almost every in-batch two-tower system.

Design lesson. Popularity bias can enter through the training procedure (negative sampling) as well as through the data. Check the sampler before blaming the logs.

14.3.3 Exposure bias and off-policy correction

Implicit feedback mixes "did not like" with "never saw". Liang et al. [14] model exposure as a latent variable (ExpoMF): a missing interaction counts as negative evidence only to the degree that the user was probably exposed to the item. Schnabel et al. [13] frame recommendation as treatments and use propensity-scored estimators for both training and evaluation of rating models under missing-not-at-random data.

At industry scale, YouTube's REINFORCE recommender (Chen et al., WSDM 2019, "Top-K Off-Policy Correction") [31] tackles the exposure bias of training a policy on logs produced by earlier policies:

  • A separate head estimates the behaviour policy beta(a|s), meaning the probability that the logged system showed item a. Gradients are importance-weighted by pi/beta, with weight capping to control variance.
  • A top-K correction multiplier, lambda_K = K * (1 - pi)^(K-1), accounts for the fact that the policy recommends a slate of K items, not a single one.
  • The paper reports that the off-policy-corrected agent increased viewing time in live experiments, and that the gains came disproportionately from items that the earlier system rarely surfaced. The correction expands exposure toward the tail.

Chapter 13 covers RL and exploration in more depth.

14.3.4 YouTube's "example age" feature: debiasing toward the past

Covington et al. [12] made a simpler but influential observation. A model trained on historical windows learns the average popularity of an item over the training window. That under-predicts fresh, viral uploads. YouTube added the age of the training example as a feature during training and set it to zero (or slightly negative) at serving. This lets the model represent time-dependent popularity and shows "now" at serving. The same paper also takes a fixed number of training examples per user, so that a small set of heavy users does not dominate the loss, which is a form of reweighting against activity bias.

14.3.5 Duration bias in watch time: Kuaishou D2Q

Short-video platforms optimise watch time. Longer videos naturally collect more watch time, so a naive regressor favours length. Kuaishou's D2Q (Zhan et al., KDD 2022) [27] treats video duration as a confounder that affects both exposure and watch time:

      duration --------> exposure (system shows long videos more)
         |                  |
         v                  v
               watch time (label)

  D2Q: split training data into duration buckets
       -> within each bucket, convert watch time into a quantile label
       -> fit one model (shared parameters) predicting the within-bucket quantile
       -> serve on quantiles: compares "how well this video holds attention
          relative to similar-length videos"

The paper reports online gains on Kuaishou over naive watch-time regression and over value-weighted baselines. Later short-video work builds on the same "normalise by length group" idea.

14.4 Diversity: From MMR to Learned Listwise Rankers

14.4.1 Classic re-ranking: MMR and topic diversification

Maximal Marginal Relevance (Carbonell and Goldstein, SIGIR 1998) [10] builds the list greedily:

next = argmax_{i not in S} [ lambda * rel(i) - (1 - lambda) * max_{j in S} sim(i, j) ]

MMR is O(N * K) similarity look-ups for K picks from N candidates. It is easy to run on the re-ranking tier and is still the default diversity baseline in many systems, including RAG retrieval today. Ziegler et al. [30] introduced intra-list similarity and topic diversification for book recommendations. User studies showed that users liked lists that were diversified even when accuracy metrics dropped slightly. That is an early piece of evidence that offline accuracy is the wrong only-metric.

Limitations of MMR: it only penalises the maximum pairwise similarity, it has no probabilistic meaning, and lambda must be tuned per surface.

14.4.2 Determinantal point processes

A DPP over a ground set of items defines P(S) proportional to det(L_S), where L is a positive semi-definite kernel. A common decomposition is

L_ij = q_i * q_j * S_ij

where q_i is item quality (relevance) and S_ij is similarity. The determinant grows with the qualities and shrinks as items become collinear, so one score covers both relevance and set-level diversity. It rewards whole-set "volume", not only pairwise distance.

YouTube: practical DPP for the home feed

Wilhelm et al., "Practical Diversified Recommendations on YouTube with Determinantal Point Processes" (CIKM 2018) [2], describe how YouTube put a DPP into its mobile home feed.

Problem. The pointwise ranker scores each video on its own, so a feed can fill up with near-duplicate content (for example, several videos on the same topic or from the same creator). Users then scroll past the whole block, and a pointwise ranker never sees that cost.

Architecture.

 candidate generators --> pointwise ranker (q_i = predicted utility)
                                   |
                                   v  top-N ranked candidates (N ~ a few hundred, approx.)
                    +-------------------------------+
                    | DPP re-ranker                 |
                    |  kernel:                      |
                    |  L_ii = q_i^2                 |
                    |  L_ij = alpha*q_i*q_j*        |
                    |        exp(-D_ij / (2 s^2))   |
                    |  D_ij from video embeddings / |
                    |  topical distance             |
                    |  greedy MAP, window by window |
                    +-------------------------------+
                                   |
                                   v
                   feed served in windows of k items; next window
                   chosen conditioned on items already selected

Key tricks.

  • Parameterised kernel with two knobs. alpha trades relevance against diversity, and sigma sets how fast similarity decays with distance. Early versions found the values by grid search against online metrics. Later the paper describes learning a deep kernel from feed interactions, treating the set of items the user engaged with in a window as a DPP sample.
  • Windowed greedy inference. The feed is long. Instead of one global MAP, the system greedily picks a window of items (roughly the number visible on a phone screen), fixes it, and moves to the next window. This keeps latency bounded.
  • Engagement as the objective. The paper reports that DPP-diversified feeds raised long-term user satisfaction and engagement metrics compared with heuristic diversity rules such as per-channel caps, which YouTube had used before.

Hulu: fast greedy MAP inference

Exact DPP MAP is NP-hard, and naive greedy costs O(M * N^3) for selecting N items from M if determinants are recomputed. Chen, Zhang and Zhou (Hulu, NeurIPS 2018) [3] made greedy DPP practical:

  • Incremental Cholesky updates. Each time an item is added, the marginal gain of every remaining candidate is updated in O(N) work per candidate, giving O(N^2 * M) total. That is fast enough for online re-ranking at hundreds of candidates and tens of selected items.
  • Sliding-window variant. For long sequences, diversity is enforced only within a window of the last w items. This matches how users perceive a scrolling feed and lowers cost further.
  • Experiments showed that the method was orders of magnitude faster than earlier greedy implementations and gave a better relevance-diversity frontier than MMR and other baselines. The paper also reports an online A/B test in a production movie-recommendation setting.

This algorithm (often called "fast greedy DPP") is the implementation most teams use in practice, including several large short-video and e-commerce platforms that describe DPP-style re-ranking.

14.4.3 Airbnb: learning to rank diversely

Airbnb's search team (Abdool et al., "Learning To Rank Diversely At Airbnb") [7] points out a basic gap in pairwise learning to rank. The loss assumes each listing's utility does not depend on what sits above it. In a marketplace, if the top 5 results are all similar high-priced lofts, a sixth loft adds little.

Design. The team keeps the trained pairwise relevance model and adds a model that scores each listing in the context of the listings already ranked above it. It learns a representation of the "query context of results so far" and ranks listing by listing (sequentially), so that a listing similar to those already placed is de-prioritised when the data shows that such redundancy lowers bookings. The paper presents this as moving from pointwise or pairwise to a listwise, context-aware formulation without hand-tuned diversity weights, and reports a statistically significant booking gain in online A/B tests.

Lesson. Diversity does not have to be a heuristic re-ranker bolted on after the model. It can be learned from outcome data once the model sees the slate context. This is the same direction taken by generative, slate-aware rankers (Chapter 6).

14.4.4 Choosing a diversity mechanism

Mechanism Objective Cost per request Tunability Learned? Production users (public)
Hard rules (per-creator cap, category quota) Constraint O(N) Very easy No Nearly everyone
MMR [10] Relevance minus max-sim O(NK) 1 knob Rarely Search, RAG, feeds
Fast greedy DPP [3] log det of quality-similarity kernel O(K^2 N) alpha, sigma Kernel can be learned [2] YouTube [2], Hulu [3]
Calibration [4] Match user's genre mix (KL) O(NK * genres) lambda No Netflix research
Listwise context model [7] Outcome (bookings) given items above Model inference per position Implicit Yes Airbnb

14.5 Calibrated Recommendations (Netflix)

Problem. Harald Steck (Netflix, RecSys 2018) [4] gives a simple example. A user watched 70% romance and 30% action. An accuracy-optimised top-10 list may be 100% romance, because romance items score highest one by one. The list is accurate but mis-calibrated: the user's minority interest disappears. Over time the feedback loop can wipe that interest out of the profile altogether.

Formulation.

  • p(g | u): the target distribution over genres g, computed from the user's watch history. Each item's genre mass is spread across its genres, and items can be weighted, for example by recency.
  • q(g | u): the genre distribution of the recommended list.
  • Mis-calibration is measured with KL divergence, C_KL(p, q) = sum_g p(g|u) log(p(g|u) / q~(g|u)). Here q~ = (1 - a) * q + a * p with a small a (the paper uses a value around 0.01) so that the divergence stays finite when the list misses a genre.

Re-ranking objective.

I* = argmax_{I, |I| = N} (1 - lambda) * sum_{i in I} s(u, i) - lambda * C_KL(p, q(I))

Steck notes that the objective is close to submodular. A greedy algorithm that adds the item with the largest marginal gain therefore has the usual (1 - 1/e) approximation guarantee and runs fast enough for post-processing. Experiments on MovieLens 20M show that a small lambda removes most of the mis-calibration at a modest accuracy cost. Lists from a standard model trained for accuracy came out more mis-calibrated for users with diverse tastes.

Why it matters for system design.

  • Calibration is a personalised form of diversity. The target mix comes from the user, not from a global "be diverse" prior.
  • The same machinery can calibrate along any categorical axis that matters to the product: content type (movies vs series), creator popularity bucket (popular vs emerging), language, or freshness. Many later "calibrated" papers do exactly that.
  • It is a cheap re-ranker over the top few hundred candidates and needs no retraining.

14.6 Cold Start

Cold start has three cases with different solutions: new users, new items, and new creators/sellers. The last is item cold start plus a marketplace-health goal.

             +-------------------+      +------------------------+
 new item -->| content encoders  |----> | ID embedding warm-up   |--> ranker
 (meta,     | (text, image,     |      | (meta-embedding [25],   |
  media)    |  audio, creator)  |      |  DropoutNet [24])       |
             +-------------------+      +------------------------+
                      |                             ^
                      v                             |
            exploration traffic (bandits [32], boosted slots, priors [5])
                      |
                      v
            real-time training (minutes) -> ID embedding converges

 new user --> onboarding signals + context (geo, device, referrer)
          --> cohort-specific gating (POSO [26]) --> popular-within-cohort fallback

14.6.1 Item cold start with content and dropout

DropoutNet (Volkovs et al., Layer 6 AI, NeurIPS 2017) [24] trains a network that takes both preference embeddings (from collaborative filtering) and content features as input. During training it randomly drops out the preference input for some users and items. The network is forced to rebuild the warm-start relevance score from content alone, so the same model works for warm, cold and partly cold entities with no separate cold model. This idea, input dropout on ID/CF features, carries over directly to modern two-tower and DLRM systems: drop ID embeddings for some examples so that content and side-feature towers learn to stand alone.

14.6.2 Meta-learned ID embeddings for new ads

Pan et al. (SIGIR 2019, Tencent-related ad data) [25] attack the new-ad problem in CTR models. A new ad's randomly initialised ID embedding is noise until it has gathered enough clicks. Meta-Embedding trains a generator that maps an ad's attributes (category, advertiser, and so on) to an initial ID embedding. It uses a two-phase, MAML-style objective: the generated embedding should (a) predict well in the cold phase and (b) adapt fast after a few gradient steps on early data. The paper reports better CTR prediction for new ads in both the cold and warm-up phases on large ad datasets. Production descendants appear across ad systems: initialise from content or neighbours, never from zero.

14.6.3 Airbnb: priors for new listings

The 2020 Airbnb paper [5] describes the cold-start issue for new listings. Engagement features such as historical booking rate are missing or noisy, so the DNN ranks new listings poorly, and fewer impressions mean even less data. Airbnb's fix was to estimate the missing engagement features for new listings from similar nearby listings (same geography, capacity and so on) instead of using defaults. The paper reports a large relative booking gain for new listings in online tests (reported as approximately double-digit percent) and a smaller but significant overall booking gain. Combined with the position debiasing above (14.2.4), this is a clear example of debiasing and cold start being the same marketplace problem.

14.6.4 New users: Kuaishou POSO

Kuaishou's POSO (Personalized Cold Start Modules, Dai et al., 2021) [26] identifies a structural problem. In a large shared ranking model, signals from new users are swamped by the majority of active users. Even when "is_new_user" is an input feature, the network mostly ignores it because it is one feature among hundreds. POSO adds user-group-specific gating (personalised modules) to existing layers such as MLP, MHA and MMoE. A small gating network driven by user-cohort features (new vs regular, activity level) rescales hidden units, so cohort differences shape the whole computation. Kuaishou reports gains in new-user engagement and retention metrics in production, at negligible serving cost.

Pattern. Give minority cohorts a structural path through the network (gates, separate experts, separate towers), not just an input feature.

14.6.5 Exploration for cold start: contextual bandits

When features cannot fill the gap, the system must explore. Li et al.'s LinUCB (Yahoo!, WWW 2010) [32] scored news articles with a linear model plus an upper-confidence bonus alpha * sqrt(x^T A^-1 x). New articles have high uncertainty, so they automatically get exploratory traffic. On the Yahoo! front page the paper reports a click lift (roughly 12.5%) over a context-free bandit, using offline replay evaluation on randomly logged traffic. Chapter 13 covers modern neural bandits and exploration budgets.

14.6.6 Real-time training as a cold-start tool

Infrastructure matters too. ByteDance's Monolith [33] (collisionless embedding tables with expiry, plus online training that syncs parameters to serving at minute-level granularity) shortens the time a new item or user spends with an untrained embedding from hours or days to minutes. For fast-churning catalogues such as short video or news, the freshness of the training loop is often the biggest cold-start lever (see Chapter 9).

14.6.7 Cold-start strategy matrix

Entity Signal available Primary technique Secondary Example
New item Content, creator, metadata Content tower / meta-embedding [25] ID dropout [24], fast online training [33] Ads CTR, short video
New user Context, onboarding choices Cohort gating [26], popular-in-cohort Bandits [32], onboarding questionnaire Kuaishou, news
New creator / seller Content + creator profile Boosted exploration slots Priors from similar suppliers [5] Airbnb hosts, marketplaces
New surface / market Transfer from other surfaces Shared embeddings, multi-domain models Calibration to local mix [4] Any multi-product platform

14.7 Fairness for Creators, Sellers and Users

In multi-sided platforms, "fairness" usually means fair exposure for suppliers: creators, artists, hosts, sellers and job candidates. User-side group fairness (for example, equal recommendation quality across demographic groups) is the other main form.

14.7.1 Fairness of exposure: the theory

Singh and Joachims (KDD 2018) [20] define fairness constraints on the exposure that ranking policies give to groups. Exposure is the position-weighted attention, using the same position-bias curves as 14.2. Examples are demographic parity of exposure and exposure proportional to merit (relevance). The optimal fair ranking policy is computed as a linear program over doubly stochastic matrices, then decomposed (Birkhoff-von Neumann) into a distribution over rankings. Position bias therefore drives both relevance debiasing and fairness: the same propensity curve sets how much exposure each slot is worth.

FA*IR (Zehlike et al.) [35] is a simpler, top-k ranking algorithm. It guarantees that every prefix of the ranking holds at least a minimum share of a protected group, checked with a binomial significance test, while staying as close as possible to the score order.

14.7.2 LinkedIn Recruiter: fairness-aware re-ranking at scale

Problem. In LinkedIn Talent Search, recruiters search for candidates. LinkedIn wanted the gender distribution of top results to match the gender distribution of the qualified candidate pool for that query, a "representative" ranking.

Design (Geyik, Ambler, Kenthapadi, KDD 2019) [21]:

 query --> candidate retrieval --> ML ranker (relevance scores)
                                         |
                                         v
            desired distribution p_q(attribute) = distribution among candidates
            matching the query (e.g., qualified pool), computed per query
                                         |
                                         v
            fairness re-ranker: per-attribute queues sorted by score;
            fill ranks greedily so that every prefix k has at least
            floor(p_a * k) and at most ceil(p_a * k) of each attribute a
            (DetGreedy / DetCons / DetRelaxed variants)
                                         |
                                         v
                              top-k shown to recruiter

Key properties.

  • Post-processing, model-agnostic. The ranker is untouched. That made the change easy to ship and audit.
  • Per-query targets. The target is the attribute mix of the qualified candidates for that query, not a global quota.
  • Prefix constraints. Fairness holds at every k the recruiter might look at, not only in aggregate.
  • Results. The paper reports deployment to all LinkedIn Recruiter users worldwide and a large increase (reported as nearly three-fold) in the share of queries with representative results, with no significant drop in business metrics in A/B tests.

14.7.3 Spotify: relevance, fairness and satisfaction trade-offs

Mehrotra et al. (Spotify, CIKM 2018) [22] studied a music recommender as a two-sided marketplace. Artists differ widely in popularity, and a pure relevance policy pushes exposure to the head. Using counterfactual (off-policy) evaluation on logged data, they estimated user satisfaction under policies that mix relevance with a supplier-fairness score (exposure across artist popularity groups). Main findings:

  • Pure fairness policies hurt satisfaction. Pure relevance policies concentrate exposure.
  • Users differ in how open they are to less-popular artists. Adaptive policies that give fairness more weight for users with broader tastes reached better trade-offs than global interpolation.

This links fairness to calibration (14.5). Pushing exposure toward emerging suppliers works best when it follows each user's demonstrated appetite.

14.7.4 Google: pairwise fairness in production recommenders

Beutel et al. (Google, KDD 2019) [23] define pairwise fairness for recommenders. Among pairs where one item was engaged with and one was not, the model should rank the engaged item higher with equal probability whether the item belongs to group A or group B (with intra-group and inter-group variants). Measuring this needs data where both items were actually exposed, which they get from randomised experiments. They add a pairwise regulariser that penalises the correlation between group membership and residual pairwise error. They report that, in a large-scale production recommender at Google, the regulariser greatly improved inter-group pairwise fairness with little engagement loss.

14.7.5 User-side fairness

Yao and Huang [36] define unfairness metrics for collaborative filtering across user groups, for example under- or over-estimating ratings for a minority group, and add them as regularisers. Abdollahpouri et al. [15] show that popularity bias is itself a user-fairness issue, because niche-taste users get worse service. In practice, user-side fairness is monitored by slicing evaluation metrics by cohort (Chapter 12) and fixed with structural cohort modelling such as POSO [26].

14.7.6 Fairness design options compared

Approach Where Guarantee Cost Examples
Prefix-constrained re-ranking Post-ranking Hard, per prefix Low LinkedIn [21], FA*IR [35]
Exposure LP / stochastic ranking Post-ranking Expected exposure Medium (LP per query) Singh and Joachims [20]
Regulariser in training Model Soft, metric-level Training only Google pairwise [23], Yao and Huang [36]
Adaptive mixing per user Policy Soft, user-aware Low Spotify [22]
Exploration boosts for new suppliers Serving Soft Exploration budget Marketplaces, creator platforms

14.8 Putting It Together: A Reference Corrective Stack

A typical large-scale feed or marketplace stack that combines the designs above:

 [Training data]
   impressions + engagements + position + device + example age + duration
     |
     |-- reweight: fixed examples per user [12]; IPS for explicit ratings [13]
     v
 [Retrieval: two-tower]
   in-batch softmax with logQ correction via streaming frequency estimator [11]
   ID dropout so content towers handle cold items [24]
   meta-embedding initialisation for new IDs [25]
     |
     v  ~ thousands of candidates
 [Ranker: multitask DNN / MMoE]
   main towers (engagement, satisfaction)
   + shallow position/device tower, additive logit, position dropout [1][5]
   duration-bucketed quantile targets for watch time [27]
   cohort gates for new users [26]
   example_age = 0 and position = missing at serving [12][1]
     |
     v  ~ hundreds of candidates
 [Re-ranking / slate construction]
   fast greedy DPP or MMR within sliding windows [2][3][10]
   calibration to user's genre / creator-popularity mix [4]
   fairness prefix constraints where policy requires [21]
   exploration slots for cold items/creators (bandit bonus) [32]
     |
     v
 [Serving + logging]  log true positions, exploration flags, propensities
                      (needed by every debiasing method above)

Key Takeaways for System Designers

  1. Log what the debiasers need. Position, device, surface, exploration flag, sampling probability and (for off-policy work) the serving policy's propensity must be in the impression logs. Without them almost none of this chapter is possible.
  2. Prefer factorised bias towers to raw IPS in industrial rankers. YouTube's additive shallow tower [1], Huawei's multiplicative PAL [9] and Airbnb's position-feature-with- dropout [5] share one recipe: let a small component absorb the bias in training, then neutralise it at serving. Dropout on the bias feature is what makes neutralisation safe.
  3. Popularity bias hides in the training procedure. In-batch negatives need logQ correction [11]. Training windows need an example-age feature [12]. Watch-time targets need duration normalisation [27].
  4. Treat diversity as a slate-level property. Pointwise rankers cannot see redundancy. Use DPP or MMR with windowing for cheap gains [2][3]. Move to learned, context-aware listwise models once you can [7].
  5. Calibrate to the user, not to a global prior. Netflix's calibration [4] and Spotify's adaptive fairness [22] both show that the best trade-off follows each user's demonstrated breadth of interest.
  6. Cold start is a structural problem, not just a missing feature. Use content towers with ID dropout [24], meta-learned embedding initialisation [25], cohort-specific gating [26], neighbour-based priors [5], and fast online training [33]. Keep an explicit exploration budget [32].
  7. Fairness of exposure reuses the position-bias curve. The same propensity model that debiases clicks tells you how much exposure each slot gives. Measure supplier exposure with it [20].
  8. Ship fairness as auditable post-processing first. LinkedIn's per-query, prefix- constrained re-ranker [21] was model-agnostic, explainable and deployed globally with no measurable business loss.
  9. Evaluate counterfactually and by cohort. Off-policy estimators [13][22][31] and cohort-sliced metrics (new users, niche users, emerging creators) catch problems that aggregate NDCG hides.
  10. Expect long-term rather than immediate wins. Diversity, calibration and fair exposure often look neutral or slightly negative on short-term engagement. The reported gains in the YouTube DPP work [2] and the off-policy REINFORCE work [31] show up in satisfaction, retention and tail coverage. Design experiments long enough to measure them.

15. Re-ranking, Blending and Whole-Page Optimization

The last stage of almost every industrial recommender gets the least attention in papers and holds the most product policy in code. After retrieval, pre-ranking and a heavy multi-task ranker have assigned each candidate a score, something still has to turn a scored set into the thing a person sees. That might be a feed of posts mixed with ads and modules, a Netflix homepage of rows, a Taobao result page or a Kuaishou session of six videos. This chapter covers that "last mile":

  • Listwise and slate re-ranking. Models that score an item in the context of the other items on the list. Examples are DLCM, PRM (Alibaba), SetRank and PEAR, plus generator-evaluator and generative rerankers such as Seq2Slate, GRN/PRS, PIER and NAR4Rec.
  • Diversification. MMR, determinantal point processes (Hulu, YouTube, X), author decay, calibration.
  • Heterogeneous feed blending. Mixing content types, sources and ads into one stream (LinkedIn, Pinterest, X/Twitter, Meta).
  • Page-level optimization. Choosing and ordering rows and shelves (Netflix, Spotify, Deezer, Amazon).
  • The business-rules and constraints layer, which every published design keeps even as models get larger.

A note on sourcing. The live web-search and fetch budget for this chapter was used up before research could start, and outbound access to arXiv and company blogs was blocked from the writing environment. The chapter therefore relies on two kinds of source. The first is primary sources already fetched and verified by other chapters of this Atlas, such as Meta, X, Pinterest, LinkedIn, Netflix and Kuaishou posts and repositories. The second is a small set of canonical, widely cited papers whose identifiers are well established. Where a number could not be checked again, it is marked approximate. Readers should treat specific online-lift figures as indicative only.

1. Why a separate re-ranking stage exists

A pointwise ranker estimates something like P(click | user, item) for each candidate on its own. Then it sorts. That rests on three assumptions that fail in real products:

  1. Independence. An item's utility does not depend on its neighbours. In reality, the fifth phone case in a row is worth less than the first. A cheap item next to an expensive one changes how both are perceived. Alibaba's work on "mutual influence aware ranking" in Taobao search was motivated directly by this [10].
  2. Single objective. One score captures everything. In practice the page must also satisfy diversity, freshness, creator exposure, ad revenue, integrity and legal constraints [1][14][15].
  3. Uniform positions. Every slot is equal apart from a position-bias discount. Real surfaces are two-dimensional (Netflix rows, Spotify shelves) or have strong cascade behaviour (carousels where only the first few cards are seen) [23][24][25].

Google's public recommender course names the three-box pipeline candidate generation, scoring and re-ranking. It assigns freshness, diversity and fairness to the last box [2]. Eugene Yan's system-design synthesis likewise ends the online path with a ranking step followed by business logic and filtering [3]. Every public funnel in Chapter 1 has some final pass: Instagram's "final reranking" with integrity, diversity and business rules [14], Facebook Feed's final pass with integrity demotions and diversity [16], X's Home Mixer heuristics [17][18], and Pinterest's Multi-Objective Blender [20].

1.1 Canonical last-mile architecture

 heavy ranker output: ~10^1-10^3 candidates, each with p_click, p_like, p_hide, ...
        |
        v
 +--------------------+   value model: score = sum w_i * p_i (+ offsets)
 | 1. score fusion    |   (Ch. 4: Meta value model, X weights, Kuaishou ensemble sort)
 +---------+----------+
           v
 +--------------------+   hard filters: integrity, blocked/muted, seen, legal,
 | 2. eligibility     |   inventory, geo, age, dedup by item / cluster
 +---------+----------+
           v
 +--------------------+   context-aware rescoring: DLCM / PRM / SetRank / PEAR
 | 3. listwise rerank |   or generator + evaluator (Seq2Slate, GRN, PIER, NAR4Rec)
 +---------+----------+
           v
 +--------------------+   MMR / DPP / author decay / calibration / cold-start lift
 | 4. diversification |
 +---------+----------+
           v
 +--------------------+   interleave content types and sources, insert ads at
 | 5. blending / slots|   allowed positions, modules (WTF, stories, carousels)
 +---------+----------+
           v
 +--------------------+   rows / shelves / modules chosen and ordered;
 | 6. page assembly   |   cross-row dedup; device templates
 +---------+----------+
           v
     response + impression log (slate, positions, propensities)

In real systems these boxes are often merged. X folds diversity, out-of-network discounts and cold-start lifts into one scoring pass before a DPP reranker [18][19]. Netflix folds row selection and title placement into "page generation" [23][24]. The logical split is still useful when designing one.

2. Rule-based and heuristic re-ranking

2.1 Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR)

MMR (Carbonell and Goldstein, SIGIR 1998) is the ancestor of every greedy diversifier. Items are picked one at a time. Each step takes the candidate that maximizes lambda * rel(i) - (1 - lambda) * max_{j in S} sim(i, j), where S is the set already selected [4]. It costs O(N*K) similarity evaluations, needs no training and has one knob. Its weakness is that it only penalizes the nearest already-picked item, not the set as a whole.

2.2 Determinantal point processes (Hulu, YouTube, X)

A DPP scores a set S by det(L_S), where the kernel L_ij = q_i * sim(i, j) * q_j combines per-item quality q_i with pairwise similarity. The determinant is large when items are both good and mutually dissimilar.

  • Hulu (NeurIPS 2018). Chen, Zhang and Zhou made greedy MAP inference for DPPs practical. They update a Cholesky factor incrementally, so selecting K items from N costs O(N*K^2) instead of a fresh determinant at every step. They also add a sliding-window variant, so diversity is enforced only among nearby positions in a long feed [5]. That window idea matters in feeds, where a user cares that adjacent items differ, not that item 3 differs from item 300.
  • YouTube (CIKM 2018). Wilhelm et al. describe deploying a DPP on YouTube's mobile home feed. They learn the kernel from user interactions, parametrizing quality from the existing ranker and similarity from embeddings plus a few learned parameters. They apply it in windows over the feed. The paper reports gains in user satisfaction metrics from the deployment. Exact lift figures are not repeated here because they could not be checked again [6].
  • X (2026). In xAI's open-sourced x-algorithm, a separate vm-ranker step reorders the scored candidates with a DPP over embeddings after value-model scoring. It gives up a little score for less similarity between neighbouring posts [18][19].

2.3 Multiplicative decays and lifts (X / Twitter)

The X value-model code is the most detailed public example of a heuristic reranking layer [18][19]:

  weighted sum of ~25 heads  -> negative-score offset (keeps scores > 0)
     -> + exploration bonus
     -> x author-diversity multiplier: (1 - floor) * decay^k + floor
            (k = number of higher-ranked posts already chosen from that author)
     -> x out-of-network factor (< 1 for unfollowed accounts)
     -> cold-start lift (new author raised to at least a target rank)
     -> DPP reorder (vm-ranker) -> visibility filters -> timeline

Two details are worth copying. The negative-score offset maps negative raw scores into a small positive band [0, OFFSET) before any multiplier runs. A multiplier below 1 therefore cannot "promote" a negatively scored item by pulling it towards zero. And the author decay is sequential: it depends on how many posts by that author already sit above the candidate, so it has to be applied greedily in rank order, not as a single vectorized pass. The 2023 Twitter Home Mixer README lists the same family of heuristics: author diversity, content balance between in-network and out-of-network, feedback fatigue, de-duplication and social proof. Ads, Who-to-Follow and other modules are mixed in afterwards [17].

2.4 Calibration as a reranking objective (Netflix)

Steck's "Calibrated Recommendations" (Netflix, RecSys 2018) re-ranks a list so that its genre distribution q(g) matches the user's historical distribution p(g). It measures miscalibration with a KL divergence C_KL(p, q) and greedily maximizes (1 - lambda) * relevance - lambda * C_KL [7]. The motivation is that accuracy-optimized lists crowd out a user's minority interests. Someone who watches 70% romance and 30% action can get a list that is 100% romance. Calibration is a distributional constraint, not a pairwise similarity penalty, and it is cheap (greedy, submodular-style).

2.5 Round-robin blending (Pinterest)

Pinterest's early home feed ranked each content type with its own specialized model, then "blended with a ratio-based round robin" to produce the final feed [21]. A round robin with fixed ratios is the simplest heterogeneous blender. It guarantees a share of each type, but it cannot trade a mediocre item of type A against an excellent item of type B. That limit motivated Pinterest's later Multi-Objective Blender inside the ranking service [20].

3. Listwise contextual re-rankers

These models take the top-K list from the ranker (K is typically tens to low hundreds) and re-score every item given the whole list. Output is still a score per item, so serving stays "sort by score". This keeps them compatible with existing infrastructure.

3.1 DLCM: a recurrent list encoder (2018)

Ai et al.'s Deep Listwise Context Model (SIGIR 2018) feeds the top-K documents from a base ranker, in reverse rank order, into a GRU. The final hidden state is a "local context" vector. An attention-style scoring function then re-scores each item against that context. Training uses a listwise attention-rank loss [8]. It established the pattern: base ranker, then list encoder, then re-scored list. Its weakness is that the RNN is order-sensitive and processes items sequentially, so distant items interact only weakly.

3.2 Groupwise scoring functions (GSF)

Ai et al. (ICTIR 2019) score small groups of documents jointly with a DNN and aggregate the group scores per document. This makes "multivariate scoring" explicit without a full sequence model [9]. It shows that cross-item features help, but the number of groups grows combinatorially, which pushed later work towards attention.

3.3 Mutual-influence-aware ranking at Taobao (MIDNN)

Zhuang et al. (Alibaba, IJCAI 2018) formalize "globally optimized mutual influence aware ranking" for Taobao search. They add list-level features to each item, such as how an item's price compares with the rest of the list, and train a DNN on them. The final permutation is chosen with beam search under an evaluator [10]. This is an early industrial instance of the generator-evaluator pattern described in Section 4.

3.4 PRM: Personalized Re-ranking Model (Alibaba, RecSys 2019)

PRM, by Pei et al., is the most-cited industrial reranker and the template for most later work [11].

Problem. The initial list in Taobao recommendation is ranked pointwise. Item-item interactions on the list, and how those interactions differ per user, are ignored. A user who cares about price reacts differently to a list of similar items than a user who cares about brand.

Architecture.

  initial list from ranker: items i_1 .. i_n  (n = list length, tens of items)
        |
        v
  per item input  x_i = [ item feature vector  ||  PV_i ]  +  PE_i
        |               PV_i = personalized vector: hidden layer of a pre-trained
        |                      CTR model taking (user, item) -> user-specific item rep
        |               PE_i = learnable position embedding (initial rank)
        v
  linear projection to d_model
        v
  N x Transformer encoder blocks (multi-head self-attention + FFN)
        |   every item attends to every other item -> O(n^2) but n is small
        v
  linear + softmax over the list  -> re-ranked scores
        v
  sort -> final list

Key ideas.

  • Self-attention instead of RNN. Any two items interact directly, whatever their distance in the list. Attention is also parallel across positions, which matters for serving latency.
  • Personalized vector (PV). Rather than feed raw user features into the reranker, PRM pre-trains a pointwise CTR model and uses its hidden-layer output for each (user, item) pair as a per-item personalized embedding. This puts user-specific item representations into the reranker cheaply.
  • Position embedding of the initial rank. The ranker's ordering is itself a strong feature. Encoding it lets PRM learn when to keep and when to override the ranker.
  • Training objective. A list-level softmax cross-entropy over clicked items in the displayed list.

Results and deployment. The paper reports offline gains over DLCM and other baselines on a public learning-to-rank dataset and on a Taobao e-commerce recommendation dataset. It reports online A/B gains in page views, clicks and GMV on Taobao's recommendation surface. The exact percentages are not repeated here because they could not be checked again [11]. The authors also released the e-commerce re-ranking dataset.

Lessons. PRM established three conventions most later rerankers keep: (1) re-rank a short list (tens of items) so quadratic attention is affordable; (2) inject personalization through embeddings from upstream models instead of retraining a big user tower; and (3) keep the original rank as an input feature.

3.5 SetRank and permutation invariance

Pang et al.'s SetRank (SIGIR 2020) argues that a reranker should be permutation-invariant with respect to its input. The result should not depend on the order in which the base ranker happened to present items. It uses stacked induced multi-head self-attention blocks without positional encodings (or with optional rank encodings) [12]. In practice industrial systems still include the initial rank as a feature, as PRM does, because it carries useful information. SetRank shows that it should be a feature, not a structural assumption.

3.6 PEAR: contextualized transformer with history (Huawei, WWW 2022)

PEAR (Li et al.) extends PRM-style models in two ways. It models both feature-level and item-level interactions inside the list. It also lets the list items attend to the user's historical interactions, so the reranker sees context from the user's past as well as from the current list. It adds an auxiliary list-level classification task that predicts whether the user engages with the list as a whole [13]. This makes the reranker partly a sequence model. The cost is more attention compute per request.

3.7 The evaluator problem

Every listwise model in this section scores items given the initial ordering. But once the reranker moves items, the context it scored them in no longer exists. Re-scoring after re-ranking is circular. This "evaluation-before-reranking" gap is what motivated the generator-evaluator and generative approaches in Section 4.

4. Generative and generator-evaluator re-ranking

4.1 Seq2Slate (Google, 2018/2019)

Bello et al.'s Seq2Slate frames re-ranking as sequence generation with a pointer network. An encoder (RNN in the original) reads the candidate set. A decoder emits one candidate per step, conditioned on what it has already placed, by attending over the inputs [27]. Because each step sees the items already chosen, the model captures "what is good next given what is above", which a scoring model cannot do. Training uses click logs. The paper proposes supervised listwise losses that treat clicked items as targets to be placed early, as well as a REINFORCE-style policy-gradient variant. It reports offline gains on learning-to-rank benchmarks and an evaluation on data from a large-scale commercial recommender at Google [27].

Serving cost is K sequential decoding steps over N candidates. That is acceptable for K of around 10-20 and N in the low hundreds, but it is the main obstacle to generative reranking at feed scale.

4.2 Generator-evaluator: Exact-K, PRS, GRN

Several Alibaba and Meituan papers split the problem in two:

            candidates (N)                      evaluator (list-wise CTR / utility model)
                |                                       ^
                v                                       | score each candidate permutation
   +---------------------------+     M candidate    +---+----------------------------+
   | generator: beam search /  | --> permutations-->| list-aware model: sees full   |
   | sampling / pointer net /  |     (M ~ tens-     | slate incl. later positions;  |
   | heuristic permutations    |      hundreds)     | predicts list reward          |
   +---------------------------+                    +---+----------------------------+
                                                        v
                                         pick argmax permutation -> serve
  • Exact-K (Alibaba, KDD 2019). Gong et al. pose "exact-K recommendation", choosing a set of exactly K items that is jointly good, as maximal-clique optimization on a graph of candidate items. They use a graph-attention encoder plus a pointer-network decoder trained with RL, with a reward from a learned evaluator [28].
  • PRS: "Revisit Recommender System in the Permutation Prospective" (2021). This paper separates a Permutation-Matching stage, which generates candidate permutations efficiently with beam search, from a Permutation-Ranking stage. The second stage scores each whole permutation with a list-wise evaluator. It reports online gains in a large production feed. The authors are at Alibaba/Taobao; the exact attribution and numbers were not re-checked [29].
  • GRN: Generative Rerank Network (2021). Feng et al. train a context-wise evaluator first, then train a pointer-network generator with policy gradient, using the evaluator's predicted list reward as the reward signal [30].

The evaluator is trained on logged slates, so it sees each item in the context it was actually shown in. It is therefore a more faithful judge of a permutation than any pointwise score. The generator only has to propose good candidates.

4.3 PIER (Meituan, WSDM 2023)

PIER (Permutation-level Interest-based End-to-end Re-ranking) addresses the cost of the generator-evaluator pattern at Meituan's scale. A Fine-grained Permutation Selection Module uses SimHash-style hashing of user interest to pick the top permutations cheaply from a very large permutation space. An Omnidirectional Context-aware Prediction Module then scores those permutations. The two modules are trained end to end, instead of with a frozen evaluator [31]. The lesson is that permutation search has to be approximated aggressively. Hashing and retrieval-style tricks from candidate generation carry over to the permutation space.

4.4 NAR4Rec: non-autoregressive generation (Kuaishou, KDD 2024)

Autoregressive generators decode one position at a time, which adds latency in proportion to slate length. Kuaishou's NAR4Rec generates all positions in parallel with a non-autoregressive model. It adds techniques for the sparse-data and position-dependency problems that come with that choice: a matching model for training and contrastive decoding to avoid repeated items. The paper reports deployment in Kuaishou's short-video app, which has hundreds of millions of daily users, with gains in engagement metrics. Specific figures are approximate and were not re-checked [32].

4.5 The generative endpoint: session-wise generation (Kuaishou OneRec)

Kuaishou's OneRec (2025) goes furthest. A single generative model produces a whole session of videos, removing the retrieve/rank/rerank cascade for that path. It is then aligned with a reward model via preference optimization [33][34]. In effect the reranker's job of choosing a jointly good list moves into the generator, and the reranker's evaluator becomes a reward model. Chapter 6 covers OneRec in depth. The relevant point here is that even OneRec's reports keep filtering and business-rule logic outside the model.

5. Slate RL and long-horizon reranking

Pointwise and listwise rerankers optimize immediate list reward. Two lines of work extend this over time.

  • SlateQ (Google, IJCAI 2019). Under a single-choice assumption (the user picks at most one item from the slate) and the assumption that rewards and transitions depend only on the item picked, the long-term value of a slate decomposes into item-level Q-values weighted by a user choice model. The slate can then be optimized exactly with a linear program for the conditional-logit choice model, or approximately with greedy top-k. SlateQ was tested in live YouTube experiments by replacing the myopic per-item score with the decomposed long-term value [35].
  • Page-wise RL (JD.com, RecSys 2018). Zhao et al. treat a whole 2-D page of items as the action. An actor-critic uses a deconvolutional actor to output the page layout, and a critic scores the page given user state and feedback on earlier pages [36].
  • Slate off-policy evaluation (Microsoft, NeurIPS 2017). Swaminathan et al.'s pseudo-inverse estimator evaluates new slate policies from logged data, assuming the slate reward is additive over (item, position) pairs. Its sample complexity is far lower than naive inverse propensity scoring over the combinatorial slate space [37]. It is the standard tool for deciding whether a new reranker is worth an A/B slot.

Chapter 13 discusses these methods at length. For reranking, the main lesson is that logging propensities for whole slates is an architectural prerequisite. Without it, neither OPE nor slate RL works.

6. Heterogeneous feed blending

A single surface often shows several kinds of thing at once. Feed posts, jobs, ads, people-you-may-know cards, stories trays and video carousels come from separate teams with separately trained, separately calibrated models. Blending is the problem of putting them on one comparable scale and one layout.

6.1 LinkedIn: first-pass rankers and a second-pass ranker

LinkedIn's 2019 feed architecture is federated. Multiple first-pass rankers (FPRs) each select and score candidates from their own inventory (network updates, jobs, recommended content and so on). A second-pass ranker (SPR) merges their outputs into one ranked list. FollowFeed, which serves updates from a member's network, was the dominant FPR, supplying more than 80% of feed updates [22].

   FollowFeed FPR ----+   (network updates; >80% of feed items in 2019 [22])
   Jobs FPR ----------+
   Recommended FPR ---+--> SPR: unified feature space, multi-objective score
   PYMK / modules ----+        (e.g. viral actions, contributions, creator side)
   Ads (separate auction) ------------+
                                      v
                          slotting: ads at allowed positions -> feed

The design matches how the organization is split, since each inventory team owns its FPR. But it pushes cross-source calibration onto the SPR. If one FPR's scores drift, its share of the feed drifts too. LinkedIn tuned the SPR's multi-objective weights with automated online search instead of by hand (secondary coverage) [38]. The 2019 post's "community-focused" work also changed the objective to account for value to creators and the poster's community, not only to the viewer [22].

6.2 Pinterest: from round-robin to a multi-objective blender

As noted in Section 2.5, Pinterest first blended type-specific rankers with a fixed-ratio round robin [21]. Its WWW 2022 home-feed funnel puts a Multi-Objective Blender after the Utility Prediction Scorer inside the Ranking Service [20]. Later work personalizes the utility weights per request: PRL-PUTS, a one-step value-based RL policy that picks a weight vector per request and exposes an empirical Pareto frontier for governance. It reports +0.13% successful sessions online with no added serving latency [39]. Moving from ratio rules, to a single learned utility, to per-request weights is the typical path for a blender.

6.3 X / Twitter: Home Mixer and modules

X's Home Mixer is built on Product Mixer, a framework of pipelines. A product pipeline selects mixer pipelines, which run candidate pipelines, and the mixer interleaves ranked tweets with ads and modules such as Who-to-Follow [17][40]. The 2026 x-algorithm describes the same orchestration as reusable Rust traits named Source, Hydrator, Filter, Scorer, Selector and SideEffect [18]. That vocabulary maps neatly onto the boxes in Section 1.1. The in-network/out-of-network balance, about 50/50 on average in 2023, is a blending decision made through an out-of-network multiplier, not a fixed quota [17][19].

6.4 Meta: Facebook Feed and Instagram

Meta's 2021 Feed post describes ranking in passes. Integrity processes run first. A lightweight model narrows more than 1,000 candidate posts per user to about 500. Multitask neural networks predict several actions. Those predictions are combined into a single value. A final pass applies contextual rules such as diversity, so that a user does not see several posts from the same source in a row [16]. Instagram Explore's 2023 architecture likewise ends with a final reranking stage applying integrity, diversity and business rules after a linear value model over MTML predictions [14]. The 2020 Instagram post explains why some rules live as constraints: suggested content in Explore had to pass integrity and quality bars before being eligible. A log-linear value model lets a negative-feedback prediction act as a near-veto [15].

Meta's public posts do not describe in detail how ads are slotted into organic feeds. The architectural pattern visible across the industry is that ads go through their own retrieval, ranking and auction (Chapter 1 summarizes Andromeda and GEM) and are then inserted into the organic stream at allowed positions. Insertion is governed by ad-load and spacing constraints, not by direct score comparison with organic items.

6.5 Ads and organic: the allocation problem

A pattern consistent with public designs and with academic literature on feed ad allocation:

 organic ranked list O = [o1, o2, ...]       ad list A = [a1, a2, ...] (auctioned)
                \                                   /
                 v                                 v
          +---------------------------------------------------+
          | allocator                                         |
          |  - candidate slots: fixed (e.g. every k-th) or    |
          |    dynamic                                        |
          |  - constraints: min gap between ads, max ad load  |
          |    per session, no ad in slot 1, category rules   |
          |  - objective: revenue(a, pos) + lambda *          |
          |    engagement_loss(pos)                           |
          |  - solver: greedy / DP over slots / RL policy     |
          +---------------------------------------------------+
                                  v
                       final feed + ad-load telemetry

The key design decisions are:

  1. Shared currency. Organic value (predicted engagement) and ad value (expected revenue) are in different units. Exchange rates (lambda) are set as policy and tuned online against long-term retention, not learned end to end.
  2. Fixed vs dynamic slots. Fixed slots are predictable and easy to audit. Dynamic slots let a high-value ad move up, or an irrelevant one move down or out, per user and session.
  3. Externalities. An ad's cost is lost engagement on the organic items it displaces and any session shortening it causes. That makes this a page-level problem, not an item-level one.

Several Chinese platforms (Meituan, ByteDance, Kuaishou) have published RL-based ad-allocation papers with this structure. Because none of them could be checked again for this chapter, they are not cited individually.

7. Whole-page optimization

7.1 Netflix: page generation

Netflix's homepage is the canonical two-dimensional recommendation surface. Gomez-Uribe and Hunt (ACM TMIS 2015) describe it as a grid of rows. A typical page had about 40 rows, each with up to about 75 titles (device-dependent). Each row is produced by a different algorithm: the Personalized Video Ranker (PVR) for genre rows, a Top-N ranker for "Top Picks", trending, continue-watching, and video-video similarity for "Because you watched" rows. A page generation algorithm selects and orders the rows [23]. The paper notes that a member typically loses interest after about 60-90 seconds of choosing, having looked at perhaps 10-20 titles, which is why page composition matters so much. It also estimates that recommendation and personalization saved Netflix more than 1 billion US dollars a year in reduced churn (approximate, as stated in the paper) [23].

Netflix's 2015 tech-blog post "Learning a Personalized Homepage" (Alvino and Basilico) describes the page-generation problem in more detail [24]:

  candidate rows: genre rows (PVR), Top Picks, Because-You-Watched, Trending,
                  Continue Watching, New Releases, ...  (each row ranks its own titles)
        |
        v
  row scoring  (relevance of row to member, given context/device)
        |
        v
  stage-wise greedy page construction:
     for slot in 1..R:
        pick row maximizing  score(row | rows already placed)
          - penalize duplicate titles across rows (dedup / diversity)
          - enforce constraints (e.g. Continue Watching near top, device limits,
            min/max of row types)
        |
        v
  render: rows top-to-bottom, titles left-to-right (2-D attention)

Points from that post:

  • Template vs row-scoring approaches. A fixed template ("row type X at position Y") is simple but not personal. Scoring rows independently and sorting gives relevance but not diversity. Rows end up redundant and repeat the same titles.
  • Stage-wise (greedy) construction. The page is built one row at a time. Each candidate row is scored given the rows already chosen, which naturally captures diversity and dedup. It is the row-level analogue of MMR.
  • Page-level metrics. Because the user scans in two dimensions, Netflix evaluates pages with 2-D extensions of ranking metrics, for example a recall over the top-m rows by top-n columns that a user is likely to see.
  • Balance. The page has to balance accuracy, diversity, discovery and freshness against constraints that differ by device.

Netflix's later posts add more page-level signals. Artwork is personalized per member with contextual bandits, and the choice of image interacts with the rest of the page [25]. Ranking has been consolidated into fewer, multi-task models serving many rows and canvases [41]. Objectives have moved towards long-term member satisfaction [42]. Netflix also uses interleaving to compare row rankers. It cannot measure page-composition effects, so those still need A/B tests [43].

7.2 Spotify home: shelves with explanations

Spotify's BaRT (RecSys 2018) is the bandit system behind the home page, a grid of shelves of playlists and albums. Each recommendation can carry an explanation ("Because you listened to X"). BaRT treats the (item, explanation) pair as the action and learns which combination to show in each shelf position. It uses counterfactual training from logged propensities [26]. It is whole-page optimization at the shelf level. The reranker chooses how a recommendation is framed as well as which item to show.

7.3 Deezer: carousels and the visibility model

Deezer models its playlist carousel as a contextual cascade bandit. Only the first L cards are visible without swiping, and cards beyond the last one the user would have seen get no feedback, so they are neither penalized nor rewarded. Users are clustered so that bandits learn per cluster (semi-personalization) [44]. The lesson for reranking: the click model of the surface has to be part of the objective, otherwise the system learns to avoid positions that were never seen.

7.4 Amazon: combinatorial page layouts

Hill et al. (Amazon, KDD 2017) optimize a page of several widgets with many possible values each, giving a combinatorial space of layouts. They use a Bayesian linear model with pairwise interaction terms, Thompson sampling, and greedy hill climbing to approximately maximize the sampled model in real time. They report about a 21% conversion improvement over the median layout in a live experiment [45]. The pattern is to sample a model, then use a cheap combinatorial optimizer. It carries over directly to row ordering and module placement.

7.5 Airbnb: diversity in search ranking

Airbnb's "Learning To Rank Diversely" (2022) addresses a whole-page effect in search. Listings ranked purely by booking probability can become homogeneous, for example all at the same price point or in the same neighbourhood. Users who would book something different then find nothing. The paper changes the training and inference of the neural ranker so that each listing's score depends on what was ranked above it, which is a contextual "similarity to listings above" mechanism. It reports a booking gain in online experiments [46].

8. The business-rules and constraints layer

Every public design keeps an explicit, non-learned layer: Netflix, Meta, X, Pinterest, LinkedIn, Kuaishou, even OneRec. Google's "Rules of Machine Learning" recommends keeping heuristics and filtering explicit and outside the model where they are policy rather than prediction [47].

8.1 What lives there

Category Examples Hard / soft Typical implementation
Eligibility blocked/muted, already seen, out of stock, geo/licensing, age gates hard filter before or after rerank [16][17]
Integrity policy-violating, borderline, low-quality hard or demotion integrity models run first; demotion multipliers [14][16]
Dedup same item, near-duplicate media, same cluster, cross-row duplicates hard hash / cluster-id sets; page-level dedup [17][24]
Diversity author/source caps, category spread, content balance soft decay multipliers, DPP, MMR [5][18][19]
Freshness / fatigue recency boosts, "seen too often" penalties soft multipliers, impression-count features [17]
Exposure cold-start creators, new items, exploration soft minimum rank, bonuses, reserved slots [18][19]
Mix / quotas in-network vs out-of-network, content-type ratios soft or hard multipliers or ratio round robin [19][21]
Monetization ad load, ad spacing, no ad in slot 1 hard allocator constraints (Section 6.5)
Layout row count, row-type limits, device templates, pinned rows hard page-generation constraints [23][24]

8.2 Design patterns

 config store (versioned, A/B-able)
      |  rules as data: {id, scope(surface, country), type(filter|cap|boost|slot),
      |                  params, priority, experiment_id}
      v
 +-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
 | rule engine in the mixer                                                |
 |  1. hard filters (set operations; cheap; run early AND re-run at end)   |
 |  2. score adjustments (multipliers/offsets; order-preserving sign care) |
 |  3. sequential constraints (greedy fill: author cap, gap rules, DPP)    |
 |  4. slot constraints (ads, modules, pinned rows)                        |
 |  5. backfill if constraints leave holes (fallback sources)              |
 +-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
      |
      v  log: which rule touched which item (for debugging and OPE)

Practical lessons from public sources:

  • Separate prediction from policy. X ships its weights and multipliers as configuration (param.rs) separate from the model, so policy changes need no retraining [18][19]. Meta tunes value-model weights to trade off online metrics [14].
  • Watch the sign and scale of scores. Multiplicative rules assume positive, calibrated scores. X's negative-score offset exists because a multiplier below 1 can raise a negative score [19]. Chapter 4 explains why calibration is the contract between the model and this layer.
  • Run filters twice. Cheap eligibility filters run before expensive models to save compute (Meta runs integrity first [16]). They run again at the end, because later stages such as blending and backfill can reintroduce items.
  • Make rules visible to learning. Rules change the logged distribution. If the reranker or ranker is trained on post-rule impressions without knowing which rule acted, it learns the rules as if they were user preferences. Logging rule decisions and propensities fixes this [37].
  • Rules accumulate. The usual failure is hundreds of interacting boosts that nobody can explain. Treat rules as code: give each one an owner and an experiment, and expire it.
