26. Marketplace and Travel Recommenders: Airbnb, Booking.com, Uber Eats, DoorDash and Others

Marketplace recommenders differ from media recommenders in a few ways that shape the whole design. The "item" is a physical supply unit that someone else owns: a listing, a hotel room, a restaurant, a driver. Supply is limited, tied to a place, and often tied to a date. A recommendation is only useful if it can actually be fulfilled: the listing is free for those dates, the restaurant is open and within delivery range, the host will accept. The label we most care about (a booking or an order) is rare, comes late, and can be undone by cancellations or host rejections. Every ranking change also moves demand between sellers, which creates fairness concerns and makes A/B tests interfere with each other.

This chapter covers the publicly documented designs from these companies. Airbnb has the richest public record: its KDD 2018 listing embeddings, the KDD 2019 and 2020 papers on deep learning for search, the multi-task "journey" ranker, learning to rank diversely, and embedding-based retrieval in 2025-2026. Booking.com's "150 successful models" paper is the best-known statement of what goes wrong between offline metrics and business value. Uber Eats contributes GNN features, a two-tower homefeed retriever and the Michelangelo platform. DoorDash contributes store embeddings, explore/exploit on the homepage and its feature platforms (Riviera, Fabricator, a Redis feature store). We also briefly cover Lyft, Expedia, Zillow, Yelp and Instacart, mostly to describe the patterns they share.

A note on sourcing. This chapter was written in an environment where the web-search budget was used up and outbound fetches to arXiv, Medium and company blogs were blocked by network policy. Facts are therefore taken from (a) sources that were fetched and checked while sibling chapters of this atlas were researched, and (b) well-established primary papers whose content is widely cited. References that could not be re-fetched are marked "not re-verified" in the reference list. Numbers from those sources are given as approximate and should be checked against the original before you quote them.

26.1 What makes marketplace recommenders different

Dimension Media feed (e.g. video) Marketplace / travel
Item Unlimited copies of a piece of content Unique, capacity-limited supply unit
Validity Almost always valid Availability, dates, delivery radius, opening hours
Primary label Watch time, engagement (dense) Booking / order (sparse, delayed, reversible)
Session length Minutes Days to weeks (travel); minutes (food)
Geo constraint Weak Hard (city, market, delivery zone)
Other side Creators, loosely coupled Hosts / merchants / drivers who can reject
Experiment interference Low High: treatment and control compete for supply
Repeat behaviour Varies Low for travel; very high for food and grocery

Three consequences come up again and again in the systems below:

  1. Geography partitions the problem. Retrieval is almost always geo-filtered first, and negatives must be sampled from the same market, or the model only learns geography.
  2. The label is a funnel. Click, then detail view, then checkout, then booking, then not cancelled. Multi-task and staged models that use the denser upper-funnel signals are standard.
  3. Offline metrics lie more often. Booking.com and Airbnb both report many cases where offline gains did not show up as business gains. Online experiments, often with interleaving or switchbacks, are the final judge.

26.2 Airbnb search ranking

Airbnb search takes a query (location, dates, number of guests, filters) and returns a ranked list of listings that are available for those dates. The public record covers the system end to end, from the GBDT era to a multi-stage deep-learning stack.

26.2.1 Overall architecture

 guest query (place, dates, guests, filters)
        |
        v
 +--------------------------+     availability, price, geo filters
 | Retrieval                |---> (inverted index; since 2025 also
 |  - geo + availability    |      two-tower EBR with IVF clusters as filters [8][9])
 +--------------------------+
        |  candidates (order of thousands, approximate)
        v
 +--------------------------+     features: listing, query, guest, real-time
 | First-pass / base ranker |     session features from embeddings [1]
 |  DNN (pairwise/listwise) |     (journey ranker: multi-task base module [5])
 +--------------------------+
        |
        v
 +--------------------------+
 | Second pass / context    |     diversity given listings above [6],
 | twiddlers, business rules|     cancellation / rejection penalties [5]
 +--------------------------+
        |
        v
  ranked results  ---> logs (impressions, clicks, bookings) ---> training
                         \--> interleaving experiments [10]

26.2.2 Real-time personalization with listing embeddings (KDD 2018)

Problem. Ranking should react to what the guest is doing in the current session. A guest who clicks on several cheap, modern apartments near the city centre should see more of those, right away, without retraining a model.

Design. Grbovic and Cheng trained word2vec-style skip-gram embeddings on search click sessions [1]. Each session is a sequence of listing IDs that a user clicked, and sessions are split when there is a gap of more than 30 minutes between clicks [1][7]. Figures reported in secondary summaries of the paper (approximate): about 800 million click sessions, about 4.5 million active listings, and 32-dimensional embeddings [1][11].

Two changes to plain skip-gram matter most:

  • Booked listing as global context. In sessions that end in a booking, the booked listing is added as a context item for every listing in the session, whether or not it falls inside the sliding window. This pulls the embedding towards "what people who looked at this eventually booked", not only towards "what was clicked next to it".
  • Market-aware negatives. Random negatives almost always come from another city, which makes them trivially easy. Airbnb adds negatives sampled from the same market as the central listing, so the model must learn differences within a market (style, price, neighbourhood), not just geography.

Cold start. A new listing has no clicks. Its embedding is set to the average of the embeddings of about three nearby listings of the same type and similar price, as described in the paper (approximate).

Long-term interest: type embeddings. Bookings are too sparse to learn per-user and per-listing embeddings from booking sequences directly. Airbnb therefore maps users and listings to coarse types, built from bucketed attributes such as market, price, room type and capacity for listings, and similar buckets for users. User-type and listing-type embeddings are learned in the same vector space from booking sequences. Host rejections are used as explicit negatives in this training, so the embedding also captures "this kind of guest tends to be rejected by this kind of listing".

How it is used.

  • Similar listings carousel. K nearest neighbours by cosine similarity, filtered by availability. Secondary summaries report about a 21% CTR increase over the previous similar-listings algorithm [11].
  • Real-time ranking features. Kafka streams record the user's clicked listings, skipped listings, long clicks, wishlisted listings and contacted listings over roughly the last two weeks. For each candidate, features such as "similarity to clicked listings" and "similarity to skipped listings" are computed online and fed to the GBDT search ranker that was in production at the time. The paper reports a booking gain from these features in an online test, and the embedding similarity features rank high in feature importance.

Lessons. (1) Cheap embeddings and simple online similarity features can give most of the benefit of session personalization, with no online model training. (2) Change the objective to match the business event (booking as global context). (3) Sample negatives from the same constraint set the user actually chooses within.

26.2.3 Moving to deep learning (KDD 2019)

"Applying Deep Learning to Airbnb Search" [2] is unusually candid. It reads as a log of what the team tried, what failed and why.

The trajectory (as described in the paper):

  1. A GBDT model with heavy hand-made features had become hard to improve.
  2. A simple neural network with one hidden layer (32 ReLU units) reached about parity with GBDT.
  3. Training with a LambdaRank-style pairwise loss (booked listing versus not-booked listings in the same search, weighted by the NDCG change of a swap) helped.
  4. An intermediate step combined GBDT and factorization-machine outputs as inputs to the neural network.
  5. The final step was a deeper network with 2 hidden layers and about 195 features, trained on the order of 1.7 billion pairs (figures approximate, as reported in [2]). This model let the team stop much of the manual feature engineering.

Things that failed (and the reasons the paper gives):

  • Listing ID embeddings. They overfit badly. Even a popular listing can be booked at most about 365 times a year, so there is very little data per ID compared with words in a language model.
  • Multi-task learning with long views. Adding a "long view" (dwell) task made views go up, but bookings did not follow. The model learned to promote listings that were nice to look at, such as expensive or unusual homes, that people did not book.
  • Features that are proxies for the label. Several offline NDCG wins did not reproduce online, which taught the team to be suspicious of offline gains.

Engineering practices that worked:

  • Normalize features so they look roughly normal: log-transform heavy-tailed features such as price, and express geo coordinates relative to the centre of the map viewport rather than as raw latitude and longitude.
  • Check feature distributions and plot model output as a function of single features, to catch features that the network uses in surprising ways.
  • Accept that the deep model is harder to explain, and invest in debugging tools.

Lesson. Moving from GBDT to DNN was not one model change. It was a journey of many small steps, and each needed an online test. The biggest gains came from scale (more training data, fewer hand-built features) once the basics (normalization, a pairwise loss) were right.

26.2.4 Architecture, bias and cold start (KDD 2020)

"Improving Deep Learning for Airbnb Search" [3] groups its changes under three headings.

Architecture: a two-tower "ideal listing" model. The team found that the DNN had learned a strong "cheaper is better" bias. Many guests have a preference for a price that is not the lowest. The new design has a query/user tower that produces an "ideal listing" vector from the query and the guest, and a listing tower that produces a vector for each listing. The score depends on the distance between the two. This makes the model favour listings close to what this guest wants, rather than ones that maximize a single monotone direction such as low price. The paper reports a booking gain online.

Bias: position as a feature, with dropout. Bookings depend strongly on rank position. Airbnb adds the listing's position as an input feature during training and applies dropout to that feature. At inference time the position is set to a constant (zero), so every listing is scored as if shown in the same position. The dropout rate trades off two failures. With too little dropout the model leans on position. With too much it cannot separate the effect of position from the effect of quality. The tuned version gave a statistically significant booking gain [3].

Cold start: estimate engagement for new listings. New listings have missing or noisy engagement features (for example historical booking rate), so the DNN ranks them low, which means they get fewer impressions and stay data-poor. Airbnb replaces the defaults with estimates computed from similar nearby listings (same geography, similar capacity and so on). The paper reports a large relative booking gain for new listings (roughly double-digit percent; around 14% as commonly quoted, approximate) and a small but significant overall booking gain [3].

   query + guest features            listing features (+ position at train time)
            |                                   |
     [ query tower ]                    [ listing tower ]
            |                                   |
       "ideal listing"  ----- distance -----  listing vector
                                |
                       score -> pairwise loss
   at serving: position feature := 0 ; new-listing engagement := neighbour estimate

26.2.5 Learning to rank diversely (2022, CIKM 2023)

Problem. A ranker that scores each listing on its own puts similar listings next to each other: same price range, same neighbourhood, same style. A guest whose taste differs from the average then finds nothing to book on the first page.

Design. Abdool et al. [6] change training and inference so that a listing's score depends on the listings already ranked above it. In effect, the model learns "what is the chance this listing gets booked, given what the guest has already seen above". Listings that look like the ones above are worth less. Ranking is done greedily, position by position. The paper reports an online booking gain.

Lesson. In a marketplace, diversity is not a nice-to-have. It is a way to cover the spread of guest preferences when the ranker cannot read them from the query.

26.2.6 Journey ranker: multi-task learning along the booking funnel (KDD 2023)

Problem. A booking is the end of a long journey: search, click, view the listing page, go to the payment page, request or instantly book, the host accepts, and the trip is not cancelled. Training only on bookings throws away the denser signals before it. Training on clicks alone optimizes the wrong thing.

Design (Tan et al., "Optimizing Airbnb Search Journey with Multi-task Learning" [5]). The Journey Ranker is built from modules:

  • Base module. A multi-task network that predicts each step of the positive funnel (click, listing page, payment page, request, booking). The final score combines the conditional probabilities along the funnel, so dense early steps help the model learn while the target is still the booking.
  • Twiddler module. Predicts negative milestones such as cancellations and host rejections, and uses them to adjust the score. This keeps the ranker from sending guests to listings that tend to fall through.
  • Context module. Lets the combination weights depend on context, for example how far ahead the trip is or what kind of guest is searching.
  • Monotonic module. Enforces monotonic relationships for some features (for example, that a better value on a quality signal should never lower the score).

The paper reports online booking gains and says the design was reused for other Airbnb search surfaces (approximate; see [5]).

Lesson. Model the funnel explicitly, including the negative outcomes that only the marketplace sees (rejections, cancellations). A booking that is later cancelled is not a success.

26.2.7 Embedding-based retrieval (2025-2026)

Airbnb's most recent public work adds a learned retrieval stage [8][9].

  • Model. Two-tower. The listing tower is run offline in a daily batch. The query tower runs online for each search.
  • Training data. Built from guest search journeys, with session-based hard negatives (listings the guest saw in the session but did not book) instead of random negatives.
  • ANN choice. HNSW gave slightly better recall in evaluation, but Airbnb chose IVF. Prices and availability change all the time, and HNSW's memory overhead on frequent updates was a problem. With IVF, a listing's cluster assignment becomes an ordinary filter in the existing search system, so retrieval is "match the query to clusters, then filter by cluster plus the usual availability filters" [8].
  • Result. The paper reports significant booking gains [9].

Lesson. When items change often and retrieval must respect hard filters, an index that fits into the existing filter engine (IVF clusters) can beat a slightly more accurate graph index (HNSW).

26.2.8 Experimentation for search: interleaving

Airbnb adapted team-draft interleaving to a two-sided marketplace with sparse, delayed bookings [10]. Only "competitive pairs", the positions where the two rankers actually differ, are used for attribution, and searches where both rankers agree are dropped. Airbnb reports roughly a 50x gain in sensitivity compared with A/B tests, and interleaving results agreed in direction with later A/B tests in most paired comparisons (approximate) [10]. Interleaving is used to screen ranking ideas quickly; A/B tests still make the final call.

26.2.9 Data platform: Zipline to Chronon

Airbnb's feature platform Zipline was rebuilt and open-sourced as Chronon, which is maintained jointly with Stripe and is described as powering all major ML applications at Airbnb [12]. It lets engineers define features in Python (GroupBy, Join) once. The same definition is used for point-in-time-correct backfills in Spark and for online serving with streaming updates. This removes the main source of train-serve skew for real-time features such as the session embedding similarities in 26.2.2. Chapter 8 covers Chronon in detail.

26.3 Booking.com: 150 models and 6 lessons

Bernardi, Mavridis and Estevez's KDD 2019 paper [4] is not about one model. It summarizes what Booking.com learned from about 150 customer-facing ML models in production. It is one of the most quoted papers on applied recommender systems.

26.3.1 Model families

The paper groups the models into families (paraphrased):

Family What it predicts Example use
Traveller preferences How flexible the user is about dates or destination Show alternative dates or places
Traveller context Trip type (family, business, couple) Adapt filters and messaging
Item space navigation Which items or destinations the user will engage with Recommendations, sorting
User interface optimization Best layout, font size, number of items UI parameters
Content curation Which reviews, photos or descriptions to show Review highlights
Content augmentation Derived facts about properties "Great value today", price trend

Most of these are not "rank the hotels" models. They are small predictions that each shape part of the experience, and their combined effect is the product.

26.3.2 The six lessons

  1. ML projects deliver value. Across families, models gave measurable business gains in randomized experiments. Even "semantic" models of hidden concepts (such as how flexible a user is) worked as building blocks for many features.
  2. Model performance is not business performance. Better offline metrics often gave no business gain. Reasons the paper gives: the value is already saturated, the model optimizes a proxy that diverges from conversion, and an "uncanny valley" effect where a prediction that is too accurate feels intrusive to users.
  3. Be on the lookout for the problem to solve. Framing the problem well (for example as regression versus classification, or picking the right label) mattered more than the learner.
  4. Prediction serving latency matters. In a controlled experiment, adding about 30% to latency cost roughly 0.5% in conversion (approximate, as reported). Tricks the paper lists: model redundancy (many replicas near the caller), in-house linear and Naive Bayes prediction, sparse models, precomputing and caching, bulking requests, and keeping feature transformation small.
  5. Get early feedback on model quality. Labels arrive late or never. Booking.com uses Response Distribution Analysis: look at the shape of the model's output distribution on live traffic. A healthy binary classifier shows a clear split; a flat or one-peaked histogram is an early warning.
  6. Test business impact with randomized controlled trials. Everything goes through A/B tests. The paper describes designs for cases where the model only applies to part of the traffic, for example triggering analysis that compares only users who would have been affected, and a three-arm design to separate the effect of the model from the effect of showing any change at all.

26.3.3 Lessons for system designers

  • Treat offline metrics as a health check, not as the goal.
  • Latency is a business metric: budget it like conversion.
  • Build monitoring that works without labels.

26.4 Expedia and the hotel-ranking problem

Expedia's best-known public contribution is a benchmark rather than a production system write-up. The 2013 Kaggle competition "Personalize Expedia Hotel Searches" released search logs with hotel features, user history, price competitiveness, position and click/booking labels [13]. Its structure is still a good model of the hotel-ranking problem:

  • Each search returns a list of hotels. The labels are graded (booked > clicked > shown), and the metric is NDCG@38.
  • The data contains both "random" and normally ranked result pages, which allowed position bias to be studied.
  • Winning solutions were mostly gradient-boosted LambdaMART models with heavy feature engineering: price normalized within the search, hotel historical CTR and booking rate, and the difference between the user's past average price or star rating and the hotel's.

The patterns it shows (graded labels, normalizing features within the query, comparing the item to the user's history) also appear in Airbnb's GBDT era and in Booking.com's work. Expedia Group has published further work on search ranking and travel recommendations on its engineering blog, but those posts could not be verified for this chapter.

26.5 Uber Eats

Uber Eats is a three-sided marketplace (eaters, merchants, couriers) with very strong locality: an eater can only order from restaurants in delivery range. Roughly 95% of users start their journey on the Homefeed, according to an Uber talk [16], so homefeed ranking is central.

26.5.1 Graph learning for dish and restaurant recommendations (2019)

Problem. Orders are sparse and local. Each eater orders from a small set of nearby restaurants, so standard collaborative filtering has little to work with [14].

Design [14]:

  • Graphs. Bipartite user-dish and user-restaurant graphs, built per city. Delivery range makes edges across cities almost meaningless. Edge weights encode how often the user ordered.
  • Model. GraphSAGE with sampled neighbourhoods and node features (dish and restaurant descriptors).
  • Loss. A max-margin ranking loss, extended with "low-rank positives". A dish ordered many times should score above a dish ordered once, which should score above a negative. The edge weights are therefore used in the loss as well as in sampling.
  • Pipeline. Embeddings are trained and generated offline every day on Uber's ML platform. Similarity between user and dish or restaurant embeddings is fed as features into the downstream ranking model and also used for candidate retrieval.

Results (approximate). The blog reports a clear offline AUC gain for the ranker when the graph features were added, with the graph similarity among the most important features, and CTR gains in online tests in the first cities [14].

 orders (per city) -> weighted bipartite graphs (user-dish, user-restaurant)
      -> GraphSAGE (sampled 2-hop, max-margin + low-rank positives), daily
      -> user / dish / restaurant embeddings
      -> similarity features ---> homefeed ranker ---> carousels and store list

Lesson. Splitting the graph by city both scales the training and encodes a real constraint. A GNN does not have to be the recommender: its embeddings used as features in an existing ranker are often the safest way to ship.

26.5.2 Two-tower embeddings for homefeed retrieval

Problem. The earlier first-pass ranker was a Deep Matrix Factorization model trained per city. As Uber expanded, this meant thousands of weekly Spark jobs and did not scale [15].

Design. A single global two-tower model [15]:

  • The store tower runs offline. Store embeddings are indexed in Uber's search platform (SIA) for approximate nearest neighbour search.
  • The eater tower runs in real time for every Homefeed request, followed by an ANN lookup against the store index, with location filters.
  • Cost drops from O(q x M) online inference (q requests, M stores) to O(M) offline plus O(q) online.

A Feature Store Summit talk gives the latency target: find the best stores out of thousands in about 50 ms [16].

26.5.3 Eats search pipeline: hydration is the hidden cost

A 2026 Uber post on the Eats search pipeline [17] reports that retrieval was returning tens of thousands of candidates, all of which were fully hydrated (all their data loaded) before the ranker discarded most of them. Removing low-yield retrieval paths saved about 120 ms. Splitting hydration into a light phase for ranking and a full phase for the results that are actually shown saved more than 100 ms more. The first-pass ranker has to stay fast "while maintaining a high recall metric" [17].

 eater request
    |
    v
 retrieval paths (lexical, embedding/ANN, geo)  --> tens of thousands of candidates
    |                                                 (before the fix)
    v
 light hydration (ranking features only)
    |
    v
 first-pass ranker (high recall, low latency)
    |
    v
 second-pass ranker (multi-objective)
    |
    v
 full hydration (presentation data) only for shown results

26.5.4 Michelangelo

Michelangelo, Uber's ML platform [18], is the infrastructure under these models. Its 2017 description covers the full lifecycle: manage data, train, evaluate, deploy, predict and monitor. Two ideas from it are now everywhere:

  • A feature store with an offline store (Hive) for training and an online store (Cassandra) for serving, fed by batch (Spark) and streaming (Kafka plus Samza, later Flink) pipelines. Features are shared across teams. The 2017 post mentions about 10,000 features in the store (approximate).
  • Transformations inside the model artifact (a DSL for selecting and transforming features), so the same code runs at training and at serving time.

Michelangelo Palette (2019) [19] extended the feature store into a feature engineering platform with a catalog, ownership, and support for batch, near-real-time and RPC feature sources.

26.5.5 Experimentation under marketplace interference

Uber's experimentation platform supports A/B tests, multi-armed bandits, switchback experiments and causal inference methods [20]. Switchbacks are the key tool for marketplaces: instead of splitting users, the whole market (a city for a time window) is switched between treatment and control, so treatment and control do not compete for the same couriers or restaurants. The platform runs on the order of 1,000 or more concurrent experiments (approximate) and uses delta-method statistics, sequential tests and CUPED-style variance reduction [20].

26.6 DoorDash

DoorDash's public writing focuses on the homepage store feed, explore/exploit, and the feature and prediction infrastructure behind them.

26.6.1 Store embeddings for the personalized store feed (2018)

DoorDash's early store-feed personalization trained store2vec: word2vec-style embeddings where each "sentence" is the sequence of stores a user viewed in a session [21]. A user vector is built by averaging the vectors of stores the user ordered from. The cosine similarity between the user vector and a candidate store becomes a feature in the store ranking model. This is the same pattern as Airbnb's listing embeddings (26.2.2): cheap sequence embeddings, used as features, not as the ranker itself. The post reports gains in click-through and conversion in experiments (details approximate) [21].

26.6.2 Homepage ranking with exploitation and exploration (2022)

Problem. A pure exploitation ranker shows the same familiar stores and cuisines. New or rarely shown merchants never collect enough data to rank well, and users who would like something different never see it.

Design [22], as described:

  • A personalized ranking model predicts how likely the user is to engage with each store or cuisine (exploitation).
  • An upper-confidence-bound (UCB) style bonus is added for items with few impressions for this user, so uncertain items get some exposure (exploration).
  • The two terms are combined into the final score, with a weight that sets how much to explore.

The post reports engagement gains in A/B tests and better discovery of new merchants (approximate).

26.6.3 Feature and prediction infrastructure

  • Sibyl is DoorDash's prediction service. It serves many models with batched feature fetches and is built to keep latency predictable [23].
  • Gigascale feature store on Redis (2020). DoorDash benchmarked Redis against other stores and used binary serialization and compression to store billions of features cheaply, with large savings in memory and CPU (figures approximate) [24].
  • Riviera (2021) is a declarative framework for real-time features on Flink: features are defined in configuration and SQL, and the framework builds the streaming job [25].
  • Fabricator (2022) is a declarative framework for batch feature engineering. A feature definition (sources, SQL, schedule, sinks) generates the pipelines, the backfills and the upload to the online store, which shortens the time from a feature idea to production [26].
 events (orders, views, ETAs) --Kafka--> Riviera (Flink, real-time features) --+
 warehouse tables -----------> Fabricator (batch, declarative)  ----------------+
                                                                                v
                                                    online feature store (Redis)
                                                                                |
 homepage request --> candidate stores (geo, open now) --> Sibyl prediction -----+
                                                           (store ranking + UCB)
                                                                  |
                                                                  v
                                               carousels + store list on homepage

26.7 Lyft

Lyft's public ML work is mostly about dispatch, pricing and ETA, not recommendation lists, but its feature serving design is a typical marketplace one. Lyft describes a feature serving system that serves both batch-computed and streaming features with low latency, and that keeps training and serving consistent by logging served values [27]. For marketplace recommenders the lesson is that ranking, pricing and dispatch draw on the same real-time supply and demand features, so a shared feature platform pays off across all of them.

26.8 Zillow, Yelp and Instacart: patterns only

These three companies have published recommender and search work on their engineering blogs. The specific posts could not be fetched for this chapter, so this section covers only the design problems their domains create, without company-specific numbers.

  • Real estate (Zillow). Each home is unique and sells once. Interaction data per item is very thin, so content features (location, price, size, photos) and user preference profiles (saved searches, favourites) carry most of the weight. Items leave the catalogue quickly when they sell, which favours models that generalize from attributes over models that memorize IDs, and makes freshness of the index important.
  • Local business discovery (Yelp). Ranking blends text relevance, distance, quality (ratings, review volume) and personal taste, and must avoid letting advertising reduce user trust. Review text is a rich content signal for both search and recommendations.
  • Grocery and retail media (Instacart). Grocery is dominated by repeat purchase ("buy it again") and replacements when an item is out of stock. Availability changes by the hour per store, so predicted availability acts as a hard filter or as a score multiplier. Sponsored products are ranked inside organic results, which needs an auction that combines bids with predicted relevance and protects user experience. Chapter 16 covers ads ranking in general.

26.10 Recurring design patterns

Sequence embeddings as features first

Airbnb (listing2vec), DoorDash (store2vec) and Uber Eats (GraphSAGE) all started by learning item embeddings from sessions or order graphs and feeding similarities as features into an existing ranker. This is low-risk: the ranker keeps its other signals, and the embedding can be refreshed daily without touching serving code.

Constrained negative sampling

Airbnb's in-market negatives, its session hard negatives in EBR, and Uber's per-city graphs are the same idea: negatives must come from the set the user really chose from. Otherwise the model learns geography or availability, which filters already handle.

Funnel-aware and outcome-aware labels

The booking is sparse, so the systems borrow signal from the funnel above it (clicks, detail views, checkout) and correct for outcomes below it (cancellations, host rejections). Airbnb's Journey Ranker is the clearest example [5]. Airbnb's 2019 failure with long-view multi-task learning [2] is the warning: an upper-funnel task must be tied to the final outcome, or the model will learn to show attractive things that do not convert.

Cold start of supply is a business problem

New hosts and new merchants need impressions to survive. Airbnb estimates engagement from similar nearby listings and removes position from scoring [3]. DoorDash adds UCB exploration [22]. Both protect the supply side of the marketplace as well as improving ranking quality.

Filters before learning

Availability, dates, delivery radius and opening hours are hard constraints. The successful designs keep them as filters in the retrieval engine, and choose ANN structures (Airbnb's IVF) and partitions (Uber's per-city graphs, geo-filtered ANN) that work with those filters.

Measure carefully, because the market is shared

Interleaving (Airbnb [10]), switchbacks (Uber [20]) and triggering and three-arm designs (Booking.com [4]) all address the same issue: marketplace experiments are noisy and biased by interference, and offline metrics are not reliable enough to decide alone.

26.11 Key takeaways for system designers

  1. Model the transaction, not the click. Use booking or order as the target, the denser funnel steps as auxiliary tasks, and cancellations and rejections as negatives. Check that every auxiliary task actually moves the final outcome online.
  2. Geography and availability come first. Partition by market or city, keep hard constraints as filters, and sample negatives inside the same constraints.
  3. Start with embeddings as features. Session or graph embeddings fed into an existing GBDT or DNN ranker are cheap, fast to ship and easy to debug.
  4. Do not memorize IDs when data per item is thin. Airbnb's listing ID embeddings overfit because each listing can be booked at most a few hundred times a year. Prefer attributes, types and content.
  5. Debias position and help new supply. Position as a feature with dropout and constant-at-serving is a simple, effective trick. Estimate missing engagement for new items from similar neighbours, and keep an explicit exploration budget.
  6. Diversify the page. When the query cannot tell you the guest's taste, cover the space. Make each listing's score depend on what is already above it.
  7. Pick the ANN index that fits the update pattern and filter engine, not only the one with the best recall. Fast-changing prices and availability favoured IVF at Airbnb.
  8. Hydrate late. Load only ranking features for the large candidate set and fetch presentation data only for the items you will show. Uber saved over 200 ms this way.
  9. Treat latency as a business metric. Booking.com measured that added latency costs conversion. Precompute, cache, replicate and keep models small where possible.
  10. Trust online experiments, and design them for marketplaces. Use interleaving to screen, switchbacks or market-level randomization for interference, label-free monitoring (response distribution analysis) for early warnings, and A/B tests for the final decision.
  11. Invest in one feature platform. Chronon, Michelangelo/Palette and Riviera/Fabricator exist because real-time marketplace features (session clicks, open stores, courier supply) are where train-serve skew is most likely.

27. The Chinese Ecosystem: Alibaba, Tencent, Meituan, Baidu, Huawei, JD, Xiaohongshu and the Architecture of Hyperscale Commerce and Content

Overview

A large share of the industrial recommender-system literature since 2017 comes from Chinese companies. Several reasons explain this. Alibaba, Tencent, Meituan, Kuaishou, ByteDance, Baidu, JD.com and Huawei each run several surfaces with hundreds of millions of daily users. Their advertising teams (Alimama at Alibaba, Tencent Ads, Baidu Phoenix Nest) publish heavily at KDD, SIGIR, CIKM, RecSys and WWW. Many of them also open-source their training stacks: XDL, DeepRec, EasyRec, Graph-Learn, Euler, Angel, embedx and PaddleRec.

This chapter maps that body of work by company. It focuses on the designs that became industry templates:

  • Alibaba / Taobao / Alimama. Target attention (DIN), interest evolution (DIEN), lifelong sequences (MIMN/UIC, SIM, ETA), entire-space multi-task learning (ESMM), graph item embeddings (EGES), learned tree indexes for retrieval (TDM, JTM), multi-interest retrieval (MIND), cost-aware pre-ranking (COLD), listwise re-ranking (PRM), and the XDL, DeepRec and Graph-Learn platforms.
  • Tencent. Multi-task learning with PLE, STEM and embedding-collapse research, WeChat look-alike retrieval (RALM), the embedx and Angel platforms, and the generative ads model GPR for WeChat Channels.
  • Meituan. Long-sequence sampling (SDIM), multi-step conversion modeling (AITM), permutation re-ranking (PIER), and generative ranking (MTGR, EGA).
  • Huawei Noah's Ark. Feature-interaction models (DeepFM, PNN family, FGCNN, EDCN, FinalMLP), position-bias modeling (PAL), re-ranking (PEAR), and the FuxiCTR/BARS benchmarks.
  • Baidu, JD.com, Xiaohongshu, Sina Weibo and a note on Pinduoduo.

Kuaishou and ByteDance are covered in Chapter 20 and appear here only for comparison.

A note on sourcing. The live web-search budget for this run was used up before research began, and outbound access to arXiv, ACM and most company blogs failed from the writing environment. Facts here come from three kinds of source. The first is primary documents that could be fetched directly: the Alibaba XDL wiki pages for DIN, DIEN, ESMM, TDM, TDM Serving, CrossMedia and Rocket Training; the READMEs of XDL, Blaze, DeepRec, EasyRec, HybridBackend, Euler, Tencent embedx and Angel, PaddleRec, FuxiCTR and DeepCTR; and the DIN and DIEN reference-code READMEs. The second is paper results recorded in other chapters of this Atlas, which were researched from the papers themselves. The third, used rarely and always flagged, is papers that could not be re-fetched. Treat any number marked approximate as approximate.

                 -> click -> conversion -> repurchase [12])

1. Alibaba: the Alimama and Taobao line

Alibaba's most influential recommender papers came from the Alimama targeted-advertising algorithm team. The XDL wiki credits DIN, DIEN, ESMM, TDM, CrossMedia and Rocket Training to that team [3][4][12][18][24][25]. All six were open-sourced together as "XDL algorithm solutions" on top of the XDL training engine [22].

1.1 DIN: Deep Interest Network (KDD 2018)

Problem. The standard Embedding&MLP CTR model of 2016 pooled a user's behaviors into one fixed-length vector. The XDL documentation states the problem directly. A Taobao user has many concurrent interests. One fixed vector V_u limits the rank of the model's solution space, and its dimension cannot grow without limit because of compute and generalization. When predicting a click on a down jacket, interest in home appliances is noise [3].

Architecture. An "activation unit" uses the candidate ad to activate the user's historical clicked items. Each behavior gets a relevance weight, and the weighted sum is the user's interest representation for this candidate. That vector is concatenated with user profile, context and ad features and fed to an MLP [3]. The weights are not softmax-normalized, so the magnitude also carries interest intensity [1].

 candidate ad emb --------------------------+
 behavior_1 emb --[act unit(b1, ad)]-- w1 --+
 behavior_2 emb --[act unit(b2, ad)]-- w2 --+--> sum_i w_i * b_i  (candidate-specific
 ...                                        |                       user interest)
 behavior_T emb --[act unit(bT, ad)]-- wT --+
        concat(user interest, profile, ad, context) --> MLP (Dice) --> pCTR

Training tricks. Two tricks are reported [1][3]:

  • Mini-batch-aware regularization. L2 is applied only to embedding rows of features present in the mini-batch, because full L2 over billions of parameters per step is infeasible. It added about 0.0031 AUC over dropout on Alibaba data.
  • Dice. An activation whose rectification point adapts to the mean and variance of its input, instead of the fixed step at zero used by ReLU or PReLU. It added about 0.0015 AUC over PReLU.

Scale and results. The production dataset had more than 2 billion samples. An online A/B test (May to June 2017) showed up to +10.0% CTR and +3.8% RPM, and DIN served the main traffic of Alibaba display advertising [1]. The authors later flagged a BatchNorm bug in the original public demo. Their corrected Amazon-Electronics GAUC table gives PNN 0.8679, DeepFM 0.8683, DIN 0.8698 and DIN with Dice 0.8711, and recommends the refactored DIEN/XDL code instead [5]. That is a useful reminder that public-benchmark gaps between these models are small. BARS found the same thing on a much larger scale (Section 5.4).

Lesson. Make the user representation a function of the candidate. Nearly every later sequence model at Alibaba, Kuaishou, Meituan, Pinterest and Meta inherits this "target attention" idea.

1.2 DIEN: Deep Interest Evolution Network (AAAI 2019)

Problem. DIN treats each behavior as an interest. The DIEN authors argue that interest is latent and behaviors are only its manifestations. Supervision from ad clicks alone cannot teach a sequence model what the user wanted at each step [4].

Architecture. DIEN has two layers [2][4]:

  • An interest-extractor GRU over the behavior sequence. An auxiliary loss asks each hidden state to predict the next clicked item against a sampled non-clicked item. The XDL docs note three benefits of this loss: it adds feedback signal, eases gradient flow on long sequences, and gives the embeddings more semantic supervision.
  • An interest-evolving layer, AUGRU. The GRU update gate is scaled by the attention score between the candidate ad and each extracted interest. Each candidate therefore gets its own evolution path, and interests unrelated to it are suppressed.

Serving. A GRU per candidate is expensive. The paper reports cutting latency from 38.2 ms to 6.6 ms with element-parallel GRU and kernel fusion, batching adjacent requests from different users on GPU, and model compression. The system served more than a million users per second at peak, and the paper reports a 20.7% CTR improvement in Taobao display ads [2]. The XDL docs state that DIEN was deployed across Alimama's targeted-ads products [4]. Serving pressure still limited production DIEN to about 50 behaviors [6].

1.3 Lifelong sequences: MIMN/UIC, SIM, ETA

This line is the clearest example of Chinese system and algorithm co-design.

  • MIMN + UIC (KDD 2019). A User Interest Center keeps a per-user memory state on the serving side. The state is updated incrementally whenever a behavior event arrives, not at request time. MIMN is a multi-channel, NTM-style memory network whose memory is exactly the UIC state. Ranking latency is therefore constant in history length, and sequences in the thousands were handled. Online (2019-03-30 to 2019-05-10), MIMN with UIC gave +7.5% CTR and +6% RPM over DIEN [6].

  • SIM (CIKM 2020). MIMN's user-only memory degraded as histories grew 10x or more. SIM splits the problem into two units [7]:

    • A General Search Unit (GSU) picks the top-K relevant behaviors from up to 54,000. Hard search keeps behaviors in the candidate's category. Soft search uses MIPS over embeddings.
    • An Exact Search Unit (ESU) runs multi-head target attention on those K behaviors.

    The two searches returned similar lists, so the cheaper hard search went online. Its index is a two-level User Behavior Tree (user_id -> category_id -> behaviors), built offline, distributed, about 22 TB. Results: +7.1% CTR and +4.4% RPM, in production since 2019 [7].

  • ETA (2021-2022). ETA replaces the separate GSU with SimHash signatures of the same embeddings the attention uses. Top-k selection by Hamming distance needs only bit operations, and retrieval becomes end-to-end trainable. Reported gains are 3.1% GMV for ETA [8], and +1.8% CTR and +3.1% GMV for ETA-Net on Taobao [9].

 UIC (event-driven)                      SIM (request-driven, two-stage)
 behavior event --> update memory        request(user, candidate c)
                    M_u in UIC             |  GSU: UBT lookup [user][cat(c)]
 request --> read M_u (O(1)) --> MIMN      |       (22 TB index, hard search)
                                           v  top-K behaviors
                                         ESU: multi-head target attn(c, top-K)
                                           v
                                         concat with short-term DIN/DIEN -> MLP

BST (DLP-KDD 2019) applied a single Transformer layer to the short behavior sequence in Taobao recommendation ranking. Its position feature is the time gap between the recommendation and the click. Offline AUC was 0.7894 against 0.7866 for DIN, and online CTR rose +7.57% against +4.55% for DIN [10].

1.4 ESMM: Entire Space Multi-Task Model (SIGIR 2018)

Problem. Alimama's docs decompose GMV as traffic x CTR x CVR x price per order, which makes CVR a direct lever [12]. CVR models trained only on clicked impressions suffer from sample selection bias (SSB), since they score all impressions but train on clicks. They also suffer from data sparsity (DS): in Taobao data CVR samples were about 4% of CTR samples [11]. Delayed feedback is a third challenge [12].

Design. pCVR is never supervised directly. The model predicts pCTR and pCTCVR = pCTR x pCVR over all impressions and supervises those two [11][12]:

 loss = sum_i CE(y_i, pCTR(x_i)) + sum_i CE(y_i AND z_i, pCTR(x_i) * pCVR(x_i))

  impression x --> [shared embedding layer] --+--> CTR tower --> pCTR ----+
                                              |                           (x)--> pCTCVR
                                              +--> CVR tower --> pCVR ----+

The product avoids dividing by small pCTR values, which is numerically unstable. The CVR tower shares embeddings with the CTR task, which has orders of magnitude more samples. That transfer is what addresses the sparsity problem [12]. Each tower can be any base network, so ESMM is a framework rather than a model [12]. The 8.9-billion-sample Taobao dataset was released as a 1% public sample, Ali-CCP [11][12].

Successors. ESM2 decomposes the post-click path into cart and wishlist actions [13]. ESCM2 adds a counterfactual regularizer because ESMM's CVR is itself biased [14]. Meituan's AITM generalizes the idea to learned information transfer across longer funnels (Section 3.2) [60]. Alibaba's delayed-feedback work, ES-DFM and DEFER, handles the third challenge [35].

1.5 EGES: billion-scale commodity embedding (KDD 2018)

Taobao's matching stage connects about a billion users to about two billion items [15]. EGES works in four steps:

  1. Build a weighted directed item graph from sessions of about one hour, filtering very short clicks and over-active users.
  2. Run DeepWalk-style weighted random walks and train skip-gram on them (BGE).
  3. Add side-information embeddings (category, shop, brand, price level), which helps cold-start items (GES).
  4. In EGES proper, learn per-item attention weights over those side embeddings.

Embedding nearest neighbors become each item's i2i candidate list, and the paper reports CTR gains over the prior CF-based matching [15]. The lesson: side-information embeddings close the cold-start gap at nearly zero serving cost.

1.6 TDM and JTM: learned tree indexes for retrieval

Problem. Item-CF and inner-product vector retrieval cannot use an expressive deep model over a corpus of tens of millions of items. Scoring every item is O(n) [18].

Design. All items are indexed as leaves of a tree, and each internal node represents a set of items, from coarse to fine. The tree need not be binary. A deep model acts as a per-node "interest discriminator". Retrieval runs layer-wise beam search: keep the top K nodes per level and expand their children. The cost of whole-corpus retrieval drops from O(n) to O(log n), and any advanced model can be used because the beam prunes aggressively [16][18]. The open-source model uses only user behaviors, split into time windows, plus node embeddings, with attention over behaviors in the style of DIN [18].

Tree and model jointly. The tree supplies training samples: positives are a positive leaf's ancestors, and negatives come from the same level. It also decides pruning at serving time. TDM therefore alternates two steps. It trains the model, then re-clusters the learned leaf embeddings hierarchically (k-means) to build a new tree, and repeats until both are stable [18]. JTM later learns the tree and model under one objective [17]. The XDL docs claim TDM was applied in video, product and news recommendation as well as Alimama ads [18].

Serving. TDM Serving is a C++ library with three layers [19]:

  • an API layer for loading data and real-time retrieval;
  • an Index layer for tree beam search, index management and business-logic filtering;
  • a Model layer for per-level DNN scoring, executed by the Blaze inference engine.

Blaze is Alimama's high-performance inference engine for ads, search and recommendation. It uses its own ULF model format, converted from XDL output [23]. Baidu's PaddleRec also ships a TDM implementation [65].

 offline (XDL)                                  online (TDM Serving)
 item embs --k-means--> tree T_k                request(user behaviors)
     ^                     |                       |
     |      samples: ancestors(+), same-level(-)   v
     +---- train DNN M_k <-+                    level 1: score children of root (Blaze)
          (repeat until stable)                  keep top-K --> expand children
                                                 ... level L: top-K leaves = items
 export: tree.pb + dense/sparse/item_emb  --->   + business filters in Index layer

1.7 MIND: multi-interest retrieval at Tmall

MIND uses capsule dynamic routing to turn a user's behaviors into K interest vectors, trained with label-aware attention. Each vector issues its own ANN query. It served major traffic on the Mobile Tmall homepage [20]. It is the inverse of DIN: DIN builds one user vector per candidate at ranking time, while MIND builds several candidate-independent user vectors so retrieval stays factorized.

1.8 COLD and pre-ranking; Rocket Training and distillation

COLD (2020) rejected the two-tower pre-ranker because it cannot use user-item cross features. COLD uses a small fully connected network with cross features. Feature selection is made under a compute budget, and the model is co-designed with serving (low precision, parallelism) and trained online [21].

Rocket Training is Alimama's co-training compression method. A large "booster" net and a small "light" net share bottom layers such as embeddings and are trained together. A hint loss pulls the light net's logits toward the booster's. A gradient block freezes the booster-only parameters on that hint term so the small net cannot drag the large one down. Only the light net serves [25].

1.9 CrossMedia / DICM and the Advanced Model Server

DICM (CIKM 2018) adds images to CTR prediction: the ad image, plus the images of items the user clicked in the past 14 days [24]. Image vectors come from a fixed VGG16 plus a trainable fully connected layer, and user-behavior images are aggregated by sum or attention pooling. Shipping images through a parameter server for billions of samples is too costly. XDL therefore built the Advanced Model Server (AMS), where servers run the image-embedding forward and backward passes. Images are stored once on the servers, and duplicate embeddings of the same image within a batch are removed [24]. This is an early form of the "compute near the parameters" pattern.

1.10 Re-ranking, RL and simulators

Taobao contributed several re-ranking and RL designs:

  • MIDNN (IJCAI 2018): list-level features plus beam search under an evaluator, for mutual-influence-aware ranking in Taobao search [75].
  • PRM (RecSys 2019): a Transformer re-ranker over the top tens of items, with pre-trained "personalized vectors" and the initial rank as an input [31].
  • Exact-K (KDD 2019): chooses an exact set of K items jointly [74].
  • Virtual-Taobao (AAAI 2019): trains a search-ranking policy in a GAN and imitation-learning simulator, reporting more than 2% online revenue gain [32].
  • PE-LTR (RecSys 2019): a Pareto-efficient algorithm for jointly optimizing GMV and CTR [34].

1.11 Platforms: XDL, DeepRec, EasyRec, Graph-Learn, Euler

  • XDL is Alimama's framework for high-dimensional sparse data. Version 1.2 added 50-100% speedups for large-batch, low-concurrency jobs, automatic global parameter placement with request merging to remove parameter-server hotspots, and full streaming-training features: feature admission, feature eviction, incremental model export and feature counting [22].
  • DeepRec is a heavily modified TensorFlow 1.15 developed since 2016. It supports Taobao search, recommendation and ads, and dozens of outside companies use it. It claims training at "trillion samples and over ten trillion parameters" [26]. Key features: EmbeddingVariable (dynamic, adaptive and multi-hash), multi-tier HBM/DRAM/PMem/SSD storage, asynchronous parameter-server training (grpc+seastar, StarServer) or synchronous collective training (HybridBackend, SOK), and delta checkpoints [26][73].
  • EasyRec / TorchEasyRec is the configuration-driven model zoo on Alibaba Cloud (MaxCompute, PAI, EAS). It supports large embeddings and online learning [72].
  • Graph-Learn (formerly AliGraph) retrains GNNs incrementally every hour [27][30]. Its Dynamic Graph Service pre-samples the graph update stream against pre-registered queries. One node (64 cores, 256 GB) answers 2-hop queries at 20 ms P99 and 20K QPS while ingesting 110 MB/s of updates [28]. Euler is the separate Alimama graph framework, with GQL and message passing [29].

1.12 Generative turn: LUM

Alibaba's LUM (2025) pre-trains a large user model generatively, queries it, and feeds its outputs into existing discriminative models. This "three-step paradigm" aims to unlock scaling laws without discarding the existing cascade [33].

2. Tencent: WeChat, Tencent Video and Tencent Ads

2.1 PLE: Progressive Layered Extraction (RecSys 2020 best long paper)

Problem. Tencent's video recommender saw a seesaw: MMoE improved one task at the expense of another when task correlations were complex [36].

Design. CGC gives each task its own experts plus a pool of shared experts. Task k's gate mixes only its own experts and the shared ones. PLE stacks CGC levels, with a shared gate feeding shared experts at the next level, so specific and shared knowledge separate progressively [36].

 level 1:  [VTR experts]   [shared experts]   [VCR experts]
              gate_A          gate_shared         gate_B
 level 2:  [VTR experts]   [shared experts]   [VCR experts]
              gate_A                              gate_B
           tower_A -> VTR (effective view, AUC)   tower_B -> VCR (completion, MSE)

Data and results. The dataset had about 1 billion samples. MMoE barely moved VCR (about +0.0001 MSE improvement), while PLE improved both tasks significantly. Online, view count rose 2.23% and watch time 1.84% over the previous multi-task model [36]. PLE is now a stock component: DeepCTR, FuxiCTR and EasyRec all ship it [53][71][72].

2.2 STEM and embedding collapse

Two Tsinghua/Tencent papers moved the multi-task and scaling debate down to the embedding layer:

  • STEM (AAAI 2024) keeps one shared embedding table plus one per task. An "All Forward Task-specific Backward" gate lets every expert contribute forward, while stop-gradient keeps a task's gradients out of other tasks' tables [37].
  • "On the Embedding Collapse" (ICML 2024) shows that embedding matrices collapse into low-dimensional subspaces as they are scaled. Its multi-embedding design keeps improving up to 10x embedding size [38].

2.3 WeChat: RALM look-alike retrieval and embedx

WeChat's article feed ("Kan Yi Kan") published RALM (KDD 2019), a real-time attention-based look-alike model for recommending fresh or long-tail content. The idea is to represent an item by the users who engaged with it ("seeds") and match new users against them. PaddleRec ships an implementation [39][65]. (The full paper could not be re-fetched. Treat this description as a summary of its title and framing, not its numbers.)

embedx is a C++ distributed embedding training and inference system. It covers graph models with billions of nodes and hundreds of billions of edges, and deep ranking and retrieval models with tens of billions of samples and features [40]. Its README lists the products it has served:

  • recommendation, search and payments at WeChat: Kan Yi Kan, WeChat Channels, WeChat Search and WeChat Pay;
  • security: WeChat Security and Tencent's anti-fraud work;
  • content and apps: Tencent News, the App Store (Yingyongbao), QQ Music, JOOX and Tencent Classroom.

Its design notes describe four things [40]:

  • Joint graph and ranking models (graphdeepfm, graphdssm). Training them together avoids the objective mismatch of the usual two-stage use of graph embeddings.
  • A minute-level online-learning loop. Recall and ranking both train and serve from the real-time stream, and changes take effect end to end within minutes.
  • Incremental parameter export and asynchronous parameter updates in serving.
  • Importance-sampling correction for the distribution shift of real-time samples.

The README claims 30-60% machine savings over open-source frameworks [40].

Angel, built by Tencent and Peking University, is the older parameter-server platform in Java/Scala on YARN, with Spark-on-Angel for ML and graph algorithms [41]. Tencent is also a listed contributor to TensorFlow Recommenders-Addons dynamic embeddings [45].

2.4 Tencent Ads: FLEN, meta-embeddings, GPR

  • FLEN (DLP-KDD 2020) is a field-aware CTR model designed for scalable serving [44].
  • Meta-Embedding (SIGIR 2019) learns a generator from ad attributes to an initial ID embedding with a MAML-style two-phase objective, which warms up cold-start ads [43].
  • GPR (2025) serves WeChat Channels ads. It is a decoder over four token types (user, organic, environment, ad). Items get RQ-KMeans+ semantic IDs, and decoding uses value-guided trie beam search. It reportedly collapsed five cascade models into one and cut latency from more than 200 ms to about 80 ms (approximate) [42].

3. Meituan: local services, food delivery and ads

Meituan's recommendation problems are shaped by location, time of day and multi-step conversion: impression, click, order, then delivery.

3.1 SDIM: sampling instead of attention (CIKM 2022)

SDIM hashes the candidate and every behavior with several hash functions and sums the behaviors that share the candidate's signature. The authors prove that this approximates target attention. Hashing runs in a separate Behavior Sequence Encoding service, so the CTR model only does a lookup. Meituan search reported +2.98% CTR and +2.69% VBR [59].

3.2 AITM: multi-step conversion (KDD 2021)

AITM targets credit-card customer acquisition, where the funnel is impression, click, application, approval, activation. An Adaptive Information Transfer module learns what to pass from earlier steps to later ones. A Behavioral Expectation Calibrator keeps later-step probabilities consistent with earlier ones. It was deployed in the Meituan app [60].

3.3 PIER: permutation re-ranking (WSDM 2023)

PIER picks top permutations cheaply with SimHash-style hashing of user interest, then scores them with an omnidirectional context-aware module, trained end to end. It makes generator-evaluator re-ranking affordable at Meituan's scale [61].

3.4 MTGR, MTGRBoost and EGA (2025)

Problem. Meituan found that a pure HSTU-style generative ranker, which drops user x item cross features, did worse than a mid-sized DLRM even at the largest size tried [57].

Design. MTGR is a Transformer encoder with HSTU-style user-level sequence compression, trained on discriminative CTR/CTCVR losses [57]:

  • Token groups: user, long sequence, real-time and candidate. Cross features are kept only on candidate tokens.
  • Group LayerNorm: separate normalization per token group.
  • Dynamic masking: real-time tokens are causal and time-gated per candidate, and candidates cannot see each other. All m candidates of a user are scored in one pass at O((n+m)^2), against O(m n^2) when scored separately.

Per-sample inference compute was about 65x that of the DLRM baseline (approximate). Meituan called it the largest offline and online gain in about two years. Training infrastructure is described in MTGRBoost [57][58].

EGA-V2 generates ads end to end. It uses RQ-VAE semantic IDs (3 levels x 1024 codes), factors generation into P(POI) x P(creative | POI), and adds a payment network that guarantees individual rationality, with approximate incentive compatibility enforced through a regret Lagrangian [62].

4. Huawei Noah's Ark: feature interactions, bias and benchmarks

Huawei's recommender research is anchored in the Huawei App Store (AppGallery) and in open benchmarks.

4.1 DeepFM (IJCAI 2017) and the PNN family

DeepFM replaces Wide&Deep's hand-crafted wide part with an FM component that shares the embedding layer with the DNN. It therefore needs no feature engineering beyond raw features. It improved AUC and logloss on Criteo and on a commercial Huawei app-store dataset [46].

PNN (ICDM 2016) inserts a product layer (inner or outer products of field embeddings) before the MLP [47]. It is one of the baselines DIN compared against [5]. A journal extension (the "PIN" product-network-in-network variant) generalizes the pairwise product to small per-pair subnetworks. It could not be re-fetched for this chapter, so its details are not stated here.

Later Huawei CTR models listed in FuxiCTR [53] include:

  • FGCNN (WWW 2019): CNN-generated new features [49];
  • EDCN (DLP-KDD 2021): information sharing between the parallel explicit and implicit towers [50];
  • FinalMLP (AAAI 2023): two MLP streams fused by bilinear interaction, plus FINAL and EulerNet (SIGIR 2023) [51];
  • MIRRN (KDD 2025): multi-granularity retrieval and refinement for long behavior sequences [56].

4.2 PAL: position bias as a probability (RecSys 2019)

PAL factorizes pCTR(click | x, pos) = pSeen(pos) x pCTR(click | x, seen). The two modules are trained jointly, and only the CTR module ranks at serving time, so position never has to be known before it is chosen. Huawei App Store A/B tests reported CTR and conversion gains over a "position as feature" baseline [48].

4.3 PEAR and cross-batch negatives

  • PEAR (WWW 2022) extends PRM-style re-ranking with list-item attention over the user's history and an auxiliary list-level engagement task [54].
  • Cross-Batch Negative Sampling (SIGIR 2021) keeps a FIFO memory of recent item embeddings and reuses them as extra negatives for two-tower training, at close to in-batch cost [55].

4.4 FuxiCTR and BARS: honesty about benchmarks

FuxiCTR is a configurable, reproducible CTR library. Its model zoo labels each model by company, and it is the easiest index of Chinese CTR work [53]. The BARS-CTR benchmark re-ran 24 models in more than 7,000 experiments and more than 12,000 GPU hours. With proper tuning, many deep models differ far less than their papers claim [52]. Read every offline AUC gain in this chapter with that result in mind.

5. Baidu, JD.com, Xiaohongshu, Weibo and Pinduoduo

5.1 Baidu

  • MOBIUS (KDD 2019) targets Baidu's sponsored-search query-ad matching. It is described as moving the matching layer from pure relevance toward the downstream business objective (CPM), so that matching and ranking are no longer optimized for different targets. The paper uses a relevance "teacher" to keep low-relevance, high-CTR pairs out, plus approximate nearest-neighbor search. (Not re-fetched for this chapter. This summary follows the published abstract as recalled; treat the details as approximate) [66].
  • PaddleRec is Baidu's open model zoo on PaddlePaddle, with parameter-server and multi-GPU training. It covers matching (DSSM, MultiView-SimNet), recall (TDM, MIND, RALM, YouTube-DNN, DeepWalk, GRU4Rec) and ranking models [65].
  • COBRA (2025) is Baidu's cascaded sparse-dense generative recommender. It generates a semantic ID and then refines it with a dense vector [64].

5.2 JD.com

JD's best-known public recommender work is page-wise RL (RecSys 2018). An actor-critic recommends a whole 2-D page at once, with a deconvolutional actor and a critic that values the page. It is trained first against an offline simulator built from logs [63]. Few JD production-architecture details (QPS, model sizes) appear in the sources gathered for this chapter.

5.3 Xiaohongshu (RedNote)

  • GenRank (2025) is generative ranking trained on hundreds of billions of exposure logs [67]:
    • An action-oriented sequence makes actions the tokens and folds items in as attributes. This halves sequence length, cuts attention compute by 75% and speeds training by 78.7%.
    • Parameter-free ALiBi-style position and time biases raise the total speedup to 94.8%.
    • Real-time features stayed important, while most historical aggregate features lost value.
  • NoteLLM (WWW 2024) compresses each note into a special LLM token for note-to-note (item-to-item) recommendation. It trains that token with contrastive learning on co-occurrence signals, alongside hashtag and category generation. (Not re-fetched; summarized from the paper as recalled) [68].

5.4 Sina Weibo

Weibo contributed two widely reused interaction modules [69]:

  • FiBiNET (RecSys 2019): SENET-style feature importance plus bilinear interactions.
  • MaskNet (2021): instance-guided multiplicative masks. MaskNet later became the backbone of Twitter's heavy ranker.

5.5 Pinduoduo

None of the sources reachable for this chapter documents Pinduoduo's recommender architecture in a primary engineering paper or blog. Pinduoduo is far less public than its peers. Designers should not assume its stack matches the Alibaba templates.

7. Architecture patterns characteristic of Chinese hyperscale

Many of these ideas exist elsewhere. Their combination and early adoption are distinctive.

  1. Ads teams drive the frontier. DIN, DIEN, MIMN, SIM, ESMM, TDM, CrossMedia, Rocket and COLD all came from Alimama's targeted-ads team [3][4][12][18][24][25]. Revenue per point of CTR or CVR justifies GPU serving and custom infrastructure earlier than organic feeds do.
  2. Model the funnel explicitly. Chinese papers treat recall -> pre-rank -> rank -> exposure -> click -> conversion -> repurchase as one chain [12]. ESMM, ESM2, ESCM2 and AITM encode that chain in the loss. COLD and Rocket make each stage as expressive as its compute budget allows.
  3. Algorithm-system co-design is the norm, not the exception. UIC moves computation to event time. SIM's 22 TB behavior tree, ETA's SimHash and SDIM's BSE service turn attention into indexing. AMS moves image embedding onto parameter servers. TDM's tree is both a training-sample generator and a serving index. DGS pre-samples graphs. MTGR's masking scores all candidates in one pass. In every case the model is shaped by what the serving system can do cheaply [6][7][8][24][18][28][57][59].
  4. Streaming everything. Feature admission and eviction, incremental export, delta checkpoints and minute-level online learning appear in XDL, DeepRec and embedx, as in ByteDance's Monolith [22][26][40].
  5. Open-source platforms as recruiting and ecosystem tools. XDL, DeepRec, EasyRec, Graph-Learn, Euler, embedx, Angel and PaddleRec are released with Chinese-first documentation and cloud integration (Alibaba Cloud PAI/MaxCompute, Baidu AI Studio) [22][26][27][29][40][41][65][72].
  6. Lifelong behavior as a first-class signal. E-commerce and short-video users accumulate 10^4 to 10^5 behaviors. The SIM -> ETA -> SDIM -> TWIN line (Kuaishou, Chapter 20) exists because Chinese platforms had both the histories and the latency pressure [7][9][59][70].
  7. Fast embrace of generative ranking with pragmatic hybrids. Kuaishou OneRec, Meituan MTGR and EGA, Tencent GPR, Xiaohongshu GenRank, Baidu COBRA and Alibaba LUM all shipped or reported production results in 2025. Several deliberately keep cross features, discriminative losses or the existing cascade [33][42][57][62][64][67][70].
         ALGORITHM-SYSTEM CO-DESIGN: WHERE THE WORK MOVES

  request-time compute  -->  moved to ...                 example
  ----------------------     ---------------------------  ----------------------
  attend over history        event-time memory update      UIC / MIMN [6]
  attend over 54K items      offline category index        SIM UBT, 22 TB [7]
  pick top-k behaviors       bit ops on SimHash codes      ETA [8], SDIM [59]
  embed images per sample    parameter-server compute      AMS / DICM [24]
  traverse graph n hops      write-time pre-sampling       DGS, 20 ms P99 [28]
  score 10^7 items           beam search on learned tree   TDM Serving [19]
  score m candidates         one pass, masked attention    MTGR [57]

Key takeaways for system designers

  1. Make the user representation candidate-aware in ranking and candidate-independent in retrieval. DIN, DIEN and SIM attend per candidate at ranking time. MIND, EGES and TDM keep retrieval factorized or indexable.
  2. Supervise in the space you serve in. ESMM's pCTCVR trick removes sample-selection bias and borrows density from the CTR task. Extend it to multi-step funnels (ESM2, AITM) and correct its residual bias (ESCM2).
  3. When attention is too expensive, turn it into retrieval. Use a two-stage GSU/ESU (SIM), hashing (ETA, SDIM) or event-time memory (UIC). Choose by whether you need candidate-awareness and end-to-end training.
  4. Learned indexes let deep models do retrieval. TDM's tree, rebuilt from learned embeddings, gives O(log n) whole-corpus scoring with arbitrary models. The price is a serving engine (beam search plus per-level scoring) and a training loop that alternates tree and model.
  5. Separate task-specific from shared capacity when you see a seesaw. PLE and CGC are the default answer. STEM pushes the separation into embeddings. Watch for embedding collapse when scaling.
  6. Budget compute per stage, and spend it where crosses pay. COLD's cross-feature pre-ranker and Rocket's booster-light co-training show how to buy quality under a latency cap.
  7. Invest in streaming infrastructure before bigger models. Feature admission and eviction, incremental export and minute-level online learning (XDL, DeepRec, embedx) are table stakes for fast-churning catalogs.
  8. Do not discard signal to be "purely generative". MTGR and GenRank show that cross features and real-time features remain decisive. Hybrid generative-discriminative designs are the production norm in 2025-2026.
  9. Discount offline gains. DIN's corrected GAUC table and the BARS benchmark both show that tuned baselines close most published gaps. Trust online A/B results and production deployment claims more than offline AUC.

28. News, Social and Content Platforms: From Click Co-visitation to Open Feed Protocols

Overview

This chapter covers recommenders for platforms where content is perishable, abundant and often user-generated: news portals (Google News, Yahoo! JAPAN, Microsoft News, The New York Times), discussion and social platforms (Reddit, Quora, Medium, Snapchat), decentralized social networks (Bluesky, Mastodon), and community or streaming services (Substack, Discord, Twitch, Hulu, Disney+, Roku).

These systems share three structural problems that set them apart from the catalog recommenders in Chapters 18 (Netflix) and 24 (Amazon):

  1. Extreme item churn. A news story or a social post is mostly worthless after hours or days. Item-ID collaborative filtering never collects enough interactions before the item dies. Content encoders such as text, entity and image models therefore do most of the work, and freshness is a primary ranking signal rather than a tie-breaker.
  2. A popularity/recency prior is a strong baseline. Reddit's "hot" formula and Mastodon's trending scores are closed-form functions of votes and age. They still serve as candidate sources, cold-start fallbacks and sanity baselines, even in platforms with heavy ML.
  3. Governance and control matter. Mastodon deliberately keeps a reverse-chronological home timeline. Bluesky moves ranking out of the platform into third-party "feed generators". Both are architecture decisions about who owns the ranking function, and they change the system design as much as any model does.

A note on sourcing for this edition. Network access during research was limited to GitHub-hosted material. Every Bluesky, Mastodon, Reddit-ranking and MIND fact below was verified against primary source code or dataset documentation fetched from GitHub [1]-[12]. Facts about older published papers (Google News, Yahoo! JAPAN, NRMS, DKN, NYT, Hulu) come from well-known peer-reviewed publications and are cited at their canonical DOIs or URLs [13]-[20], but were not re-fetched in this session. Those claims are kept to the papers' headline contributions, and any numbers from them are marked approximate. For several platforms (Snapchat Spotlight/Discover, Quora, Medium, Substack, Discord, Twitch, Disney+, Roku), primary engineering detail could not be retrieved. Those sections say so explicitly instead of filling gaps.
