1. Neighborhood collaborative filtering

1.1 User-based kNN

Problem. Predict a user's interest in an item from the behaviour of similar users.

Mechanism. Build user-user similarities from co-rated items, usually with Pearson correlation or cosine similarity. Pick the k most similar neighbours who interacted with the target item. Predict a similarity-weighted average of their (mean-centred) ratings.

Why it fell out of favour at scale. The user space is far larger and changes far faster than the item space. A user's neighbourhood changes with every new interaction, so the similarity matrix has to be recomputed constantly. Sparse overlap between users also makes similarities noisy. Amazon's engineers gave exactly these reasons for moving away from user-based CF [1][2].

1.2 Item-to-item CF (Amazon)

Problem. Amazon needed recommendations for tens of millions of customers and millions of products. Results had to be computed in real time on every page view, and had to react to what the customer had just put in the cart [1].

Architecture. The key move was to swap the roles of users and items. Item-item relatedness is much more stable than user-user similarity, so it can be computed offline. The online step is then a cheap lookup and merge:

 OFFLINE (batch, periodic)                          ONLINE (per request, ms)
 ------------------------------------------------   -------------------------------
 for each item i1 in catalog:                        user context:
   for each customer c who bought i1:                  recent purchases / cart / views
     for each item i2 bought by c:                           |
        record co-purchase(i1, i2)                           v
   for each i2: sim(i1,i2) = cosine over customers    lookup top-N similar items
 store top-N similar items per item  ------------->   for each seed item
   (item -> [(item, score), ...])                            |
                                                             v
                                                      merge, de-dup, remove owned,
                                                      re-rank (business rules)

Scale properties. The worst-case offline cost is O(N^2 M), where N is the number of items and M the number of customers. In practice it is closer to O(NM), because most customers buy very few items. Online cost depends only on how many items the user has interacted with, not on catalogue size or user count [1]. The 2003 IEEE Internet Computing paper later received the journal's "test of time" recognition. Its 2017 retrospective, "Two Decades of Recommender Systems at Amazon.com", describes how the basic item-to-item idea was refined: correcting relatedness for purchase base rates, handling time and context, and using it far beyond the "customers who bought" widget [2].

Academic formalisation. Sarwar, Karypis, Konstan and Riedl (WWW 2001) studied item-based CF systematically. They compared cosine, adjusted-cosine and correlation similarities, and showed that item-based models could be precomputed and gave better quality than user-based kNN on sparse data [25].

1.3 SAR: item-kNN with time decay as a production recipe

Microsoft's open-source Recommenders repository ships SAR (Simple Algorithm for Recommendation), a cleaned-up item-kNN that works as a strong first baseline [15][21]:

  1. Co-occurrence matrix C (m x m). c_ij counts the users who interacted with both item i and item j.
  2. Similarity S by rescaling C. Jaccard is s_ij = c_ij / (c_ii + c_jj - c_ij), a "compromise between popularity and discovery". Lift is s_ij = c_ij / (c_ii * c_jj), which favours niche and serendipitous items. Raw counts favour popular items.
  3. Affinity matrix A (n x m) with event weights and exponential time decay. a_ij = sum over events k of w_k * (1/2)^((t0 - t_k)/T), where T is a half-life.
  4. Scores = A x S. Previously seen items can optionally be filtered out [21].

The example notebook uses Jaccard similarity, a 30-day half-life and top-10 on MovieLens. It reports NDCG@10 of about 0.385 and Precision@10 of about 0.33 [21]. The notebook also says plainly that the single-node implementation is not meant for very large data, because the dense item-item work becomes expensive [21]. That trade-off holds for every item-item model: quality is strong and the model is simple, but memory grows as O(m^2) unless similarities are sparsified to top-k per item.

1.4 Graph random walks: P3alpha and RP3beta

The Dacrema et al. evaluation suite includes two graph baselines next to kNN: P3alpha and RP3beta [16]. Both score items by the probability of a three-step random walk user -> item -> user -> item on the bipartite interaction graph. P3alpha raises transition probabilities to a power alpha. RP3beta also divides by item popularity raised to beta, which pushes the ranking towards the long tail. They are item-item models in disguise: the walk collapses into a sparse item-item matrix, so serving is the same as kNN. In the reproducibility studies these cheap models often matched or beat neural baselines [16][17].

2. Matrix factorization for explicit feedback: Funk-SVD, SVD++, timeSVD++

2.1 The Netflix Prize context

The Netflix Prize (2006-2009) offered USD 1M for a 10% RMSE improvement over Cinematch. It released about 100M ratings from about 480K users on about 17,770 movies. Latent-factor models became the mainstream approach as a result [3][4]. The summary of the winning techniques by Koren, Bell and Volinsky, "Matrix Factorization Techniques for Recommender Systems" (IEEE Computer, 2009), is the standard reference [3].

Biased MF (Funk-SVD). Predict r_ui = mu + b_u + b_i + q_i^T p_u. Here mu is the global mean, b_u and b_i are user and item biases, and p_u and q_i are f-dimensional factors. Fit by stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on observed ratings only, with L2 regularisation. The bias terms explain much of the variance in ratings. Leaving them out is still one of the most common reasons a "baseline" looks weak [3][26].

SVD++. In "Factorization Meets the Neighborhood" (KDD 2008), Koren added implicit information: the set N(u) of items the user rated, whatever the ratings were. The user representation becomes p_u + |N(u)|^(-1/2) * sum over j in N(u) of y_j. The fact that a user chose to rate an item carries signal. The same paper combined factor and neighbourhood models in one objective [4].

timeSVD++. This variant lets biases and user factors drift over time, because user taste and item popularity are not stationary. It was one of the strongest single models in the winning ensemble [3].

Lesson from production. The Netflix Prize also showed the cost of ensembles. The grand-prize blend combined on the order of a hundred models. Netflix said publicly that it adopted the core MF and RBM components, but did not put the full blend into production, because the extra accuracy did not justify the engineering cost. The company was also moving from DVD ratings to streaming implicit signals [3]. That shift, from rating prediction (RMSE) to ranking over implicit feedback, is what the rest of this chapter covers.

3. Implicit-feedback MF: confidence-weighted ALS (Hu, Koren, Volinsky)

3.1 Problem

Most real systems never see ratings. They see views, plays, purchases and dwell time. Such data has several properties that break rating-style MF [5]:

  • There is no negative feedback. A missing entry may mean dislike, or may mean the user never saw the item.
  • The data is noisy. A watched show may have been playing in the background.
  • The numeric value shows confidence, not preference. Watching a show many times makes it more likely the user likes it, but the count is not a rating.
  • Evaluation must be ranking-based.

3.2 Model

Hu, Koren and Volinsky (ICDM 2008) built the method on TV-viewing data from a digital set-top box service: roughly 300K households and about 17K programmes [5]. They split each observation r_ui into:

  • Preference p_ui = 1 if r_ui > 0, else 0.
  • Confidence c_ui = 1 + alpha * r_ui. A log variant, c_ui = 1 + alpha * log(1 + r_ui / epsilon), is also proposed. The paper reports alpha of about 40 working well on their data.

The objective covers all user-item pairs, observed or not:

 min over x_*, y_*:  sum_{u,i} c_ui (p_ui - x_u^T y_i)^2
                     + lambda ( sum_u ||x_u||^2 + sum_i ||y_i||^2 )

Summing over all m*n cells is the point of the method: unobserved cells act as low-confidence negatives. The engineering problem is that this dense sum is intractable if done naively.

3.3 The ALS trick that makes it scale

With item factors Y fixed, each user's factor has a closed form:

 x_u = (Y^T C^u Y + lambda I)^(-1) Y^T C^u p(u)
     where  Y^T C^u Y = Y^T Y  +  Y^T (C^u - I) Y
                        ^^^^^     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
                    precompute     only n_u nonzero rows (items u touched)
                    once, O(f^2 n)

Y^T Y is shared by all users. The correction term only touches the n_u items the user interacted with, so one sweep over users costs O(f^2 N + f^3 m). N is the number of non-zeros, f the number of factors and m the number of users. The cost is linear in the data, not in the full matrix [5]. Items are handled the same way. Every user (and every item) solves independently, so the problem is embarrassingly parallel. That is why ALS rather than SGD became the default for distributed implicit MF.

The same paper also gives explanations. Because the solve is linear, a user's score for an item can be written as a weighted sum over the items they consumed. "Because you watched X" falls out of the algebra [5].

3.4 Industrial implementations

Implementation Algorithm(s) Execution model Notes
Spark MLlib ALS [6] explicit ALS, implicit ALS (Hu et al.) distributed, block-partitioned parameters rank, regParam, alpha, implicitPrefs; coldStartStrategy to drop NaN predictions
Facebook Giraph CF [7] SGD and ALS on Apache Giraph graph-parallel "rotational" scheme reported on graphs of roughly 100B ratings (approx.)
benfred/implicit [22] iALS (incl. conjugate gradient), BPR, logistic MF, item-kNN (cosine/TF-IDF/BM25) multi-threaded Cython/OpenMP, CUDA kernels for ALS and BPR integrates Annoy, NMSLIB and Faiss for ANN; advises disabling BLAS threading for big speedups
Google iALS / iALS++ [18] iALS, block (subspace) iALS++ single-machine research code embedding dims up to 2048 (ML-20M) and 8192 (MSD)
TensorFlow WALS (historical) weighted ALS distributed TF basis of earlier Google Cloud recommendation tutorials (approx.)

Facebook's rotational hybrid. Facebook's 2015 engineering post "Recommending items to more than a billion people" describes running MF on Giraph [7]. Workers hold partitions of users, and item factors rotate between workers in a ring. This avoids broadcasting the full item matrix, which standard Giraph and Spark ALS would do. Facebook reported that the approach handled datasets of around 100 billion ratings, which was much larger than the open-source alternatives of the time could handle. The post also covers approximate top-k serving by grouping items. Figures are approximate here because the post could not be re-read during this session.

The implicit library's practical tips. Set OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 or MKL_NUM_THREADS=1 so BLAS threading does not fight the library's own OpenMP parallelism. Use GPU kernels for ALS and BPR. Serve with an ANN index (Annoy, NMSLIB, Faiss) rather than brute-force scoring [22].

3.5 iALS revisited (2021-2022)

Rendle, Krichene, Zhang and Koren re-ran iALS on the benchmarks that neural papers use. These were the NCF setups (ML-1M, Pinterest) and the Mult-VAE setups (ML-20M, Million Song Dataset) [18]. The released configurations show what "properly tuned" means [18]:

Benchmark Dim Reg Unobserved weight Epochs
ML-1M (NCF protocol) 192 0.007 0.3 12
Pinterest (NCF protocol) 192 0.02 0.007 16
ML-20M (VAE protocol) 256 (2048 in headline table) 0.003 0.1 16
MSD (VAE protocol) 256 (8192 in headline table) 0.002 0.02 16

Three details carried most of the gain [18]:

  1. A separate weight on unobserved entries, rather than the implicit weight of 1 in the original formulation.
  2. Frequency-scaled regularisation (the "reg exp" exponent).
  3. Much larger embedding dimensions than papers usually allow, up to 2048 and 8192.

The companion iALS++ paper uses block (subspace) coordinate descent so that these large dimensions are cheap enough to train [18]. The conclusion of the revisiting paper was that a well-tuned iALS is competitive with the strongest published results on these benchmarks, including Mult-VAE and EASE. The numbers are in the paper's Tables 3 and 4 and are not reproduced here.

4. Pairwise learning to rank: BPR and WARP

4.1 BPR (Rendle et al., UAI 2009)

Problem. Pointwise regression on 0/1 implicit data optimises the wrong thing. What matters is that observed items rank above unobserved ones for each user.

Model. BPR assumes that for user u, an observed item i should be preferred to an unobserved item j. It maximises the posterior

 sum over (u,i,j) in D_S of  ln sigma( xhat_uij )  -  lambda ||Theta||^2
   with xhat_uij = xhat_ui - xhat_uj

This is a smooth surrogate for AUC [8]. BPR is a criterion, not a model. xhat can come from MF (BPR-MF), item-kNN (BPR-kNN) or anything differentiable.

Training. The full set of (u, i, j) triples is huge, so BPR uses LearnBPR: SGD with bootstrap sampling of triples, drawn uniformly with replacement. The paper argues this converges much faster than user-wise sweeps [8].

Lessons from later practice.

  • Uniform negative sampling gives mostly easy negatives late in training, so gradients vanish. This led to popularity-aware, adaptive and hard negative sampling, and to WARP.
  • BPR-MF is in every evaluation suite. In Dacrema et al., BPRMF sits next to iALS, PureSVD, FunkSVD and SLIM-BPR [16].
  • It needs careful tuning: learning rate, regularisation and the number of sampled negatives all matter a lot.

4.2 WARP and LightFM

WARP (Weighted Approximate-Rank Pairwise). For each positive, sample negatives until one violates the margin. The number of draws needed estimates the positive's rank, and the update is weighted by a function of that rank. This focuses learning on the top of the list. LightFM implements both BPR and WARP losses, and its quickstart uses LightFM(loss='warp') [9].

5. Sparse and dense linear item-item models: SLIM and EASE

5.1 SLIM (Ning and Karypis, ICDM 2011)

Idea. Learn the item-item weight matrix W directly rather than computing it from a similarity heuristic:

 min_W  1/2 ||A - A W||_F^2 + beta/2 ||W||_F^2 + lambda ||W||_1
 s.t.   W >= 0,  diag(W) = 0

A is the user-item matrix. The L1 + L2 (elastic net) penalty makes W sparse, so serving is as cheap as item-kNN. The zero-diagonal constraint stops the trivial solution of each item predicting itself. The non-negativity keeps W interpretable. Each column of W is its own regression, so training splits by item.

System notes. The KarypisLab SLIM library is a multi-threaded C implementation with command-line tools (slim_learn, slim_predict, slim_mselect for model selection) and a Python interface [10]. It offers coordinate descent and an ADMM solver (which needs Intel MKL). The README says ADMM usually wins when there are few items relative to users and many non-zeros [10]. In the Dacrema et al. suite, SLIM ElasticNet and SLIM BPR are among the strongest baselines [16].

5.2 EASE (Steck, WWW 2019)

Idea. Drop the L1 penalty and the non-negativity constraint from SLIM and keep only L2 and the zero diagonal. The problem then has a closed-form solution:

 min_B ||X - X B||_F^2 + lambda ||B||_F^2   s.t. diag(B) = 0

 P   = (X^T X + lambda I)^(-1)                 # item-item, m x m
 B_ij = - P_ij / P_jj   for i != j ,  B_jj = 0
 scores(u) = x_u B                             # dense item-item "autoencoder"

An open-source implementation [11b] follows exactly this recipe: build the sparse user-item matrix, form the regularised Gram matrix X^T X + lambda I, invert it, take B with a zeroed diagonal, score with X B, filter seen items and take the top-k.

Why it matters. EASE is a linear autoencoder with no hidden layer, which is why the title calls it "embarrassingly shallow". It matched or beat deep autoencoders such as Mult-VAE on the standard ML-20M, Netflix and MSD benchmarks [11]. Training is one m x m inversion, with cost roughly O(m^3) in the number of items. That cost does not depend on the number of users, and m in the low tens of thousands fits comfortably in memory. Its two limits are the m^2 memory of a dense B and the cubic inversion. Beyond about 10^5 items you need item pruning, sparse approximations or blockwise methods. Steck also observed that the learned weights include many negative item-item weights, which carry useful information. SLIM's non-negativity constraint throws that information away [11].

Follow-ups. The main deep model EASE was measured against was Mult-VAE [27]. Steck's later work extended the linear family, with higher-order relations and denoising views of the linear autoencoder (not re-verified this session). It also pointed out pitfalls of using cosine similarity on learned embeddings [28]. In 2026 EASE is still the default "is your fancy model actually better?" check in the major benchmarking frameworks.

  Linear item-item models: what each one learns

               similarity source           constraints            training cost
  item-kNN     cosine / Jaccard heuristic  top-k sparsify         O(nnz * avg deg)
  SAR          co-occurrence + rescale     time-decayed A         O(nnz + m^2)
  RP3beta      3-step random walk          popularity penalty     sparse mat-mults
  SLIM         learned (elastic net)       W >= 0, diag 0         m regressions
  EASE         learned (ridge)             diag 0                 one m x m inverse

6. Word2vec-style item embeddings: item2vec, prod2vec, Airbnb

6.1 item2vec (Barkan and Koenigstein, 2016)

Apply skip-gram with negative sampling (SGNS) to item sets, such as the items in one user's basket or listening list. Each set is treated as a "sentence" in which every pair of items is context, because order is ignored. The learned vectors give item-item similarity that is competitive with SVD-based item similarity, and it was evaluated on Microsoft Store and music data [12]. The appeal for systems is that SGNS is cheap, scales linearly with the number of co-occurrences, and gives dense vectors that drop straight into an ANN index.

6.2 prod2vec and bagged-prod2vec (Yahoo, KDD 2015)

Grbovic et al. ("E-commerce in Your Inbox") learned product embeddings from purchase sequences mined from e-mail receipts. Receipts were ordered in time per user, and products in the same receipt formed context. They added user embeddings (user2vec), and a "bagged" variant that treats each receipt as an unordered bag. This was one of the first web-scale industrial uses of word2vec for recommendation, serving product ads in Yahoo Mail. It reported clear CTR gains over popularity-based targeting (exact figures not re-verified here) [13].

6.3 Airbnb listing embeddings (KDD 2018 best paper)

Airbnb trained listing embeddings on click sessions, roughly 800 million of them. A session is split when consecutive clicks are more than 30 minutes apart. Approximate details from the KDD paper and the Airbnb engineering post [14]:

  • 32-dimensional embeddings for about 4.5M active listings.
  • Booked listing as global context. In booked sessions, the booked listing is kept in every context window. Every click in the session is then pulled towards the conversion.
  • Market-aware negatives. Extra negatives are sampled from the same market, so embeddings separate listings within a city instead of just learning geography.
  • Cold start. A new listing's embedding is the average of its three nearest listings by type, price and location (approx.).
  • User-type and listing-type embeddings trained on bookings to handle sparsity for long-horizon personalisation.
  • Production use: similar-listing carousels, and real-time personalisation features in search ranking. They reported a meaningful CTR lift on similar-listing recommendations (approx. 21%, not re-verified this session).
 Airbnb-style session embedding pipeline
 --------------------------------------
  click logs --> sessionize (30-min gap) --> filter (dwell >= threshold)
       |
       v
  SGNS training (window, negatives = random + same-market, global ctx = booking)
       |
       v
  listing vectors (d=32) --> ANN index --> "similar listings" candidates
       |
       +--> real-time features: sim(candidate, recently clicked / skipped)
                                  --> fed to GBDT/NN search ranker

Lesson. Each of these word2vec variants is the same algorithm. What made them work was domain-specific sessionisation, context design and negative sampling. Treat embedding quality as a data-engineering problem first.

7. Content-based and hybrid recommenders

7.1 Content-based filtering

Content-based recommenders represent items by features: text, tags, categories, audio or image embeddings. They represent users by aggregating the features of items they liked, then score candidates by similarity or a learned classifier. Microsoft Recommenders includes a TF-IDF content baseline for text datasets [15]. The Dacrema et al. suite includes CBF-kNN and a CF+CBF hybrid kNN [16]. Strengths: cold start for new items, transparency, and no need for other users' data. Weaknesses: over-specialisation (the "more of the same" filter bubble), and quality capped by feature quality. In 2026 that cap has been raised a lot by pretrained text and image encoders.

7.2 Hybrids: LightFM as the canonical design

LightFM (Kula, RecSys 2015 workshop, built at Lyst) represents each user and item as the sum of the latent vectors of its features [9]. Feature sets usually include a per-entity indicator feature plus metadata such as tags, brand and category. The model:

 user u  -> features f_u (one-hot id + metadata)  -> e_u = sum_{j in f_u} E_U[j]
 item i  -> features f_i (one-hot id + metadata)  -> e_i = sum_{j in f_i} E_I[j]
 score(u,i) = e_u . e_i + b_u + b_i     trained with BPR or WARP (or logistic)

With only indicator features, LightFM is plain MF. With only metadata features, it is a content model. With both, a new item with no interactions still gets a meaningful embedding from its tags [9]. This structure is conceptually a two-tower model with linear, bag-of-features towers. It is the direct ancestor of the neural two-tower retrieval in Chapter 2. Factorization machines (xLearn FM/FFM in Microsoft Recommenders [15]) generalise the same idea to arbitrary feature crosses.

7.3 Hybridisation patterns in production

  • Feature augmentation. CF embeddings (iALS, item2vec) become features in a GBDT or neural ranker. Airbnb does this [14].
  • Switching. Use content and popularity for cold users and items, and CF once there are enough interactions.
  • Candidate-source union. Item-kNN, MF, content and trending sources each supply candidates. A learned ranker merges them. This is the "classic models as retrieval sources" pattern that most large systems still use (see Chapter 1).

8. The reproducibility crisis: why classic baselines still matter

8.1 Dacrema, Cremonesi and Jannach (RecSys 2019, best paper)

"Are We Really Making Much Progress? A Worrying Analysis of Recent Neural Recommendation Approaches" examined 18 top-N recommendation algorithms. All were neural and published at major venues (KDD, SIGIR, WWW, RecSys) in the preceding years. The findings [16][17]:

  • Only 7 of 18 could be reproduced with reasonable effort, using the authors' code and data.
  • Of those 7, 6 were often outperformed by comparatively simple heuristics: nearest-neighbour or graph methods tuned properly.
  • The remaining one beat the simple baselines but did not consistently beat a well-tuned non-neural linear ranking method.

8.2 The TOIS extension (2021)

"A Troubling Analysis of Reproducibility and Progress in Recommender Systems Research" widened the study [17]. Roughly 12 of 26 examined neural methods could be reproduced, and 11 of those 12 were outperformed by simple, well-tuned baselines (approximate counts as stated in the paper's abstract). The accompanying code base [16] ported the neural methods:

  • CollaborativeDL, CollaborativeVAE, MCRec, DELF, DMF, ConvNCF, CoupledCF, NeuRec, CFM, NeuMF, Mult-VAE, SpectralCF and CMN.

It evaluated them against 17 baselines, all with systematic hyperparameter search:

  • Random and TopPop.
  • UserKNN and ItemKNN.
  • CBF and CF+CBF kNN.
  • P3alpha and RP3beta.
  • PureSVD, NMF, iALS, BPRMF and FunkSVD.
  • EASE-R, SLIM-BPR and SLIM-ElasticNet.

A 2021 maintenance note fixed an HR/NDCG implementation issue that affected a few NDCG numbers, and stated that "the analysis and conclusions of the study are not affected" [16].

A companion CIKM 2020 paper went after a specific architectural claim. It showed that the reported benefit of applying CNNs to the outer-product "embedding map" of user and item vectors (ConvNCF and relatives) did not come from the convolutions [16].

8.3 Converging evidence from other groups

  • Rendle, Krichene, Zhang and Anderson (RecSys 2020), "Neural Collaborative Filtering vs. Matrix Factorization Revisited." On NCF's own datasets and protocol (ML-1M, Pinterest; embedding sizes swept from 16 to 192, 8 repeats), a properly set-up dot-product MF beat NeuMF. A second experiment showed that an MLP needs very large capacity and data to learn even a plain dot product [19]. The systems corollary: dot-product scoring is also what makes ANN retrieval possible, which an MLP scoring function rules out.
  • Rendle, Zhang and Koren (2019), "On the Difficulty of Evaluating Baselines." On MovieLens-10M and the Netflix Prize data, carefully tuned classic methods (Bayesian timeSVD++ flipped and similar) beat many recently published results. The conclusion was that the reported baseline numbers had been far too weak [26].
  • Rendle et al., iALS revisited (2021-2022). Tuned iALS matched EASE and Mult-VAE on ML-20M and MSD [18].
  • Anelli et al. (UMAP 2022), "Top-N Recommendation Algorithms: A Quest for the State of the Art." A large Elliot-based comparison on MovieLens-1M (about 1M interactions), Amazon Digital Music (about 1.58M interactions, 840K users) and Epinions (about 300K interactions) [20]. It again found classic linear and neighbourhood models highly competitive. It also examined beyond-accuracy dimensions such as novelty, diversity and popularity bias, where rankings differ.
  • Krichene and Rendle (KDD 2020), "On Sampled Metrics for Item Recommendation." Evaluating with 1 positive vs. 100 sampled negatives, the protocol inherited from NCF, can change the ranking of algorithms compared with full ranking [29]. That puts many published comparisons in doubt.
  • Session-based recommendation. Ludewig, Jannach and colleagues found that session-kNN variants are often competitive with GRU4Rec and later neural session models [30].

8.4 Root causes, and the fixes the community adopted

Failure mode Typical symptom Fix adopted by benchmark frameworks
Untuned baselines baseline uses defaults; proposed model tuned for weeks equal hyperparameter budget (Bayesian or random search) for all models [16][23]
Weak baseline choice only BPR-MF / NeuMF as baselines always include ItemKNN, RP3beta, SLIM/EASE, iALS, TopPop [16][20]
Sampled metrics 1 positive + 100 negatives full-ranking evaluation [29]
Data leakage, inconsistent splits test info used for early stopping or tuning explicit train/validation/test splits; temporal splits
Missing code or data cannot reproduce released configs and seeds (Elliot, RecBole, Dacrema repo) [16][23][24]
Single-metric reporting only HR@10 accuracy + beyond-accuracy + significance tests (Elliot has Wilcoxon and paired t-test) [23]

Frameworks now encode these practices:

  • Elliot (SIGIR 2021) runs the whole pipeline, from loading and splitting through hyperparameter optimisation to statistical testing. It covers BPRMF, FunkSVD, SVD++, kNN, SLIM, VAE, NeuMF and more [23].
  • RecBole offers 94 algorithms across general, sequential, context-aware and knowledge-based tasks, with BPR as its quick-start default [24].
  • Microsoft Recommenders wraps ALS (PySpark), BPR (Cornac), SAR, LightFM, Surprise SVD, xLearn FM/FFM and TF-IDF next to neural models [15].

9. Comparison: classic algorithms as a system designer sees them

Algorithm Feedback Training cost (approx.) Serving pattern Cold start Typical role in 2026 stacks
User-kNN explicit or implicit O(n^2) user sims or on-the-fly neighbour lookup per request poor rarely used at scale
Item-kNN / item-to-item [1][25] implicit O(nnz * deg), offline batch precomputed top-N per item, merge poor for new items "similar items" widgets, candidate source
SAR [21] implicit + time co-occurrence O(m^2) memory A x S, or top-N per item poor quick strong baseline
P3alpha / RP3beta [16] implicit sparse matrix products precomputed item-item poor strong baseline, long-tail boost
Funk-SVD / SVD++ [3][4] explicit ratings SGD, O(nnz * f) per epoch dot product poor rating prediction, legacy
iALS [5][18] implicit O(f^2 nnz + f^3 (n+m)) per sweep dot product + ANN poor (fold-in possible) retrieval source, embedding features
BPR-MF [8] implicit SGD over sampled triples dot product + ANN poor baseline; sampling research
SLIM [10] implicit m elastic-net regressions sparse x_u W poor strong accuracy, sparse serving
EASE [11] implicit one m x m inverse, O(m^3) dense x_u B poor strongest simple baseline for m < ~1e5
item2vec / prod2vec [12][13] sequences / baskets SGNS, linear in co-occurrences ANN on item vectors poor (fixable via averaging) similar items, session features
Content-based (TF-IDF etc.) [15] item features feature extraction similarity search good cold start, explanations
LightFM hybrid [9] implicit/explicit + metadata SGD (BPR/WARP) dot product + ANN good small/mid-scale hybrid, cold-start retrieval

10. Reference architecture: classic models in a modern pipeline

                              +----------------------------+
   interaction logs --------> | batch training (daily)     |
   (views, plays, buys)       |  - item-kNN / RP3beta      |----> item->topN table (KV)
                              |  - iALS / BPR (Spark/GPU)  |----> item & user factors
                              |  - EASE (if m small)       |----> B matrix / top-N
                              |  - item2vec on sessions    |----> item vectors
                              +-------------+--------------+
                                            |
                                    ANN index build (Faiss/ScaNN/Annoy)
                                            |
 request --> context (recent items, user id) v
         --> candidate generation: union of
               [kNN lookups of recent items] + [ANN on user factor]
               + [content / trending for cold users]          (~100s-1000s)
         --> feature join (incl. CF scores, embedding sims as features)
         --> learned ranker (GBDT or DNN)                           (~10s)
         --> business rules, diversity, dedup  --> response

Here the classic models do three jobs:

  1. Candidate sources. They are cheap and high-recall.
  2. Features for the ranker. Examples: an iALS dot product, an item2vec similarity to the last clicked item, a co-occurrence count.
  3. Baselines and guardrails. A new model has to beat them offline on full-ranking metrics, and online in A/B tests, before it ships.

Key takeaways for system designers

  1. Tune baselines before building new models. In the reproducibility studies, ItemKNN, RP3beta, SLIM, EASE and iALS beat most published neural recommenders once they were tuned [16][17][18][19]. Give every baseline the same hyperparameter-search budget as the new model.
  2. Pick item-item over user-user for online serving. Item relationships are stable and can be precomputed. Online cost then depends on the user's history length, not on catalogue size [1][2].
  3. For implicit data, weight by confidence and count the unobserved entries. The Hu-Koren-Volinsky formulation, made tractable by the Y^T Y precompute trick, is still the right mental model. Modern tuning adds a separate weight for unobserved entries, frequency-scaled regularisation and large dimensions [5][18].
  4. Prefer dot products. They are as accurate as MLP scorers in fair comparisons, and they are what makes ANN retrieval and caching possible [19].
  5. EASE is the cheapest strong baseline when the catalogue is small enough. One matrix inverse, no SGD and no sampling. Move to SLIM (sparse), item-kNN, iALS or blockwise approximations as m grows past about 1e5 [10][11].
  6. Embedding quality depends on the training data you construct. item2vec-style models succeed or fail on sessionisation, context windows and negative sampling, as with Airbnb's booked-listing global context and same-market negatives [14].
  7. Hybrids solve cold start. Building entity embeddings as sums of feature embeddings (LightFM) is the simplest way to embed new items. Today's two-tower models are the neural version of the same idea [9].
  8. Evaluate with full ranking, fixed splits and significance tests. Sampled metrics can reorder algorithms [29]. Use a framework such as Elliot, RecBole or the Dacrema code base, and release configs [16][23][24].
  9. Retire classic models with care. Many production stacks still use kNN and MF as candidate sources and ranker features even after adding deep models, because they are cheap, interpretable and robust.

37. Real-Time and Session-Based Recommendation: Streaming Updates, Online Learning, Nearline Pipelines and In-Session Intent

A recommender reacts to user behaviour on several clocks. The item corpus changes by the minute: new videos, posts, listings and ads appear constantly. User intent changes within a session: a user who has just saved three kitchen Pins wants kitchens now, whatever their 90-day profile says. Model parameters go stale as the world drifts: Facebook showed in 2014 that prediction quality degrades measurably for every day the training data falls behind the serving day [3]. Real-time recommendation is the set of designs that shorten these clocks without breaking cost, latency or stability budgets.

This chapter surveys the public designs along four axes:

  1. Fresh features. Streaming counters, real-time action sequences and session embeddings computed from event streams (Kafka plus Flink, Heron or Samza) and served from a low-latency store. Examples: Twitter's aggregation framework, Airbnb's session embeddings, Chronon's tiled Flink aggregations, DoorDash Riviera.
  2. Fresh candidates. Indexes and graphs that absorb new edges and items within seconds. Examples: GraphJet, Pixie, Manas realtime HNSW and X's Thunder.
  3. Fresh user representations inside the model. Real-time sequence encoders that read the last N actions at request time. Examples: TransAct, TransAct V2, SIM/TWIN-style search over long histories, and the academic session-based line GRU4Rec, SASRec and BERT4Rec.
  4. Fresh parameters. Online or continual training with streaming label joins and incremental parameter sync. Examples: Facebook's online joiner, Google Photon, ByteDance Monolith, Kuaishou PERSIA, and delayed-feedback corrections from Twitter and Alibaba.

The recurring tension is freshness versus stability. Fresher means more infrastructure, more ways to diverge between training and serving, more exposure to feedback loops and noise, and less diversity. The best designs pair a cheap, stable long-term component (a batch embedding, a daily model, a lifelong history) with a small, fast real-time component, and they measure the decay curve before buying freshness.

Sourcing note. The sandbox egress proxy blocked direct fetches of arXiv, Medium and company blogs. The chapter therefore draws on two kinds of material. The first is primary sources (papers, engineering posts and open-source READMEs) that sibling chapters of this Atlas had already fetched and summarized (Chapters 5, 8, 9, 11, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 26 and 28). The second is a later research pass of about 25 web searches, whose result abstracts and snippets added references [53]-[63]. Figures marked "approx." come from secondary summaries or could not be re-verified here.

37.1 The landscape: where freshness lives

37.1.1 Offline, nearline, online: the Netflix blueprint (2013)

Netflix's "System Architectures for Personalization and Recommendation" by Amatriain and Basilico is still the clearest vocabulary for placing computation [27]. It separates where computation runs from what is computed:

 member events (plays, ratings, browsing, search)
        |
        +--> OFFLINE  (Hadoop/Hive/Pig): training, batch scoring; no data or
        |             complexity limit, but stale and context-blind
        |
        +--> NEARLINE (event-driven, no request waiting): e.g. on a play event
        |             recompute member factors and scores; results written to
        |             Cassandra / EVCache / MySQL
        |
        v
     ONLINE (per request, strict SLA): fetch precomputed + live signals,
            light model eval, filtering, context; FALLBACK to precomputed
            or unpersonalized results on timeout

Key rules from the post [27]:

  • Nearline is the middle tier. It reacts to events within seconds, can be more complex than online code because no request waits on it, and writes its results to fast stores.
  • Events vs data. Events are small, time-sensitive messages that must be processed fast and flow over a pub/sub system (Hermes in the post). Data is the denser record collected into Hadoop for later processing.
  • A model can be split across tiers. Item factors are trained offline, while user-dependent parts are re-solved nearline when the member acts. Netflix slides from the period describe re-solving a member's MF factors on a play event (approx.).

Amatriain's 2023 "10th anniversary" revisit says the split still holds, but "nearline" has grown into streaming feature platforms and near-real-time training [28]. Almost every system in this chapter can be placed in one of the three tiers.

Netflix's later stack shows how far the nearline tier has grown. Third-party summaries of Netflix talks describe Keystone, a managed Kafka routing service with Flink on top, running on the order of 20,000 Flink jobs. One stated use case is replacing day-old batch jobs for personalization signals such as "take fraction" (plays divided by impressions), which previously had a delay of hours to days (approx.) [62].

Eugene Yan's survey of real-time recommendations frames the trade-off from the operator's side [61]:

  • Batch recommendations are computed once a day and cached, so a failed compute step has no customer-facing impact.
  • Real-time recommendations aggregate streamed events and generate results on demand. They lose batch's economies of scale and are considerably trickier to run in production.

37.1.2 Four kinds of freshness

Freshness kind Typical latency Mechanism Representative systems
Feature freshness ms to seconds Stream processor -> KV store; request-time sequence fetch Twitter RTA [24], Chronon tiles [32], Airbnb [30], TransAct [9]
Candidate freshness seconds In-memory graphs, incremental ANN inserts GraphJet [18], Pixie [15], Manas realtime [16], Thunder [26]
Representation freshness per request Real-time sequence encoder in the ranker TransAct [9], TransAct V2 [11], TWIN [46]
Parameter freshness minutes to hours Online joiner + streaming trainer + incremental sync FB 2014 [3], Monolith [1], PERSIA [47]

These are complementary, not alternatives. A short-video feed typically uses all four. A marketplace like Airbnb can get most of the benefit from feature freshness alone [30].

37.2 Event backbone: a canonical action stream

Every real-time design starts with a reliable, low-latency stream of user actions with stable keys. Two public examples:

Twitter/X Unified User Actions (UUA). UUA is described as "a centralized, real-time stream of user actions". It merges client-side and server-side events into one Kafka stream, which is replicated to HDFS, Pub/Sub, GCS and BigQuery [22]. The User Signal Service then standardizes explicit and implicit signals (likes, retweets, follows, video views and so on) so that retrieval and ranking consume one schema [23].

Recos-Injector. For Twitter's GraphJet-based services, Recos-Injector is the streaming preprocessor. It consumes favorites, retweets, follows and client events, filters and combines them, and publishes them to a dedicated Kafka topic per GraphJet service [21].

Design rules that recur across sources:

  • Mint an impression or request ID at serving time and carry it into every downstream event. Facebook's online joiner, Google Photon and Monolith all depend on such a key for the label join [1][3][4].
  • Log features at serving time rather than recomputing them later. This is the only robust defence against training/serving skew for real-time features, because the value served at time t is hard to reconstruct offline [1][34].
  • Per-consumer topics. Recos-Injector's per-service topics let each consumer get a filtered, compact stream and scale independently [21].

Pinterest real-time user signal serving. Pinterest's log path runs from the Singer logging agent on serving hosts into Kafka. The Merced archiver copies Kafka to S3 for long retention, and a unified Flink source concatenates archived and live data behind one API, which the team calls "an unlimited log" [54]. On top of this, the real-time user signal service works in three steps [53]:

  1. It consumes trimmed engagement events (user ID, Pin ID, action type).
  2. A materialization step enriches each event with Pin and query features.
  3. It writes the result to a time-series store that rankers query online.

The post reports about 1.2 million events/s and a p99 of about 10 seconds from engagement to servable signal [53]. Services such as TransAct read their "last N actions" from this kind of store (Section 37.5.1).

37.3 Streaming features: counters, windows and tiles

37.3.1 Twitter's aggregation framework: one definition, two engines

Problem. The Home ranker, push notifications and email recommendations all need user, author, user x author and tweet engagement aggregates, conditioned on content type and engagement label, both over long horizons and over the last few minutes [24].

Design. An AggregateGroup declares keys (for example USER_ID or (USER_ID, AUTHOR_ID)), features, labels, metrics and half-lives (exponential decay rather than hard windows). The same definition drives a daily summingbird-scalding batch job, whose output is uploaded to Manhattan, and a summingbird-storm/Heron real-time job backed by memcached [24].

            client events (Kafka client-event topics)
                 |                               |
   daily DataRecord dumps (HDFS)        Storm/Heron (summingbird)
                 |                               |
   batch aggregates -> Manhattan KV     real-time aggregates -> memcached
                 \___________________   _________________/
                                     \ /
              Home Mixer / pushservice feature hydration

Scale. The 2023 open-source release describes ranking features kept over long windows (50 days) and real-time windows (under 3 days, typically 30 minutes), with roughly 6,000 features hydrated per ranked candidate for the For You heavy ranker (approx.) [24][25].

Tricks. Decayed counters are monoid-friendly: an old value plus elapsed time is enough to roll forward, so each key stores O(1) state instead of a window of events. The real-time path also updates "realtime features" such as like, reply and retweet counts on tweets for Earlybird-based retrieval [25].

37.3.2 Airbnb/Stripe Chronon: tiled Flink aggregation

Chronon (open-sourced by Airbnb and co-maintained with Stripe) makes the freshness model an explicit part of the feature definition.

  • A GroupBy with accuracy = SNAPSHOT is refreshed daily and backfilled as of the previous midnight. With TEMPORAL (the default when a Kafka topic is set) it is updated in real time online and backfilled with millisecond point-in-time accuracy offline [33].
  • Untiled vs tiled serving. In the untiled design the streaming job writes individual events and the fetcher folds them at request time. With 10 events/s for one key and a 12-hour window, one request has to fold 432,000 events. In the tiled design a stateful Flink job pre-aggregates events into tiles of intermediate representations (for example sum and count for an average), and the fetcher reads 12 or 13 one-hour tiles. Stripe reported a 33% reduction in feature-serving latency after the initial tiled rollout [32].
  • The Flink job evaluates the same Spark SQL expressions as the batch engine by embedding Catalyst inside Flink, so batch and streaming share one expression language [35].
  • Chronon logs served values and runs a daily job comparing them with backfilled values. It names the inherent sources of skew: Kafka plus KV write latency makes streaming features lag by milliseconds to seconds, and batch features are inconsistent "centered around midnight" until the bulk upload finishes [34].
 Kafka -> Flink [source] -> [Spark SQL eval] -> [tiling: IRs per tile] -> KV
 fetcher: get(key, tiles in [now - W, now)) -> merge IRs -> finalize -> feature
 batch upload holds hop-aligned partials; stream covers everything after batch end

37.3.3 Marketplace variants: DoorDash Riviera, Uber, Lyft

DoorDash's Riviera (2021) is a declarative framework for real-time features on Flink: features are defined in configuration and SQL, and the framework builds the streaming job. Its output lands in a Redis-based online feature store next to batch features from Fabricator [36]. Uber's Michelangelo used the same dual-path pattern: Kafka plus streaming jobs (Samza, later Flink) for near-real-time features such as a restaurant's recent average prep time, written to the same Cassandra store as batch features (approx.; see Chapter 8).

Instacart's account of moving to real-time ML shows the same shape. Its pipeline reads raw service events from Kafka, transforms them into features with Flink, and sinks them into a feature store for on-demand access. The motivation was that batch-only features made predictions stale during a shopping journey. The post also names an organizational trap: different teams had adopted three different streaming tools, which made cross-team event features hard to build [57]. A secondary case study of Instacart's Griffin ML platform lists session-based recommendations among the applications this streaming path enabled (approx.) [58].

Lesson. The streaming feature problem is solved. The remaining design work is (1) one declarative definition for batch, stream and backfill, (2) pre-aggregation on the write path for hot keys, and (3) logging served values to measure and remove skew.

37.4 Real-time candidate generation

37.4.1 GraphJet (Twitter, VLDB 2016)

Problem. Tweets have a useful life of hours. Collaborative filtering on a nightly batch graph is too stale, so Twitter needed "users who engaged with X also engaged with Y" over roughly the last day, with new edges visible within seconds [18].

Architecture. GraphJet "maintains a full graph index over a sliding time window in memory on a single server" [19]. The bipartite graph has users on one side and tweets (or URLs, hashtags) on the other. The index is a sequence of time-sliced segments: new edges go into the newest segment and whole segments are dropped when they leave the window, which avoids per-edge deletion and garbage-collection pressure. Recommendations come from SALSA-style personalized random walks [18].

Metric (per server, from README [19]) Value
Edge ingestion up to 1,000,000 edges/s
Recommendations, steady state up to 500/s
Edge reads "several million" per second

Production descendant: UTEG. The User-Tweet-Entity-Graph service is "a Finagle thrift service built on the GraphJet framework". It produces the "XXX liked" out-of-network tweets on the home timeline. It is fed by Kafka through Recos-Injector, keeps in-memory engagements for the past 24-48 hours, takes the viewer's RealGraph-weighted followees as input, and returns tweets ranked by weighted followee engagement [20][21]. Twitter's 2023 blog attributes roughly 15% of For You tweets to this kind of social-graph traversal (approx.) [25].

 Kafka (fav, RT, follow, client events)
        |
  recos-injector (filter, combine, per-service topic)
        |
  UTEG / GraphJet (24-48 h window, all in RAM, full replica per server)
        |  input: viewer's weighted followees
        v
  tweets ranked by followee engagement, with social proof

37.4.2 Thunder (X, 2026)

In the 2026 open-source X algorithm, in-network retrieval moved from the Lucene-based Earlybird search cluster to Thunder, "an in-memory post store and realtime ingestion pipeline". It consumes post create and delete events from Kafka, serves the posts of the viewer's followees, trims posts older than a retention period, and promises "sub-millisecond lookups for in-network content without hitting an external database". It also receives the already-seen list so it can exclude those posts at the source [26]. Architecturally this is GraphJet again: a time-windowed in-memory index replacing a general-purpose search engine for very fresh content.

37.4.3 Pixie (Pinterest, WWW 2018)

Problem. Recommend from more than 3 billion Pins to more than 200 million users and react to what the user just did. The previous Hadoop system precomputed results and could not react within a session [15].

Design. A pruned Pin-Board bipartite graph of about 3 billion nodes and 17 billion edges, about 120 GB, is loaded into RAM on each server. Every server holds a full replica, so walks never cross machines. The graph is rebuilt offline. The query is real time: the user's most recent Pins, each weighted, seed many short random walks with restarts. Per-Pin visit counts are combined as V[p] = (sum over q of sqrt(V_q[p]))^2, which rewards candidates reached from several query Pins. Walks stop early once enough Pins pass a visit threshold [15].

Scale. p99 latency under 60 ms, about 1,200 requests/s per server and about 100,000 requests/s across the cluster, with up to 50% higher engagement than the Hadoop system [15].

Lesson. Freshness can come from the query, not the index. A daily graph with real-time seed actions already gives in-session responsiveness.

37.4.4 Manas realtime HNSW (Pinterest)

Pinterest's ANN platform Manas added a realtime HNSW mode in which new Pins are inserted incrementally into the graph index, so embedding-based retrieval can surface fresh content without waiting for a full rebuild. Filtering was first done by over-fetching K neighbours and post-filtering [16]. Streaming filters later reused the inverted index as the filter store, with bitmap and array-backed posting lists replacing skiplists for faster lookups [17].

37.4.5 Google News co-visitation (2007)

The earliest large-scale example of the split is Google News personalization [49]. MinHash user clusters and PLSI classes are computed in batch with MapReduce. Co-visitation counts (two stories clicked by the same user within a time window) and per-cluster click counts are updated online in Bigtable, so a story gets a score as soon as clicks arrive. Serving blends the three signals linearly. The pattern of batch structure plus streaming counts is the same one Twitter and Pinterest later used.

37.5 Real-time user intent inside the ranker

37.5.1 Pinterest TransAct (KDD 2023)

Problem. Pinterest's user embedding PinnerFormer is computed in a daily batch. It was explicitly trained to tolerate staleness: moving from real-time to daily inference cut Recall@10 by 13.9% with a next-action objective but only by 8.3% with the dense all-action objective [13]. Even so, a daily embedding cannot react to what the user did seconds ago [9].

Hybrid design. TransAct encodes the user's most recent actions (on the order of 100) in real time inside the Homefeed ranker (Pinnability), while PinnerFormer and other batch features provide long-term context. The authors present this as combining real-time responsiveness with the cost efficiency of batch representations [9].

 real-time action stream                                  candidate Pin
         |                                                      |
 latest ~100 actions: PinSage emb + action type + timestamp     |
         |                                                      |
 early fusion: concat each action with candidate embedding <---+
         v
 small Transformer encoder
         v
 compress (first K tokens + max pooling) -> flatten
         v
 concat with PinnerFormer + other features -> DCN v2 -> MLP
         v
 multi-task heads (repin, click, hide, ...) -> utility

Findings and tricks [9][10]:

  • Early fusion of each action with the candidate makes the sequence encoder target-aware.
  • Action-type embeddings mattered more than positional encodings.
  • Random time-window masking during training hides the most recent actions for some examples, so the model does not over-rely on the last few clicks. This protects diversity (as reported in summaries).
  • The paper lists production problems: serving complexity, reduced diversity, and engagement decay, which means the model needs frequent retraining.
  • Serving. The new model raised CPU latency by more than 20x, so Pinterest moved Homefeed ranking to GPU serving to stay latency-neutral at the same cost [10].
  • Results. Secondary summaries report about +11% Homefeed repin volume and -10% hides (approx.). TransAct was deployed in Homefeed, Related Pins, Notifications and Search [9].

37.5.2 TransAct V2 (2025): real-time plus lifelong

TransAct V2 extends Homefeed ranking from about 100 real-time actions to lifelong histories of up to about 16,000 actions [11][12]. It keeps three sequences, lifelong, real-time and impressions, and selects a short subsequence by candidate-anchored nearest-neighbour search in PinSage space. The most recent real-time actions are always kept, so in-session intent is never lost to the long-history search [11].

  • Each token carries a timestamp, a multi-hot action type, the surface and a 32-d PinSage embedding. Lifelong actions are stored with int8 quantization [11].
  • An auxiliary Next Action Loss predicts what the user does next [11].
  • Serving kernels (fused dequantization plus NN search, a single-kernel Triton Transformer) improved end-to-end inference latency by 103x (p50), 338x (p90) and 250x (p99) over the unoptimised baseline [11].
  • Reported online results: +6.35% repins, +1.41% time spent, -12.8% hides [12].
  • A literature review of the paper reports offline gains over the real-time-only TransAct baseline: +13.31% HIT@3 on repins and -11.25% HIT@3 on hides. It also notes that only the nearest-neighbour features are logged at request time, and the NN search is recomputed offline for training (approx.) [63].

37.5.3 Long histories with real-time recency: SIM and TWIN

Alibaba's SIM (CIKM 2020) introduced the two-stage pattern for lifelong histories. A General Search Unit (GSU) retrieves behaviours relevant to the candidate. In production this is "hard search" by category over a User Behavior Tree keyed by user ID then category ID, about 22 TB in size. An Exact Search Unit (ESU) then runs target attention over the top-K. The output is concatenated with short-term, real-time DIN features. SIM modelled up to 54,000 behaviours and reported +7.1% CTR and +4.4% RPM in display advertising [45].

Kuaishou's TWIN (KDD 2023) makes the GSU use the same target-attention relevance as the ESU. It keeps it affordable by precomputing and caching linear projections of item-inherent features per item, and compressing user-item cross features into a scalar attention bias. The CP-GSU scores about 10^4 behaviours, keeps the top 100, and the authors report a 99.3% reduction of the compute bottleneck, enough to deploy on main traffic [46].

The real-time lesson: lifelong and real-time are separate inputs with separate freshness. The long history is indexed or cached and can lag. The last few minutes of actions are streamed and always included.

37.5.4 Airbnb: session embeddings as real-time features (KDD 2018)

Problem. Search ranking should react to what the guest is doing in this session, for example clicking several cheap, modern apartments near the centre, without retraining a model [30].

Design. Grbovic and Cheng trained skip-gram listing embeddings on click sessions, splitting sessions at gaps of more than 30 minutes. They added two changes: the booked listing as a global context for every listing in a booking session, and same-market negatives. Secondary summaries report about 800 million click sessions, about 4.5 million active listings and 32-dimensional embeddings (approx.) [30][31].

Real-time use. Kafka streams record the user's clicked, skipped, long-clicked, wishlisted and contacted listings over roughly the last two weeks. For each candidate the ranker computes features such as "similarity to clicked listings" and "similarity to skipped listings" online and feeds them to the GBDT ranker in production at the time. The paper reports an online booking gain, and the embedding similarity features ranked high in importance [30].

Lesson. Freshness can come from cheap online similarity features over a streamed short history, with no online training at all. Skipped items are a valuable real-time negative signal.

37.5.5 Netflix: in-session adaptation for search

Netflix research described augmenting search with recommendations adapted to the member's current session. Browsing and partial-query signals in the session predict intent before or while the member types, which matters most on TV devices where typing is slow (approx.) [29].

37.5.6 Instagram Explore: online user tower, offline item tower

Instagram Explore's main ML retrieval source is a two-tower network. Item embeddings are computed offline (typically daily) and indexed, and a fresh user embedding is computed at request time from online features before ANN search. The first-stage ranker reuses two towers for cacheability, and some users' heavy-stage results are precomputed off-peak [37]. This asymmetry, where the user side is fresh and the item side is batched, is the standard compromise for two-tower retrieval.

37.6 Session-based models: the academic line

Session-based recommendation predicts the next item from a short, often anonymous, sequence. It is the modelling counterpart of real-time intent.

Model Year / org Core idea Notable result or caveat
GRU4Rec [38] 2015, Gravity R&D / Telefonica GRU over session clicks; session-parallel mini-batches; in-batch negatives; BPR/TOP1 ranking losses Beat item-kNN in the paper
Session-kNN [39] 2017, Jannach & Ludewig Nearest-neighbour over sessions Beat GRU4Rec in most tested setups; hybrids best
HRNN [44] 2017 Hierarchical RNN: session RNN initialized from a user-level RNN Personalizes sessions for logged-in users
SASRec [40] 2018, UCSD Causal self-attention for next item About 10x faster than CNN/RNN baselines
BERT4Rec [41] 2019, Alibaba Bidirectional Cloze training Not consistently better than SASRec on replication [42]
gSASRec [42] 2023, Glasgow SASRec + gBCE to fix negative-sampling overconfidence +9.47% NDCG vs BERT4Rec on ML-1M; ~73% faster training
Transformers4Rec [43] 2021, NVIDIA Library bridging NLP Transformers and session recs Used in competitions and industry pipelines

Key details:

  • GRU4Rec made RNNs practical for sessions with session-parallel mini-batches: many sessions run in parallel, and when one ends the next takes its slot and its hidden state is reset. Scoring is restricted to items in the mini-batch, an early form of in-batch negatives [38].
  • Strong simple baselines. Jannach and Ludewig showed that session-based nearest neighbours often beat GRU4Rec, and the best results came from combining the two [39]. Co-visitation-style item-to-item methods (as in Google News [49]) remain hard to beat for very short sessions.
  • Loss and sampling matter more than architecture. gSASRec traces most of the BERT4Rec vs SASRec gap to overconfidence caused by negative sampling [42].

From academia to production. Industrial systems rarely deploy a pure session model. Instead the session encoder becomes one component: a real-time sequence feature in a ranker (TransAct [9]), a user tower in retrieval (Instagram [37]), or the short-term branch next to a lifelong search unit (SIM [45], TWIN [46]). Meta's HSTU goes further, treating recommendation as sequential transduction over a single chronological stream of content and action tokens per user. The paper motivates the design explicitly by high-cardinality, non-stationary streaming data [48].

37.7 Online learning: streaming labels and continual training

37.7.1 Facebook ads online joiner (2014)

He et al. describe an online data joiner. Impressions and clicks are keyed by request ID. Impressions wait in a window: a click within the waiting window makes a positive, and otherwise a negative is emitted when the window closes. The labeled stream feeds an online trainer for the logistic-regression layer on top of boosted-tree feature transforms, and models are pushed back to the ranker [3].

  • Waiting-window trade-off. Too short and late clicks become false negatives, biasing CTR down. Too long and examples arrive late and need more buffer memory.
  • Safety. The joiner needs anomaly protection, for example alarms and cutting off the trainer if the click stream stops [3].
  • Freshness evidence. Normalized entropy worsens as training data falls days behind evaluation, which motivates daily or online training [3].
  • Negative downsampling with recalibration q = p / (p + (1 - p)/w) became the standard correction [3].

37.7.2 Google Photon (2013): exactly-once joins

Photon joins clicks to queries across datacenters with exactly-once semantics, because each joined click is billed and used for training. A Paxos-replicated IdRegistry records joined event IDs, so duplicate processing in several datacenters never emits a click twice. Clicks that arrive before their query are retried. The paper reports millions of joined events per minute with end-to-end latency of seconds (approx.) [4]. The lesson for recommenders is that the join must be idempotent: duplicate positives inflate CTR and break calibration.

37.7.3 ByteDance Monolith (2022): minute-level training at TikTok scale

Problem. ByteDance's feed and ads models face an unbounded, non-stationary sparse ID space, long-tailed feature frequency and concept drift within hours. Standard TensorFlow keeps batch training and serving "completely separated", and fixed-size hashed tables cause collisions [1].

Architecture.

 client actions --> Kafka: actions ---+
 serving-time feature log --> Kafka --+
                                      v
           Flink online joiner (join on request key; in-memory cache +
           on-disk KV for late actions; negative sampling)
                  |                                     |
          Kafka: training examples              HDFS (batch dumps)
                  |                                     |
          online training workers <--- same code ---> batch training
                  |
          training PS: Cuckoo-hash tables (frequency admission + expiry)
                  |  sparse: incremental sync of touched IDs (minute-level)
                  |  dense : synced far less often
                  v
          serving PS -> online inference

Key tricks [1][2]:

  • Collisionless embeddings. Cuckoo-hash key-value tables on the parameter servers give every ID its own row. Frequency filtering admits an ID only after it has been seen a threshold number of times, and expirable embeddings evict inactive IDs. Together they bound memory.
  • One codebase, two modes. Batch training on HDFS bootstraps the model, and online training then consumes the Kafka example stream indefinitely.
  • Asymmetric parameter sync. Pushing terabytes every minute is impractical. Only sparse rows touched since the last sync are pushed, at minute-level intervals, while dense weights, which change slowly, are synced much less often.
  • Cheap fault tolerance. Daily PS snapshots lose little quality on failure, because each shard holds a small fraction of IDs and online training heals quickly.

Results. Collisionless tables beat hashed ones. Shorter sync intervals (from hours down toward about 30 minutes in the experiments, approx.) gave consistently higher online AUC, and real-time training beat batch training for ads [1]. The repository is TensorFlow plus Bazel and was archived by ByteDance in October 2025 [2].

37.7.4 ShareChat: batch-to-real-time training with Kafka and Flink (2024)

ShareChat's OARS 2024 workshop paper is one of the few public accounts of migrating an existing recommender from batch to real-time training [55]:

  • Stack. The team moved event ingestion from Google Pub/Sub to Kafka. It used Flink for streaming joins of feature and label events, with RocksDB state and checkpointing.
  • Semantics. The paper works through causal dependencies between events, event time versus processing time, and exactly-once versus at-least-once delivery.
  • Cost. Avro schemas plus compression cut event throughput by about 85%, and the redesign cut cost by about 40%.

A companion ShareChat study analyses embeddings on a short-video app with more than 180 million users [56]. Embeddings trained in real time converge toward their final vectors faster than batch-trained ones, needing about one fifth as many views to mature. Batch-trained embeddings end up with markedly higher norms, which the author links to popularity bias. This is quantitative evidence that real-time training changes what is learned, not only when.

37.7.5 Kuaishou PERSIA (2022)

PERSIA splits training the same way. Embedding layers are updated asynchronously on CPU parameter servers, because sparse updates tolerate staleness, and the dense network is trained synchronously on GPUs, because its accuracy suffers under asynchrony. It reports models up to 100 trillion parameters in production at Kuaishou [47]. Monolith and PERSIA agree: the sparse part is fast-moving and staleness-tolerant, and the dense part is slow-moving and sensitive.

37.7.6 Delayed feedback in streaming training

Online training on conversions faces labels that arrive minutes to weeks late.

Strategy Freshness Bias handling Source
Waiting window Delayed by window Late positives become false negatives Facebook [3]
Delay model (exponential delay) Medium Joint conversion + delay likelihood Criteo, Chapelle [8]
Fake negatives, no wait Best FN-weighted or FN-calibrated loss Twitter [5]
Elapsed-time sampling Good Short wait + re-emit late positives + importance weights Alibaba ES-DFM [6]
Real negatives re-ingest Good Also re-ingest real negatives after window Alibaba DEFER [7]

Twitter's design (Ktena et al., RecSys 2019) ingests every eligible impression immediately as a negative and again as a positive when the engagement arrives. FN-weighted and FN-calibrated losses undo the bias, and they beat waiting-window and delay-model baselines offline and in an online A/B test [5]. For continuous training this is the freshest option and has become a common default.

37.7.7 Online learning for the policy layer

Freshness also applies to exploration and fusion. Yahoo's LinUCB updates a per-article ridge regression online for a small, fast-changing pool of news stories [50].

YouTube Online Matching (RecSys 2023). Batch-trained recommenders are slow to find good new videos. YouTube therefore added a real-time bandit as an extra retrieval source in candidate generation [59]. Its parts:

  • An offline pipeline builds a sparse bipartite graph between users (or user clusters) and items.
  • An online agent aggregates bandit parameters in real time from the feedback stream.
  • Diag-LinUCB, an extension of LinUCB, makes the parameter updates distributable, which lets the system serve billions of users and millions of items.

The paper reports a policy-update latency of about 45 minutes at p50 and 74 minutes at p95. Live experiments on two use cases, fresh-content discovery and corpus exploration, showed significant top-line gains [59]. The design pattern is a hybrid: the expensive structure (the graph) is offline, and only a small set of bandit statistics is real time. Kuaishou's Pantheon learns personalized fusion weights jointly with its real-time ranker, deployed for about 400 million daily users [52]. When the candidate pool churns faster than a model can be retrained, a bandit or online-updated policy layer on top of a slower ranker is a cheap way to stay fresh.

37.8 TikTok and the short-video case

TikTok's 2020 newsroom post describes the For You feed as ranking on user interactions (likes, shares, follows, comments, content created), video information and, with lower weight, device and account settings. Signals are weighted by strength: finishing a longer video is a stronger signal than shared country. It also describes diversity rules (no two consecutive videos from the same creator or with the same sound) and cold start through interest selection, which "early interactions quickly replace" [51].

Short video stresses every clock at once. A user may swipe through dozens of items in minutes, each swipe is a label, and the corpus churns hourly. ByteDance's published answer is the Monolith loop: streaming joins, online training, and minute-level sparse sync [1]. Kuaishou's is PERSIA plus real-time sequence features and TWIN-style lifelong search [46][47].

     +---------------- short-video real-time stack (composite) ----------------+
     | client swipe/watch events -> Kafka                                      |
     |   |-> Flink features (counters, last-N actions) -> KV  -> ranker input  |
     |   |-> fresh-item / graph indexes (incremental insert)  -> retrieval     |
     |   '-> Flink joiner(serving feature log) -> online trainer               |
     |          sparse rows: minute-level incremental push -> serving PS       |
     |          dense weights: hourly or slower                                |
     | request: lifelong history (cached, may lag) + last-N actions (fresh)    |
     +-------------------------------------------------------------------------+

37.9 Freshness versus stability

Freshness has costs, and the sources name them explicitly.

  1. Feedback loops and over-reaction. A model that reacts to the last click can collapse diversity. TransAct reports reduced diversity and uses random time-window masking to stop the model from over-weighting the most recent actions [9]. TikTok describes explicit diversity rules on top of the ranker [51].
  2. Train/serve skew in real-time features. Streaming features lag by milliseconds to seconds, and batch features have a "midnight" inconsistency until upload finishes [34]. Logging served values and backfilling with the same freshness semantics (SNAPSHOT vs TEMPORAL) is the fix [33][34].
  3. Label bias in fast training. Short waiting windows create false negatives, and fake-negative pipelines duplicate positives. Both need loss corrections [3][5][6].
  4. Operational risk. An online trainer can be poisoned by a broken stream. Facebook recommends alarms and automatic trainer cutoff [3]. Monolith keeps a batch path and snapshots for recovery [1].
  5. Cost. TransAct's real-time encoder raised CPU latency more than 20x and forced a move to GPU serving [10]. Untiled streaming aggregation can force 432,000-event folds per request [32].
  6. Engagement decay. Real-time models degrade quickly if not retrained. TransAct names engagement decay as a reason for frequent retraining [9].

How designs balance it.

  • Pair slow and fast components. PinnerFormer (daily, trained to be robust to staleness) plus TransAct (real-time) [9][13]. SIM/TWIN lifelong search plus short-term DIN features [45][46]. Instagram's offline item tower plus online user tower [37].
  • Split by parameter type. Sparse embeddings fast, dense weights slow [1][47].
  • Bound the window. GraphJet and UTEG keep 24-48 hours, and Thunder trims by retention [20][26].
  • Measure the decay curve first. Facebook's NE-versus-delay curve [3] and PinnerFormer's real-time-versus-daily Recall@10 gap (13.9% vs 8.3%) [13] are examples of quantifying the value of freshness before paying for it.

37.11 Key takeaways for system designers

  1. Decide which clock you are shortening. Feature, candidate, representation and parameter freshness have different costs. Many products (Airbnb [30], Pixie [15]) get most of the value from fresh features or fresh query seeds without online training.
  2. Build one canonical action stream first. A deduplicated Kafka stream with stable request and impression IDs (UUA [22], Recos-Injector [21]) is the foundation for features, graphs and label joins.
  3. Log features at serving time and join by request ID. This is how Facebook, Photon and Monolith make streaming labels trustworthy [1][3][4]. Make the join idempotent.
  4. Declare features once and compile to batch and stream. Twitter's AggregateGroup and Chronon's GroupBy are the templates [24][33]. Pre-aggregate into tiles on the write path for hot keys [32].
  5. Use decayed counters and bounded windows. Exponential half-lives give O(1) state per key [24]. Sliding-window in-memory graphs (GraphJet, UTEG, Thunder) keep fresh candidates cheap [18][20][26].
  6. Put a real-time sequence encoder in the ranker, next to a batch user embedding. TransAct plus PinnerFormer is the reference hybrid [9][13]. Always include the most recent actions even when you also search a lifelong history [11][45].
  7. Train the stable component to be robust to staleness. PinnerFormer's dense all-action loss shrank the real-time-vs-daily gap from 13.9% to 8.3% [13].
  8. For online training, sync sparse fast and dense slow. Use collisionless dynamic tables with admission and expiry for churning ID spaces [1][47].
  9. Handle delayed labels explicitly. Prefer fake-negative ingestion with FN-weighted or calibrated loss, or elapsed-time sampling, over long waiting windows [5][6][7].
  10. Guard stability. Use time-window masking or recency dropout to avoid over-reaction [9], diversity rules on the final slate [51], stream anomaly alarms with trainer cutoff [3], and a batch fallback path [1][27].
  11. Respect simple session baselines. Session kNN and co-visitation counts remain strong for short anonymous sessions [39][49]. Fix losses and negative sampling before adding architecture [42].
  12. Budget the serving cost of freshness. Real-time encoders can multiply latency (20x at Pinterest) and may require GPUs and fused kernels to ship [10][11].
